qs.q: The number 5837_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 4.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. The multiples of 4 with a tens digit of 7 are 72 and 76, so the smallest digit is 2.

qs.q: The 6-digit number 63_514 has a missing thousands digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: The number ends in 4, so it is already even and will be divisible by 6 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The known digits sum to \(6 + 3 + 5 + 1 + 4 = 19\), and the next multiple of 3 is 21, so the smallest digit is \(21 - 19 = 2\).

qs.q: The 6-digit number 5184_6 has a missing tens digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 4.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. Testing two-digit numbers ending in 6, 06 is not divisible by 4, but 16 is, so the smallest digit is 1.

qs.q: The 8-digit number 47162_83 has a missing hundreds digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. The sum of the known digits is \(4 + 7 + 1 + 6 + 2 + 8 + 3 = 31\), and the next multiple of 9 is 36, so the smallest digit is \(36 - 31 = 5\).

qs.q: The 7-digit number 6318_45 has a missing hundreds digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. The sum of the known digits is \(6 + 3 + 1 + 8 + 4 + 5 = 27\), which is already divisible by 9, so the smallest digit that can be inserted is 0.

qs.q: The 6-digit number 39251_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 6 if it is even and the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The known digits add to \(3 + 9 + 2 + 5 + 1 = 20\), and among the even possibilities for the last digit (0, 2, 4, 6, 8), the smallest that makes the sum divisible by 3 is 4 since \(20 + 4 = 24\).

qs.q: The number \(52\,46\_\) has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 3.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The sum of the known digits is \(5 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 17\), so the smallest digit to reach the next multiple of 3 (which is 18) is \(18 - 17 = 1\).

qs.q: The number \(39\,57\_\) has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 4.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. The multiples of 4 in the 70s are 72 and 76, so the smallest missing digit is 2.

qs.q: The number \(26\,75\_\) has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. The sum of the known digits is \(2 + 6 + 7 + 5 = 20\), so the smallest digit to reach the next multiple of 9 (which is 27) is \(27 - 20 = 7\).

qs.q: The number \(71\,82\_\) has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 6 if it is even and the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The sum of the known digits is \(7 + 1 + 8 + 2 = 18\), which is already divisible by 3, so the smallest even digit that keeps the sum a multiple of 3 is 0.

qs.q: The number \(42\,38\_\) has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: For the number to be divisible by 6, it must be even and the sum of its digits must be divisible by 3. The sum of the known digits is \(4 + 2 + 3 + 8 = 17\), so the missing digit must make the sum a multiple of 3 (\(1, 4, \text{or } 7\)) and be even, which gives 4 as the smallest digit.

qs.q: The 7-digit number \(9\,142\,7\_6\) has a missing tens digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by both 4 and 9.
qs.s: To be divisible by 4, the last two digits must form a multiple of 4, so the tens digit must be odd (\(1, 3, 5, 7, \text{or } 9\)). For divisibility by 9, the sum of the digits \(9 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 7 + d + 6 = 29 + d\) must equal 36, giving \(d = 7\), which is odd and therefore satisfies both rules.

qs.q: The 6-digit number \(\_45\,63\_\) begins and ends with the same missing digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: The leading digit of a 6-digit number cannot be 0, and divisibility by 6 requires the units digit to be even, restricting the digit to \(\{2, 4, 6, 8\}\). The sum of the digits is \(d + 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 + d = 18 + 2d\), which is divisible by 3 only when \(d = 6\) among the allowed even digits.

qs.q: The 7-digit number \(5\,821\,5\_6\) has a missing tens digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by both 4 and 6.
qs.s: Divisibility by 4 requires the tens digit to be odd (\(1, 3, 5, 7, \text{or } 9\)) so that the last two digits form a multiple of 4. The number already ends in 6 (even), and divisibility by 6 requires the sum \(5 + 8 + 2 + 1 + 5 + d + 6 = 27 + d\) to be divisible by 3 (\(d \in \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\)), so the smallest digit satisfying both is 3.

qs.q: The 6-digit number \(471\,8\_2\) has a missing tens digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by both 3 and 4.
qs.s: For the number to be divisible by 4, the tens digit must be odd (\(1, 3, 5, 7, \text{or } 9\)) so that the last two digits form a multiple of 4. For divisibility by 3, the sum \(4 + 7 + 1 + 8 + d + 2 = 22 + d\) must be a multiple of 3 (\(d \in \{2, 5, 8\}\)), making 5 the smallest digit satisfying both conditions.

qs.q: The 6-digit number \(7\_3\,84\_\) has the same missing digit in the ten-thousands place and the units place. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: Divisibility by 6 requires the units digit to be even (\(0, 2, 4, 6, \text{or } 8\)) and the sum of the digits \(7 + d + 3 + 8 + 4 + d = 22 + 2d\) to be divisible by 3. Testing the even digits gives sums of 22 for \(d = 0\), 26 for \(d = 2\), and 30 for \(d = 4\), so the smallest digit is 4.

qs.q: The number 2584_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: The sum of the given digits is \(2 + 5 + 8 + 4 = 19\). To make the sum of the digits a multiple of 9, the missing digit must be \(27 - 19 = 8\).

qs.q: The number 4869_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: The sum of the known digits is \(4 + 8 + 6 + 9 = 27\), which is already divisible by 9. Because 0 is a valid digit and \(27 + 0 = 27\), the smallest digit is 0.

qs.q: The number 7418_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 4.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. The two-digit multiples of 4 starting with 8 are 80, 84, and 88, so the smallest digit is 0.

qs.q: The number 4316_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: To be divisible by 6, the number must end in an even digit and have a digit sum divisible by 3. Testing even digits with the existing sum of 14, the smallest digit that gives a sum divisible by 3 is 4, since \(14 + 4 = 18\).

qs.q: The number 5182_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 3.
qs.s: The sum of the given digits is \(5 + 1 + 8 + 2 = 16\). The smallest digit that can be added to make the sum a multiple of 3 is 2, since \(16 + 2 = 18\).

qs.q: The 7-digit number 5d8d3d5 has three identical missing digits represented by \(d\). Determine the smallest digit \(d\) so that the number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: The sum of the digits is \(5 + 8 + 3 + 5 + 3d = 21 + 3d\). For the sum to be a multiple of 9, set \(21 + 3d = 27\), which gives \(3d = 6\) and \(d = 2\).

qs.q: The 8-digit number 8374925_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 6 if it ends in an even digit and has a digit sum divisible by 3. The known digits sum to 38, and testing the even digits shows that 4 is the smallest digit yielding a multiple of 3 (\(38 + 4 = 42\)).

qs.q: The 6-digit number 352a1b has two missing digits, \(a\) and \(b\). If the number is divisible by both 4 and 9, determine the smallest possible value of the digit \(a\).
qs.s: For divisibility by 4, the last two digits \(1b\) must form a multiple of 4, so \(b = 2\) or \(b = 6\). For divisibility by 9, the digit sum \(11 + a + b\) must be a multiple of 9, giving \(a = 5\) when \(b = 2\) and \(a = 1\) when \(b = 6\), so the smallest possible value of \(a\) is 1.

qs.q: The 8-digit number 52d416d3 has two identical missing digits represented by \(d\). Determine the smallest digit \(d\) so that the number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: The sum of the known digits is \(5 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 6 + 3 = 21\), so the total sum is \(21 + 2d\). Setting \(21 + 2d = 27\) gives \(2d = 6\), so the smallest digit is \(d = 3\).

qs.q: The 7-digit number 673d24d has two identical missing digits represented by \(d\), where one is the last digit. Determine the smallest digit \(d\) so that the number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: Because \(d\) is the units digit, \(d\) must be an even digit (\(0, 2, 4, 6, 8\)) for the number to be divisible by 6. Testing these even digits in the total sum \(22 + 2d\), the smallest digit that produces a multiple of 3 is \(d = 4\), since \(22 + 2(4) = 30\).

qs.q: The number 3714_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. The sum of the given digits is \(3 + 7 + 1 + 4 = 15\), so the missing digit must be \(18 - 15 = 3\).

qs.q: The number 6841_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 5.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 5 if its last digit is 0 or 5. Therefore, the smallest digit that makes the number divisible by 5 is 0.

qs.q: The number 5183_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 3.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The sum of the given digits is \(5 + 1 + 8 + 3 = 17\), so the smallest digit to make the sum a multiple of 3 is 1 (since \(17 + 1 = 18\)).

qs.q: The number 7285_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. The sum of the given digits is \(7 + 2 + 8 + 5 = 22\), so the missing digit must be \(27 - 22 = 5\).

qs.q: The number 7315_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 5-digit number is divisible by 4.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. The two-digit numbers starting with 5 that are divisible by 4 are 52 and 56, so the smallest missing digit is 2.

qs.q: The number 582,7_0 has a missing tens digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 6-digit number is divisible by both 3 and 4.
qs.s: For divisibility by 4, the tens digit must be in \(\{0, 2, 4, 6, 8\}\) so that the last two digits form a multiple of 4. For divisibility by 3, the digit sum \(5 + 8 + 2 + 7 + d + 0 = 22 + d\) must be a multiple of 3, which is satisfied among the even candidates by \(d = 2\) and \(d = 8\), giving 2 as the smallest digit.

qs.q: The number 4,812,_13 has a missing hundreds digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 7-digit number is divisible by 9.
qs.s: A whole number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. The sum of the known digits is \(4 + 8 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 19\), so the missing digit must be \(27 - 19 = 8\).

qs.q: The number 714,82_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 6-digit number is divisible by both 5 and 9.
qs.s: For divisibility by 5, the last digit must be 0 or 5. The sum of the first five digits is \(7 + 1 + 4 + 8 + 2 = 22\), and adding 5 yields \(22 + 5 = 27\) (divisible by 9) while adding 0 yields 22 (not divisible by 9), so the smallest digit is 5.

qs.q: The number 839,5_2 has a missing tens digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 6-digit number is divisible by 4.
qs.s: A whole number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. The two-digit numbers ending in 2 that are multiples of 4 are 12, 32, 52, 72, and 92, so the smallest missing tens digit is 1.

qs.q: The number 5,381,72_ has a missing last digit. Determine the smallest digit so that the 7-digit number is divisible by 6.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 6 if it is even and the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The sum of the known digits is \(5 + 3 + 8 + 1 + 7 + 2 = 26\), so the missing digit must be from \(\{1, 4, 7\}\) to make the sum a multiple of 3, and it must also be even, making 4 the smallest valid digit.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about whole numbers is true?
qs.a: If a number is divisible by both 2 and 5, its last digit must be 0.
d: If a number is divisible by 5, its last digit must be 5.
If a number ends in 2, it must be divisible by 4.
If a number is divisible by 10, its last two digits must be 00.
qs.s: Divisibility by 2 requires the last digit to be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, and divisibility by 5 requires it to be 0 or 5, so only numbers ending in 0 satisfy both.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about divisibility is true for all whole numbers?
qs.a: If a number is divisible by 8, then it must also be divisible by 4.
d: If a number is divisible by 4, then it must also be divisible by 8.
If a number is divisible by 3, then it must also be divisible by 6.
If a number is divisible by 2, then it must also be divisible by 4.
qs.s: Since 8 is a multiple of 4 (\(8 = 4 \times 2\)), every multiple of 8 is necessarily a multiple of 4; counterexamples like 12, 9, and 6 disprove the remaining statements.

qs.q: A student tests four proposed divisibility rules. Which rule is correct?
qs.a: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
d: A number is divisible by 5 only if its last digit is 5.
A number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
A number is divisible by 10 if the sum of its digits is 10.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 3 if and only if the sum of its digits is a multiple of 3; testing numbers like 20, 12, and 19 shows that the other rules fail.

qs.q: Which of the following divisibility statements is true for all whole numbers?
qs.a: A number is divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4.
d: A number is divisible by 4 if its last digit is divisible by 4.
A number is divisible by 3 if its last digit is divisible by 3.
A number is divisible by 6 if its last digit is 6.
qs.s: Because 100 is divisible by 4, any whole number is divisible by 4 if and only if its last two digits form a multiple of 4; counterexamples like 14, 16, and 26 disprove the other choices.

qs.q: Which of the following statements regarding divisibility is true?
qs.a: A number is divisible by 6 if it is an even number whose digits sum to a multiple of 3.
d: A number is divisible by 6 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 6.
A number is divisible by 6 if its last digit is even.
A number is divisible by 6 if it is divisible by 2 or divisible by 3.
qs.s: A whole number is divisible by 6 if and only if it is divisible by both 2 (making it even) and 3 (the sum of its digits is divisible by 3).

qs.q: Which of the following statements is true for every positive integer \(n\)?
qs.a: The sum of any three consecutive integers, \(n + (n + 1) + (n + 2)\), is always divisible by 3.
d: The sum of any three consecutive integers, \(n + (n + 1) + (n + 2)\), is always divisible by 6.
The sum of any four consecutive integers, \(n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) + (n + 3)\), is always divisible by 4.
The product of any two consecutive integers, \(n(n + 1)\), is always divisible by 4.
qs.s: Simplifying the sum yields \(3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)\), which is always a multiple of 3; testing \(n = 2\) gives \(2 + 3 + 4 = 9\) (not divisible by 6), \(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10\) (not divisible by 4), and \(2 \times 3 = 6\) (not divisible by 4).

qs.q: Which of the following statements regarding divisibility rules is true?
qs.a: A number is divisible by 25 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 25.
d: A number is divisible by 25 if its last digit is 5.
A number is divisible by 50 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 5.
A number is divisible by 16 if the number formed by its last three digits is divisible by 16.
qs.s: Because 100 is divisible by 25, any number \(100k + r\) is divisible by 25 if and only if its last two digits \(r\) are divisible by 25; 1000 is not divisible by 16, which disproves the three-digit rule for 16 using 1016.

qs.q: Which of the following general statements about divisibility is true?
qs.a: A number is divisible by 36 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4 and the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
d: A number is divisible by 36 if it is divisible by both 3 and 12.
A number is divisible by 36 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 36.
A number is divisible by 18 if it is an even number whose digits sum to a multiple of 6.
qs.s: Since \(\gcd(4, 9) = 1\), a number is divisible by 36 if and only if it satisfies the separate rules for 4 and 9; 24 disproves the 3 and 12 rule, 9999 disproves the digit-sum rule for 36, and 42 disproves the rule for 18.

qs.q: Which of the following divisibility rules is correct for all whole numbers?
qs.a: A number is divisible by 15 if its last digit is 0 or 5 and the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
d: A number is divisible by 15 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 15.
A number is divisible by 20 if it is divisible by both 2 and 10.
A number is divisible by 45 if its last digit is 5 and the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
qs.s: Because 15 factors into the coprime numbers 3 and 5, a number must satisfy the rule for 5 (last digit 0 or 5) and the rule for 3 (digit sum divisible by 3); counterexamples like 69, 30, and 90 disprove the others.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine which of the following statements about divisibility by 11 is true.
qs.a: A four-digit number with digits \(a, b, c, d\) (in order) is divisible by 11 if \((a + c) - (b + d)\) is divisible by 11.
d: A four-digit number with digits \(a, b, c, d\) is divisible by 11 if \(a + b + c + d\) is divisible by 11.
A four-digit number with digits \(a, b, c, d\) is divisible by 11 if the two-digit number formed by \(cd\) is divisible by 11.
A four-digit number with digits \(a, b, c, d\) is divisible by 11 if \(a - d\) is divisible by 11.
qs.s: A number is divisible by 11 if the alternating sum of its digits is divisible by 11, which for $abcd$ is \((a + c) - (b + d)\). For example, testing 1331 gives \((1 + 3) - (3 + 1) = 0\), confirming that 1331 is divisible by 11.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine which of the following statements is false.
qs.a: If a number is divisible by both 2 and 4, then it must be divisible by 8.
d: If a number is divisible by 6, then it must be an even number.
If a number is divisible by both 2 and 5, then it must be divisible by 10.
If a number is divisible by 10, then its last digit must be 0.
qs.s: Testing 12 shows that 12 is divisible by both 2 and 4, but \(12 \div 8 = 1.5\), which is not an integer. Therefore, being divisible by both 2 and 4 does not guarantee divisibility by 8.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine which of the following statements is true.
qs.a: A number is divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4.
d: A number is divisible by 4 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 4.
A number is divisible by 4 if its last digit is divisible by 4.
A number is divisible by 4 if its last digit is an even number.
qs.s: The number 100 is divisible by 4, so any whole number is divisible by 4 if and only if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. Testing 13 shows that a digit sum of 4 does not make a number divisible by 4 (\(13 \div 4 = 3.25\)).

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 20 if it is divisible by both 4 and 5.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: True, because every common multiple of 4 and 5 is divisible by 20.
d: False, because 10 is divisible by both 4 and 5, but not by 20.
False, because 40 is divisible by both 4 and 5, but not by 20.
True, but only for numbers that end in 00.
qs.s: The least common multiple of 4 and 5 is 20 because 4 and 5 share no common prime factors. Therefore, any number divisible by both 4 and 5 must be a multiple of 20, making the statement true.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 24 if it is divisible by both 4 and 6.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: False, because 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6, but not by 24.
d: False, because 18 is divisible by both 4 and 6, but not by 24.
True, because any multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 24.
qs.s: Testing common multiples of 4 and 6 gives 12, 24, 36, and so on. Since 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6 but is not divisible by 24, the statement is false.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 8 if it is divisible by both 2 and 4.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: False, because 4 is divisible by both 2 and 4, but not by 8.
d: False, because 6 is divisible by both 2 and 4, but not by 8.
True, because all even numbers are divisible by 8.
qs.s: Testing numbers divisible by both 2 and 4 gives 4, 8, 12, and so on. Since 4 is divisible by both 2 and 4 but not by 8, the statement is false.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 18 if it is divisible by both 3 and 6.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: False, because 6 is divisible by both 3 and 6, but not by 18.
d: False, because 9 is divisible by both 3 and 6, but not by 18.
True, because any number divisible by 6 is also divisible by 18.
qs.s: Testing numbers divisible by both 3 and 6 gives 6, 12, 18, and so on. Since 6 is divisible by both 3 and 6 but not by 18, the statement is false.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 15 if it is divisible by both 3 and 5.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: True, because every common multiple of 3 and 5 is divisible by 15.
d: False, because 5 is divisible by both 3 and 5, but not by 15.
False, because 45 is divisible by both 3 and 5, but not by 15.
True, but only for numbers ending in 5.
qs.s: Since 3 and 5 are prime numbers with no common factors, their least common multiple is \(3 \times 5 = 15\). Any number divisible by both 3 and 5 is a multiple of 15, so the statement is true.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 36 if it is divisible by both 3 and 12.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: False, because 12 is divisible by both 3 and 12, but not by 36.
d: False, because 18 is divisible by both 3 and 12, but not by 36.
True, because any multiple of 12 is also a multiple of 36.
qs.s: Common multiples of 3 and 12 start at \(\text{LCM}(3, 12) = 12\). Since 12 is divisible by both 3 and 12 but not by 36, the statement is false.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 72 if it is divisible by both 8 and 9.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: True, because every common multiple of 8 and 9 is divisible by 72.
d: False, because 36 is divisible by both 8 and 9, but not by 72.
False, because 144 is divisible by both 8 and 9, but not by 72.
True, but only for numbers that have an even sum of digits.
qs.s: Because 8 and 9 share no prime factors (their greatest common factor is 1), their least common multiple is \(8 \times 9 = 72\). Every common multiple of 8 and 9 is divisible by 72, so the statement is true.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 90 if it is divisible by both 6 and 15.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: False, because 30 is divisible by both 6 and 15, but not by 90.
d: False, because 45 is divisible by both 6 and 15, but not by 90.
True, because any multiple of 15 is divisible by 90.
qs.s: The least common multiple of 6 and 15 is 30, not 90. Since 30 is divisible by both 6 and 15 but not by 90, the statement is false.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 60 if it is divisible by 2, 5, and 6.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: False, because 30 is divisible by 2, 5, and 6, but not by 60.
d: False, because 20 is divisible by 2, 5, and 6, but not by 60.
True, because any number divisible by both 5 and 6 must be divisible by 60.
qs.s: The least common multiple of 2, 5, and 6 is 30. Because 30 is divisible by 2, 5, and 6 but not by 60, the statement is false.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true or false: 'A number is divisible by 120 if it is divisible by 3, 5, and 8.' Which conclusion is correct?
qs.a: True, because every common multiple of 3, 5, and 8 is divisible by 120.
d: False, because 60 is divisible by 3, 5, and 8, but not by 120.
False, because 40 is divisible by 3, 5, and 8, but not by 120.
True, but only for numbers that end in two zeros.
qs.s: The numbers 3, 5, and 8 are pairwise coprime, meaning their least common multiple is \(3 \times 5 \times 8 = 120\). Every number divisible by all three must be a multiple of 120, so the statement is true.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine which of the following divisibility statements is true.
qs.a: A number is divisible by 14 if it is divisible by both 2 and 7.
d: A number is divisible by 12 if it is divisible by both 2 and 6.
A number is divisible by 18 if it is divisible by both 3 and 6.
A number is divisible by 24 if it is divisible by both 4 and 6.
qs.s: Since 2 and 7 share no common prime factors, any number divisible by both must be a multiple of their least common multiple, which is \(2 \times 7 = 14\). For the other statements, counterexamples include 6 (divisible by 2 and 6, but not 12; divisible by 3 and 6, but not 18) and 12 (divisible by 4 and 6, but not 24).

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine which of the following divisibility statements is false.
qs.a: A number is divisible by 16 if it is divisible by both 2 and 8.
d: A number is divisible by 10 if it is divisible by both 2 and 5.
A number is divisible by 21 if it is divisible by both 3 and 7.
A number is divisible by 20 if it is divisible by both 4 and 5.
qs.s: Testing 8 reveals that it is divisible by both 2 and 8, but it is not divisible by 16, which proves the statement is false. The other three statements are all true because the pairs of divisors share no common factors other than 1.

qs.q: By testing numbers, determine whether the statement is true: A number is divisible by 15 if it is divisible by both 3 and 5.

qs.s: Write the prime factorizations: \(8 = 2^3\), \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), and \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\). The LCM is the product of the highest power of each prime, which gives \(2^3 \times 3^2 = 72\).

qs.q: Find the least common multiple: 36, 54, 90, 108
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), \(54 = 2 \times 3^3\), \(90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5\), and \(108 = 2^2 \times 3^3\). The LCM is \(2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5 = 540\).

qs.q: Find the least common multiple: 48, 72, 80, 120
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(48 = 2^4 \times 3\), \(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\), \(80 = 2^4 \times 5\), and \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\). The LCM is \(2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 720\).

qs.q: Find the least common multiple: 22, 33, 44, 55
qs.s: Write the prime factorizations: \(22 = 2 \times 11\), \(33 = 3 \times 11\), \(44 = 2^2 \times 11\), and \(55 = 5 \times 11\). The LCM is \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 11 = 660\).

qs.q: Find the least common multiple: 45, 60, 75, 120
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(45 = 3^2 \times 5\), \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\), \(75 = 3 \times 5^2\), and \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\). The LCM is \(2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 1800\).

qs.q: Find the least common multiple: 14, 24, 35, 40, 42
qs.s: Write the prime factorizations: \(14 = 2 \times 7\), \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(35 = 5 \times 7\), \(40 = 2^3 \times 5\), and \(42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7\). The LCM is \(2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 840\).

qs.q: Three city buses leave a transit station at the same time. Route A departs every 5 minutes, Route B departs every 6 minutes, and Route C departs every 15 minutes. How many minutes will pass before all three buses depart from the station at the same time again?
qs.s: Find the LCM of 5, 6, and 15. The prime factorizations are \(5 = 5\), \(6 = 2 \times 3\), and \(15 = 3 \times 5\), giving \(\text{LCM}(5, 6, 15) = 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30\) minutes.

qs.q: Three traffic signals turn green at intervals of 8, 10, and 12 seconds respectively. If all three signals just turned green at the exact same moment, how many seconds will pass before they all turn green at the same time again?
qs.s: Find the LCM of 8, 10, and 12. Since \(8 = 2^3\), \(10 = 2 \times 5\), and \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(\text{LCM}(8, 10, 12) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120\) seconds.

qs.q: Three runners begin running around a circular track at the same time from the starting line. They take 6, 8, and 9 minutes respectively to complete one full lap. How many minutes will pass before all three runners cross the starting line together again?
qs.s: Find the LCM of 6, 8, and 9. Factoring into primes gives \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(8 = 2^3\), and \(9 = 3^2\), so \(\text{LCM}(6, 8, 9) = 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72\) minutes.

qs.q: Three church bells toll at intervals of 4, 7, and 14 minutes respectively. If all three toll together right now, how many minutes will pass before they toll together again?
qs.s: The time until they toll together again is the LCM of 4, 7, and 14. Factoring gives \(4 = 2^2\), \(7 = 7\), and \(14 = 2 \times 7\), so \(\text{LCM}(4, 7, 14) = 2^2 \times 7 = 28\) minutes.

qs.q: Three lighthouses flash their lights at intervals of 4, 6, and 10 seconds respectively. If all three flash at the same instant, how many seconds will pass before they next flash at the same instant again?
qs.s: The time until they flash together is \(\text{LCM}(4, 6, 10)\). Using prime factors, \(4 = 2^2\), \(6 = 2 \times 3\), and \(10 = 2 \times 5\), so \(\text{LCM}(4, 6, 10) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\) seconds.

qs.q: Three commuter trains depart from a central station at regular intervals of 42, 56, and 70 minutes respectively. If all three trains depart together at 6:00 AM, how many minutes will pass before all three depart at the same time again?
qs.s: Using prime factorizations, \(42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7\), \(56 = 2^3 \times 7\), and \(70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7\). The LCM is \(2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 840\) minutes.

qs.q: Three automated security sirens sound at intervals of 15, 20, and 24 minutes. If all three sirens sound simultaneously at 8:00 AM, how many times will all three sirens sound together again over the next 12 hours?
qs.s: The sirens sound together every \(\text{LCM}(15, 20, 24) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120\) minutes (or 2 hours). Over the next 12 hours, they will sound together again \(\frac{12}{2} = 6\) times.

qs.q: Three cyclists ride around a circular track at steady speeds, taking 24, 30, and 40 seconds respectively to complete one full lap. If they start together from the starting line, how many laps will the fastest cyclist have completed when all three cyclists next cross the starting line together?
qs.s: All three cyclists cross the line together every \(\text{LCM}(24, 30, 40) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120\) seconds. Since the fastest cyclist takes 24 seconds per lap, they will have completed \(\frac{120}{24} = 5\) laps.

qs.q: Three industrial machines require scheduled maintenance. Machine A is serviced every 36 days, Machine B every 45 days, and Machine C every 60 days. If all three machines are serviced today, how many days will pass before they are all serviced on the same day again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), \(45 = 3^2 \times 5\), and \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\). The LCM is \(2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180\) days.

qs.q: Four cargo ships depart from the same port on recurring delivery routes that take 14, 21, 28, and 35 days respectively. If all four ships depart the port together today, how many days will pass before all four ships return to the port together on the same day?
qs.s: Factoring each number gives \(14 = 2 \times 7\), \(21 = 3 \times 7\), \(28 = 2^2 \times 7\), and \(35 = 5 \times 7\). Thus, \(\text{LCM}(14, 21, 28, 35) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 420\) days.

qs.q: Three bus routes depart from the central transit station at regular intervals: Route A departs every 15 minutes, Route B every 25 minutes, and Route C every 30 minutes. If buses on all three routes depart at the same time, how many minutes will pass before they next depart together?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(15 = 3 \times 5\), \(25 = 5^2\), and \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\). The least common multiple is \(\text{LCM}(15, 25, 30) = 2 \times 3 \times 5^2 = 150\) minutes.

qs.q: Three lighthouse beacons flash at regular intervals of 12 seconds, 18 seconds, and 20 seconds respectively. If all three flash at the exact same moment, how many seconds will pass before they all flash together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), and \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\). The least common multiple is \(\text{LCM}(12, 18, 20) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180\) seconds.

qs.q: Three church bells ring at regular intervals of 16 minutes, 20 minutes, and 24 minutes. If they toll at the exact same moment, how many minutes will pass before they all toll together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(16 = 2^4\), \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\), and \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\). The least common multiple is \(\text{LCM}(16, 20, 24) = 2^4 \times 3 \times 5 = 240\) minutes.

qs.q: Four runners start together at the starting line of a circular track. They complete a lap every 24, 36, 40, and 60 seconds, respectively. After how many seconds will all four runners cross the starting line together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), \(40 = 2^3 \times 5\), and \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\). The least common multiple is \(\text{LCM}(24, 36, 40, 60) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360\) seconds.

qs.q: Four research satellites orbit the Earth and pass directly over a ground station every 8, 12, 18, and 28 hours respectively. If all four satellites are directly over the station right now, in how many hours will they all be over the station at the same time again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(8 = 2^3\), \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), and \(28 = 2^2 \times 7\). Thus, \(\text{LCM}(8, 12, 18, 28) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 7 = 504\) hours.

qs.q: Five periodic comets visit the inner solar system every 18, 24, 35, 42, and 60 years respectively. If all five comets appeared in the inner solar system together in the year 2020, how many years will pass before they all appear together again?
qs.s: Factoring the periods gives \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(35 = 5 \times 7\), \(42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7\), and \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\). The least common multiple is \(2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520\) years.

qs.q: Three pointers on concentric dials complete one full rotation in 24 seconds, 36 seconds, and 54 seconds respectively. If all three pointers start together pointing straight up, how many full rotations will the slowest pointer have completed when they next point straight up simultaneously?
qs.s: The time to align is \(\text{LCM}(24, 36, 54) = 2^3 \times 3^3 = 216\) seconds. The slowest pointer takes 54 seconds per rotation, so it completes \(216 \div 54 = 4\) full rotations.

qs.q: Four automatic signals beep at intervals of 15, 20, 24, and 30 seconds respectively. They all beep together at 12:00 noon. Including the beep at 12:00 noon, how many times will all four signals beep simultaneously between 12:00 noon and 12:30 PM, inclusive?
qs.s: The signals beep together every \(\text{LCM}(15, 20, 24, 30) = 120\) seconds, or 2 minutes. Over the 30-minute span from 12:00 to 12:30, they beep \((30 \div 2) + 1 = 16\) times.

qs.q: Two cyclists and a runner train on a circular track. Cyclist 1 completes a lap in 48 seconds, Cyclist 2 completes a lap in 72 seconds, and the runner completes a lap in 120 seconds. They all start at the finish line at the same moment. When all three first cross the finish line together again, how many more laps will Cyclist 1 have completed than the runner?
qs.s: They cross together at \(\text{LCM}(48, 72, 120) = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 720\) seconds. Cyclist 1 completes \(720 \div 48 = 15\) laps and the runner completes \(720 \div 120 = 6\) laps, giving a difference of \(15 - 6 = 9\) laps.

qs.q: Three factory warning sirens are tested periodically: Siren A sounds every 45 minutes, Siren B sounds every 60 minutes, and Siren C sounds every 75 minutes. If all three sirens sound simultaneously at 7:00 AM on Monday, at what time will they next sound together?
qs.s: The sirens align every \(\text{LCM}(45, 60, 75) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 900\) minutes, which is equal to 15 hours. Adding 15 hours to 7:00 AM on Monday yields 10:00 PM Monday.

qs.q: Three cargo vessels, the Atlantic, the Pacific, and the Arctic, dock at the same port. The Atlantic docks every 12 days, the Pacific every 15 days, and the Arctic every 18 days. If all three vessels are in port together on July 1, what is the next date when all three will be in port together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(15 = 3 \times 5\), and \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), giving \(\text{LCM}(12, 15, 18) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180\) days. Counting 180 days after July 1 (30 days in July, 31 in August, 30 in September, 31 in October, 30 in November, and 28 in December) gives December 28.

qs.q: Three security officers, Davis, Evans, and Foster, are assigned night patrol at a warehouse. Davis patrols every 4 days, Evans every 6 days, and Foster every 10 days. If all three patrol together on May 1, what is the next date when all three will patrol together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(4 = 2^2\), \(6 = 2 \times 3\), and \(10 = 2 \times 5\), giving \(\text{LCM}(4, 6, 10) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\) days. Counting 60 days after May 1 (30 days remaining in May and 30 in June) gives June 30.

qs.q: Three volunteers, Maya, Liam, and Noah, work shifts at an animal shelter. Maya works every 6 days, Liam every 8 days, and Noah every 9 days. If all three work together on September 1, what is the next date when all three will work together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(8 = 2^3\), and \(9 = 3^2\), giving \(\text{LCM}(6, 8, 9) = 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72\) days. Counting 72 days after September 1 (29 days remaining in September, 31 in October, and 12 in November) gives November 12.

qs.q: Three tour boats leave a harbor at 8:00 AM. Boat A returns to dock every 15 minutes, Boat B every 18 minutes, and Boat C every 24 minutes. If they all departed at 8:00 AM, at what time will all three next return to the dock together?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(15 = 3 \times 5\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), and \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), giving \(\text{LCM}(15, 18, 24) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360\) minutes. Since 360 minutes equals 6 hours, adding 6 hours to 8:00 AM gives 2:00 PM.

qs.q: Three maintenance technicians, Carlos, Dan, and Eric, service a factory generator. Carlos services it every 6 days, Dan every 9 days, and Eric every 15 days. If all three service the generator together on March 1, what is the next date when all three will service it together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(9 = 3^2\), and \(15 = 3 \times 5\), giving \(\text{LCM}(6, 9, 15) = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 90\) days. Counting 90 days after March 1 (30 days remaining in March, 30 in April, and 30 in May) gives May 30.

qs.q: A community center is assembling identical art kits. Markers are sold in packs of 24, sketchpads in packs of 36, and sticker sheets in packs of 40. The center wants to buy the same number of each item with none left over. What is the minimum total number of packages (marker packs + sketchpad packs + sticker packs) the center must purchase?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), and \(40 = 2^3 \times 5\), giving \(\text{LCM}(24, 36, 40) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360\) items of each type. The minimum total number of packages is \(\frac{360}{24} + \frac{360}{36} + \frac{360}{40} = 15 + 10 + 9 = 34\).

qs.q: Three harbor lighthouses flash at regular intervals: Lighthouse A flashes every 45 seconds, Lighthouse B every 60 seconds, and Lighthouse C every 75 seconds. If all three flash simultaneously at 9:00 PM, at what time will they flash together for the second time after 9:00 PM?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(45 = 3^2 \times 5\), \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\), and \(75 = 3 \times 5^2\), giving \(\text{LCM}(45, 60, 75) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 900\text{ seconds} = 15\text{ minutes}\). Since they flash together every 15 minutes, the second simultaneous flash occurs at \(9:00\text{ PM} + 2(15\text{ min}) = 9:30\text{ PM}\).

qs.q: Three scientists take remote field shifts. Dr. Patel takes a field shift every 24 days, Dr. Quinn every 30 days, and Dr. Rivera every 36 days. If all three begin a field shift together on January 1 of a non-leap year, what is the next date when all three will begin a field shift together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\), and \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), giving \(\text{LCM}(24, 30, 36) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360\) days. Since a non-leap year has 365 days, 360 days after January 1 is \(365 - 1 - 360 = 4\) days before December 31, which is December 27.

qs.q: Four delivery services visit a supermarket warehouse: Service A visits every 6 days, Service B every 8 days, Service C every 10 days, and Service D every 15 days. If all four services visit together on April 15, what is the next date when all four will visit together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(8 = 2^3\), \(10 = 2 \times 5\), and \(15 = 3 \times 5\), giving \(\text{LCM}(6, 8, 10, 15) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120\) days. Counting 120 days after April 15 (15 days remaining in April, 31 in May, 30 in June, 31 in July, and 13 in August) gives August 13.

qs.q: Three commuter trains, the Red, Blue, and Green lines, depart from a central terminal. The Red line departs every 12 minutes, the Blue line every 18 minutes, and the Green line every 30 minutes. All three lines depart together at 6:00 AM. If the terminal operates continuously until 11:00 PM that evening, how many times after 6:00 AM will all three trains depart together at the same time?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\), and \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\), so \(\text{LCM}(12, 18, 30) = 180\text{ minutes} = 3\text{ hours}\). From 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM is 17 hours, and \(17 \div 3 = 5\) with a remainder of 2, so they depart together 5 times after 6:00 AM.

qs.q: At a summer camp, counselors can divide campers evenly into activity groups of 6, 8, or 10 campers with no one left over. What is the smallest number of campers that allows for this?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(8 = 2^3\), and \(10 = 2 \times 5\). The least common multiple is \(2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120\) campers.

qs.q: A bookstore clerk wants to arrange a delivery of books into equal stacks of 4, 7, or 10 books with none left over. What is the smallest number of books that can be stacked evenly in any of these three ways?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(4 = 2^2\), \(7 = 7\), and \(10 = 2 \times 5\). The LCM is \(2^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 140\) books.

qs.q: A music teacher wants to organize students into ensembles of 4, 9, or 10 musicians with no students left over. What is the smallest number of students that can be split evenly into any of these three ensemble sizes?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(4 = 2^2\), \(9 = 3^2\), and \(10 = 2 \times 5\). The LCM is \(2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180\) students.

qs.q: A bakery packages cookies into bags of 6, 8, or 9 cookies with none left over. What is the smallest total number of cookies the baker can make so that they can be packaged completely into bags of any one of these three sizes?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(8 = 2^3\), and \(9 = 3^2\). The LCM is \(2^3 \times 3^2 = 8 \times 9 = 72\) cookies.

qs.q: Three lighthouses along a coastline flash their beacons at intervals of 6 seconds, 10 seconds, and 14 seconds. If they all flash at the same instant, after how many seconds will all three beacons flash together again?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(10 = 2 \times 5\), and \(14 = 2 \times 7\). The LCM is \(2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 210\) seconds.

qs.q: A picnic coordinator is buying hot dogs that come in packages of 12, buns in packages of 15, and cheese slices in packages of 20. She wants to have the exact same number of each item with none left over. What is the minimum total number of packages she must buy altogether?
qs.s: The LCM of 12, 15, and 20 is \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\) items. She needs \(60 \div 12 = 5\) packages of hot dogs, \(60 \div 15 = 4\) packages of buns, and \(60 \div 20 = 3\) packages of cheese slices, totaling \(5 + 4 + 3 = 12\) packages.

qs.q: A marching band can be arranged into complete rows of 28, 35, or 42 musicians with no musicians left over. If the total number of musicians in the band is known to be greater than 1,000, what is the smallest possible number of musicians in the band?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(28 = 2^2 \times 7\), \(35 = 5 \times 7\), and \(42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7\), giving an LCM of \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 420\). The smallest multiple of 420 greater than 1,000 is \(420 \times 3 = 1260\).

qs.q: A factory packages manufactured bolts into boxes of 16, 24, 30, or 36 bolts with none left over. What is the smallest number of bolts that can be completely packed into boxes of any of these four sizes?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(16 = 2^4\), \(24 = 2^3 \times 3\), \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\), and \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\). The LCM is \(2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 16 \times 9 \times 5 = 720\) bolts.

qs.q: Three runners start running laps around a track at the exact same moment from the starting line. Runner A completes a lap every 48 seconds, Runner B every 60 seconds, and Runner C every 72 seconds. How many laps will Runner A have completed when all three runners first cross the starting line together again?
qs.s: The LCM of 48, 60, and 72 is \(2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 720\) seconds, so they meet again after 720 seconds. Runner A completes \(720 \div 48 = 15\) laps.

qs.q: Three transit buses leave the central terminal together at 7:00 a.m. Route A completes its circuit every 24 minutes, Route B every 36 minutes, and Route C every 40 minutes. At what time will all three buses next depart from the central terminal at the same time?
qs.s: The LCM of 24, 36, and 40 is \(2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360\) minutes, which is 6 hours. Adding 6 hours to 7:00 a.m. gives 1:00 p.m.

exercises.name: Finding LCM using the GCF formula

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 14 and 21.
qs.s: The GCF of 14 and 21 is 7, and their product is \(14 \times 21 = 294\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 294 \div 7 = 42\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 27 and 36.
qs.s: The GCF of 27 and 36 is 9, and their product is \(27 \times 36 = 972\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 972 \div 9 = 108\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 12 and 20.
qs.s: The GCF of 12 and 20 is 4, and their product is \(12 \times 20 = 240\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 240 \div 4 = 60\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 16 and 28.
qs.s: The GCF of 16 and 28 is 4, and their product is \(16 \times 28 = 448\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 448 \div 4 = 112\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 15 and 25.
qs.s: The GCF of 15 and 25 is 5, and their product is \(15 \times 25 = 375\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 375 \div 5 = 75\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 72 and 120.
qs.s: The GCF of 72 and 120 is 24, and their product is \(72 \times 120 = 8640\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 8640 \div 24 = 360\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 84 and 126.
qs.s: The GCF of 84 and 126 is 42, and their product is \(84 \times 126 = 10584\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 10584 \div 42 = 252\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 108 and 144.
qs.s: The GCF of 108 and 144 is 36, and their product is \(108 \times 144 = 15552\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 15552 \div 36 = 432\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 54 and 90.
qs.s: The GCF of 54 and 90 is 18, and their product is \(54 \times 90 = 4860\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 4860 \div 18 = 270\).

qs.q: Using the method of dividing the product of two numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF), find the least common multiple (LCM) of 140 and 175.
qs.s: The GCF of 140 and 175 is 35, and their product is \(140 \times 175 = 24500\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = 24500 \div 35 = 700\).

exercises.name: Finding LCM using the GCF formula

qs.q: Find the LCM of 54 and 90 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(54 = 2 \times 3^3\) and \(90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5\), so \(\text{GCF}(54, 90) = 2 \times 3^2 = 18\). Dividing their product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = \frac{54 \times 90}{18} = 270\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 80 and 120 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(80 = 2^4 \times 5\) and \(120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5\), which gives \(\text{GCF}(80, 120) = 2^3 \times 5 = 40\). Dividing the product by the GCF yields \(\text{LCM} = \frac{80 \times 120}{40} = 240\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 60 and 84 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\) and \(84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\), giving \(\text{GCF}(60, 84) = 2^2 \times 3 = 12\). Dividing their product by the GCF yields \(\text{LCM} = \frac{60 \times 84}{12} = 420\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 56 and 84 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(56 = 2^3 \times 7\) and \(84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\), so \(\text{GCF}(56, 84) = 2^2 \times 7 = 28\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = \frac{56 \times 84}{28} = 168\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 48 and 72 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(48 = 2^4 \times 3\) and \(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\), so \(\text{GCF}(48, 72) = 2^3 \times 3 = 24\). Dividing the product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = \frac{48 \times 72}{24} = 144\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 1050 and 1400 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(1050 = 2 \times 3 \times 5^2 \times 7\) and \(1400 = 2^3 \times 5^2 \times 7\), so \(\text{GCF}(1050, 1400) = 2 \times 5^2 \times 7 = 350\). Dividing the product by the GCF yields \(\text{LCM} = \frac{1050 \times 1400}{350} = 4200\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 168 and 252 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(168 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7\) and \(252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7\), which gives \(\text{GCF}(168, 252) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84\). Dividing their product by the GCF yields \(\text{LCM} = \frac{168 \times 252}{84} = 504\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 288 and 432 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(288 = 2^5 \times 3^2\) and \(432 = 2^4 \times 3^3\), so \(\text{GCF}(288, 432) = 2^4 \times 3^2 = 144\). Dividing their product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = \frac{288 \times 432}{144} = 864\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 198 and 264 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(198 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 11\) and \(264 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 11\), giving \(\text{GCF}(198, 264) = 2 \times 3 \times 11 = 66\). Dividing their product by the GCF gives \(\text{LCM} = \frac{198 \times 264}{66} = 792\).

qs.q: Find the LCM of 315 and 441 by taking the product of both numbers and dividing that product by the GCF.
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(315 = 3^2 \times 5 \times 7\) and \(441 = 3^2 \times 7^2\), giving \(\text{GCF}(315, 441) = 3^2 \times 7 = 63\). Dividing their product by the GCF yields \(\text{LCM} = \frac{315 \times 441}{63} = 2205\).

qs.q: A global climate symposium is held every 6 years and was held in 2020. A clean energy summit is held every 5 years and was held in 2023. What is the next year in which both events will take place in the same year?
qs.s: The climate symposium occurs in years 2020, 2026, 2032, 2038, and the clean energy summit occurs in years 2023, 2028, 2033, 2038. The next year both events occur together is 2038.

qs.q: A national music festival is held every 3 years and was held in 2019. A national dance festival is held every 5 years and was held in 2021. What is the first year after 2021 in which both festivals will be held in the same year?
qs.s: The music festival occurs in years 2019, 2022, 2025, 2028, 2031, while the dance festival occurs in years 2021, 2026, 2031. Both festivals will first be held together in 2031.

qs.q: An international film festival is held every 4 years and was held in 2021. A cultural expo is held every 5 years and was held in 2022. What is the next year in which both events will be held in the same year?
qs.s: The film festival takes place in years 2021, 2025, 2029, 2033, 2037, and the expo takes place in years 2022, 2027, 2032, 2037. The earliest year they coincide is 2037.

qs.q: The Turing Youth Bowl is held every 3 years and took place in 2020. The Lovelace Robotics Championship is held every 4 years and took place in 2022. What is the first year after 2022 in which both competitions will take place in the same year?
qs.s: The Turing Youth Bowl is held in years 2020, 2023, 2026, and the Lovelace Championship is held in years 2022, 2026. Thus, both competitions will first coincide after 2022 in the year 2026.

qs.q: A prestigious fiction award is presented every 4 years and was presented in 2017. A poetry award is presented every 6 years and was presented in 2019. What is the next year in which both awards will be presented in the same year?
qs.s: The fiction award is given in years 2017, 2021, 2025, and the poetry award is given in years 2019, 2025. The next year both awards will be given together is 2025.

qs.q: A city conducts a major transit review every 12 years; the last one was completed in 2014. A regional environmental audit is conducted every 15 years; the last one was completed in 2011. What is the second year after 2014 in which both events will take place in the same year?
qs.s: Both events first coincide in the year 2026 (\(2014 + 12 = 2026\) and \(2011 + 15 = 2026\)). Since \(\text{LCM}(12, 15) = 60\), they coincide every 60 years, so the second common year after 2014 is \(2026 + 60 = 2086\).

qs.q: A national heritage festival is held every 8 years and was held in 2004. A folklore festival is held every 6 years and was held in 2008. What is the last year in the 21st century (up to and including the year 2100) in which both festivals will be held in the same year?
qs.s: The festivals first coincide in 2020 and recur together every \(\text{LCM}(8, 6) = 24\) years. Adding 24 repeatedly gives the common years 2020, 2044, 2068, and 2092, making 2092 the last occurrence in the 21st century.

qs.q: Three international academic competitions are held periodically. The Youth Math Olympiad is held every 4 years and was held in 2022. The Science Decathlon is held every 6 years and was held in 2020. The Informatics Challenge is held every 5 years and was held in 2023. What is the first year after 2023 in which all three competitions will be held in the same year?
qs.s: The Math and Science competitions both occur in 2026 and repeat every \(\text{LCM}(4, 6) = 12\) years (2026, 2038, 2050, ...). Checking these with the Informatics Challenge (held every 5 years after 2023), \(2038 - 2023 = 15\) is a multiple of 5, making 2038 the first year all three coincide.

qs.q: An international chemistry congress meets every 12 years and last met in 2008. A physics convention meets every 16 years and last met in 2004. How many times during the 21st century (from 2001 through 2100 inclusive) will both events take place in the same year?
qs.s: Both events first coincide in 2020 and repeat every \(\text{LCM}(12, 16) = 48\) years. Within the 21st century (2001–2100), they coincide only in 2020 and \(2020 + 48 = 2068\), for a total of 2 times.

qs.q: A suspension bridge is inspected every 8 years and was inspected in 2018. A highway tunnel is inspected every 12 years and was inspected in 2014. A water aqueduct is inspected every 9 years and was inspected in 2023. What is the first year after 2023 in which all three structures will be inspected in the same year?
qs.s: The bridge and tunnel both undergo inspection in 2026 and recur together every \(\text{LCM}(8, 12) = 24\) years, in 2026, 2050, and so on. Checking the aqueduct inspection years (\(2023 + 9k\)), \(2050 - 2023 = 27 = 3 \times 9\), so 2050 is the first common inspection year.

exercises.name: Common multiple of a range of integers

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 1 to 8?
qs.s: The highest prime powers among the numbers from 1 to 8 are \(2^3 = 8\), \(3\), \(5\), and \(7\). The least common multiple is \(8 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 840\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 1 to 7?
qs.s: The highest power of each prime from 1 to 7 is \(2^2\), \(3\), \(5\), and \(7\). Multiplying these gives \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 420\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 1 to 6?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(2 = 2\), \(3 = 3\), \(4 = 2^2\), \(5 = 5\), and \(6 = 2 \times 3\). Taking the highest power of each prime present gives \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 8 to 11?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(8 = 2^3\), \(9 = 3^2\), \(10 = 2 \times 5\), and \(11 = 11\). The least common multiple is \(2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 11 = 8 \times 9 \times 5 \times 11 = 3960\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 6 to 9?
qs.s: The prime factorizations are \(6 = 2 \times 3\), \(7 = 7\), \(8 = 2^3\), and \(9 = 3^2\). Taking the highest power of each prime gives \(2^3 \times 3^2 \times 7 = 8 \times 9 \times 7 = 504\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 1 to 12?
qs.s: The highest prime powers from 1 to 12 are \(2^3 = 8\), \(3^2 = 9\), \(5\), \(7\), and \(11\). The least common multiple is \(8 \times 9 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11 = 27720\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 1 to 13?
qs.s: The highest prime powers from 1 to 13 are \(2^3 = 8\), \(3^2 = 9\), \(5\), \(7\), \(11\), and \(13\). Multiplying gives \(8 \times 9 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11 \times 13 = 27720 \times 13 = 360360\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 12 to 16?
qs.s: Factoring the numbers gives \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\), \(13 = 13\), \(14 = 2 \times 7\), \(15 = 3 \times 5\), and \(16 = 2^4\). Taking the highest power of each prime gives \(2^4 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13 = 16 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13 = 21840\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 14 to 18?
qs.s: Factoring the numbers gives \(14 = 2 \times 7\), \(15 = 3 \times 5\), \(16 = 2^4\), \(17 = 17\), and \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\). Taking the highest power of each prime gives \(2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 17 = 16 \times 9 \times 5 \times 7 \times 17 = 85680\).

qs.q: What is the smallest positive whole number divisible by every whole number from 10 to 15?
qs.s: Factoring each number gives highest prime powers of \(2^2 = 4\), \(3\), \(5\), \(7\), \(11\), and \(13\). Multiplying these yields \(4 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11 \times 13 = 60060\).

qs.s: Prime factorizing 1225 gives \(5^2 \times 7^2\), so the square root is \(5 \times 7 = 35\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 15876
qs.s: Prime factorizing 15876 gives \(2^2 \times 3^4 \times 7^2\), so the square root is \(2 \times 3^2 \times 7 = 2 \times 9 \times 7 = 126\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 44100
qs.s: Since \(44100 = 441 \times 100 = 21^2 \times 10^2\), the square root is \(21 \times 10 = 210\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 7056
qs.s: Prime factorizing 7056 gives \(2^4 \times 3^2 \times 7^2\), so the square root is \(2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 4 \times 3 \times 7 = 84\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 11025
qs.s: Prime factorizing 11025 gives \(3^2 \times 5^2 \times 7^2\), so the square root is \(3 \times 5 \times 7 = 105\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 5184
qs.s: Prime factorizing 5184 gives \(2^6 \times 3^4\), so the square root is \(2^3 \times 3^2 = 8 \times 9 = 72\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 3600
qs.s: Write \(3600\) as \(60 \times 60\), or note that \(\sqrt{3600} = \sqrt{36 \times 100} = 6 \times 10 = 60\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 1600
qs.s: Write \(1600\) as \(40 \times 40\), or note that \(\sqrt{1600} = \sqrt{16 \times 100} = 4 \times 10 = 40\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 400
qs.s: Write \(400\) as \(20 \times 20\), or note that \(\sqrt{400} = \sqrt{4 \times 100} = 2 \times 10 = 20\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator: 4356
qs.s: Using prime factorization, \(4356 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 11^2\), so \(\sqrt{4356} = 2 \times 3 \times 11 = 66\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{100}{361}\)
qs.s: Because \(10^2 = 100\) and \(19^2 = 361\), the square root is \(\frac{10}{19}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{36}{289}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the square root of the numerator and denominator gives \(\sqrt{36} = 6\) and \(\sqrt{289} = 17\), yielding \(\frac{6}{17}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{121}{256}\)
qs.s: Since \(11^2 = 121\) and \(16^2 = 256\), the square root is \(\frac{11}{16}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(1\frac{87}{169}\)
qs.s: Convert to an improper fraction: \(1\frac{87}{169} = \frac{169 + 87}{169} = \frac{256}{169}\). Then evaluate \(\sqrt{\frac{256}{169}} = \frac{16}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{72}{338}\)
qs.s: Simplify the fraction by dividing both terms by 2 to get \(\frac{36}{169}\). Then take the square root to obtain \(\frac{6}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{484}{729}\)
qs.s: By prime factorization, \(484 = 2^2 \times 11^2\) so \(\sqrt{484} = 22\), and \(729 = 3^6 = 27^2\) so \(\sqrt{729} = 27\), giving \(\frac{22}{27}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{98}{242}\)
qs.s: Divide the numerator and denominator by their common factor of 2 to simplify to \(\frac{49}{121}\), whose square root is \(\frac{7}{11}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(2\frac{34}{81}\)
qs.s: Rewrite the mixed number as an improper fraction: \(2\frac{34}{81} = \frac{162 + 34}{81} = \frac{196}{81}\). Taking the square root gives \(\frac{\sqrt{196}}{\sqrt{81}} = \frac{14}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{5}{45}\)
qs.s: Divide both the numerator and denominator by 5 to simplify \(\frac{5}{45}\) to \(\frac{1}{9}\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}} = \frac{1}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{50}{72}\)
qs.s: Divide the numerator and denominator by 2 to reduce \(\frac{50}{72}\) to \(\frac{25}{36}\). Evaluating the square root gives \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} = \frac{5}{6}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{8}{50}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\frac{8}{50}\) by dividing both the numerator and denominator by 2 to get \(\frac{4}{25}\). The square root is \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{25}} = \frac{2}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{18}{32}\)
qs.s: Divide the numerator and denominator by 2 to simplify \(\frac{18}{32}\) to \(\frac{9}{16}\). Then take the square root of both parts to get \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{3}{4}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{27}{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\frac{27}{75}\) by dividing the numerator and denominator by 3 to get \(\frac{9}{25}\). The square root is \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{288}{338}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\frac{288}{338}\) by dividing numerator and denominator by 2 to get \(\frac{144}{169}\). Since \(\sqrt{144} = 12\) and \(\sqrt{169} = 13\), the square root is \(\frac{12}{13}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{392}{578}\)
qs.s: Divide the numerator and denominator by 2 to simplify \(\frac{392}{578}\) to \(\frac{196}{289}\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{\frac{196}{289}} = \frac{14}{17}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{75}{432}\)
qs.s: Divide the numerator and denominator by 3 to simplify \(\frac{75}{432}\) to \(\frac{25}{144}\). The square root is \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{144}} = \frac{5}{12}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect square root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{300}{588}\)
qs.s: Simplify \(\frac{300}{588}\) by dividing the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor, 12, to obtain \(\frac{25}{49}\). The square root is \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{49}} = \frac{5}{7}\).

exercises.name: Determining and evaluating perfect cube roots

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 1
qs.s: Since \(1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1\), 1 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 1.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 27
qs.s: Since \(3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27\), 27 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 3.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 16
qs.s: Since \(2^3 = 8\) and \(3^3 = 27\), there is no integer whose cube equals 16, so a perfect cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 64
qs.s: Since \(4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64\), 64 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 4.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 125
qs.s: Since \(5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125\), 125 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 5.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 1728
qs.s: Prime factorizing gives \(1728 = 2^6 \times 3^3 = (2^2 \times 3)^3 = 12^3\), so the perfect cube root is 12.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 512
qs.s: Factoring gives \(512 = 2^9 = (2^3)^3 = 8^3\), so the perfect cube root is 8.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 3375
qs.s: Prime factorizing gives \(3375 = 3^3 \times 5^3 = (3 \times 5)^3 = 15^3\), so the perfect cube root is 15.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{8}{25}\)
qs.s: Although the numerator is a perfect cube (\(2^3 = 8\)), the denominator 25 is not a perfect cube, so a rational cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{27}{125}\)
qs.s: Since \(\frac{27}{125} = \frac{3^3}{5^3} = \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3\), the cube root is \(\frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 8
qs.s: Since \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\), 8 is a perfect cube and its cube root is 2.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 25
qs.s: Since \(2^3 = 8\) and \(3^3 = 27\), no integer cubed equals 25 (25 is \(5^2\), a square rather than a cube).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 256
qs.s: The prime factorization of 256 is \(2^8\); because the exponent 8 is not divisible by 3, 256 is not a perfect cube.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 729
qs.s: Factoring gives \(729 = 3^6 = (3^2)^3 = 9^3\), so the cube root is 9 (27 is its square root).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 500
qs.s: The prime factorization of 500 is \(2^2 \times 5^3\); because the factor 2 is not cubed, 500 is not a perfect cube.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 343
qs.s: Using continuous division by primes, \(343 = 7 \times 7 \times 7 = 7^3\), so the cube root of 343 is 7.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 216
qs.s: The prime factorization of 216 is \(2^3 \times 3^3 = (2 \times 3)^3 = 6^3\), so the perfect cube root is 6.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 2744
qs.s: The prime factorization of 2744 is \(2^3 \times 7^3 = (2 \times 7)^3 = 14^3\). Therefore, the perfect cube root is 14.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{64}{125}\)
qs.s: Taking the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately gives \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\) and \(\sqrt[3]{125} = 5\), so the cube root is \(\frac{4}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{27}{343}\)
qs.s: Taking the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately gives \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[3]{343} = 7\), so the cube root is \(\frac{3}{7}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 36.
qs.s: Factoring gives \(36 = 2^2 \times 3^2\), which cannot be written as three identical integer factors. Therefore, 36 does not have a perfect cube root.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 2700.
qs.s: Factoring gives \(2700 = 3^3 \times 2^2 \times 5^2\), where the exponents of 2 and 5 are not multiples of 3. Therefore, 2700 is not a perfect cube and its cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{16}{54}\).
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction by dividing numerator and denominator by 2 gives \(\frac{8}{27}\). Since \(8 = 2^3\) and \(27 = 3^3\), the perfect cube root is \(\frac{2}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{64}{729}\).
qs.s: Since \(64 = 4^3\) and \(729 = 9^3\), evaluating the root gives \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{64}{729}} = \frac{4}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 81
qs.s: Since \(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\), 81 lies between two consecutive perfect cubes and cannot be written as the cube of an integer. Therefore, the perfect cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 4000
qs.s: The prime factorization of 4000 is \(2^5 \times 5^3\), and because the exponent of 2 is not a multiple of 3 (note \(15^3 = 3375\) and \(16^3 = 4096\)), 4000 is not a perfect cube. Therefore, the perfect cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{8}{27}\)
qs.s: Taking the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately gives \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{27}} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{8}}{\sqrt[3]{27}} = \frac{2}{3}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator. 1000
qs.s: Since \(10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10^3 = 1000\), the cube root is \(\sqrt[3]{1000} = 10\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{343}{729}\)
qs.s: Since \(343 = 7^3\) and \(729 = 9^3\), evaluating the root of the fraction gives \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{343}{729}} = \frac{7}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator. \(\frac{54}{250}\)
qs.s: Simplify the fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by 2 to get \(\frac{27}{125}\), then find \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{125}} = \frac{3}{5}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{8}{729}\)
qs.s: Find the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately: \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{729} = 9\). Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{729}} = \frac{2}{9}\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 5832
qs.s: Prime factorize \(5832\) into \(2^3 \times 3^6 = (2 \times 3^2)^3 = 18^3\). Therefore, the perfect cube root is \(\sqrt[3]{5832} = 18\).

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 225
qs.s: Prime factorization gives \(225 = 3^2 \times 5^2\). Since the exponents are not multiples of 3, 225 is not a perfect cube.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{64}{343}\)
Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{27}{100}\)
qs.s: While the numerator is a perfect cube (\(27 = 3^3\)), the denominator \(100 = 10^2\) is not a perfect cube. Therefore, a rational cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 243.
qs.s: The prime factorization of 243 is \(3^5\). Because the exponent 5 is not divisible by 3, 243 is not a perfect cube, so its perfect cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 3125.
qs.s: Factoring 3125 gives \(5^5\). Since the exponent 5 is not divisible by 3, 3125 is not a perfect cube, so its perfect cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 1331.
qs.s: Testing prime divisibility reveals that \(1331 = 11 \times 11 \times 11 = 11^3\). Therefore, the perfect cube root of 1331 is 11.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: 2048.
qs.s: Factoring 2048 into prime factors yields \(2^{11}\). Since the exponent 11 is not divisible by 3, 2048 is not a perfect cube, so its perfect cube root does not exist.

qs.q: Find the perfect cube root, if it exists, without a calculator: \(\frac{125}{216}\)
qs.s: Take the cube root of the numerator and denominator separately: \(\sqrt[3]{125} = 5\) and \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), giving \(\frac{5}{6}\).

qs.q: A softball diamond is shaped like a square with an area of \(3600\text{ ft}^2\). What is the distance from home plate to first base?
qs.s: The distance from home plate to first base is one side of the square, which is \(s = \sqrt{3600} = 60\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A square garden has an area of \(576\text{ m}^2\). What is the length of one side of the garden?
qs.s: The side length of a square is the square root of its area, so \(s = \sqrt{576} = 24\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A square dance floor has an area of \(1225\text{ ft}^2\). What is the length of one side of the dance floor?
qs.s: Taking the square root of the area gives the side length, \(s = \sqrt{1225} = 35\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A square painting has an area of \(784\text{ in.}^2\). What is the width of the painting?
qs.s: The width of the square painting is the square root of its area, so \(w = \sqrt{784} = 28\text{ in.}\)

qs.q: A square checkerboard has an area of \(400\text{ cm}^2\). What is the length of one side of the checkerboard?
qs.s: The side length is found by taking the square root of the area, so \(s = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A square park has an area of \(4356\text{ m}^2\). What is the perimeter of the park?
qs.s: First find the side length \(s = \sqrt{4356} = 66\text{ m}\). Then the perimeter is \(P = 4s = 4(66) = 264\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular playground is made of 3 identical square sections placed side by side in a row. If the total area of the playground is \(1083\text{ m}^2\), what is the width of the playground (the side length of one square)?
qs.s: The area of each square section is \(1083 \div 3 = 361\text{ m}^2\). The width is the side length of one square, \(s = \sqrt{361} = 19\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A large square field has an area of \(7056\text{ m}^2\). If it is divided into 4 equal smaller square plots, what is the side length of each smaller plot?
qs.s: The side length of the entire field is \(\sqrt{7056} = 84\text{ m}\). Since 4 identical squares form a \(2 \times 2\) grid, the side length of each smaller plot is \(84 \div 2 = 42\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A square garden with an area of \(529\text{ m}^2\) is surrounded on all sides by a walkway of uniform width. If the total area of the garden and walkway combined is \(841\text{ m}^2\), what is the width of the walkway?
qs.s: The side length of the garden is \(\sqrt{529} = 23\text{ m}\), and the total side length including the walkway is \(\sqrt{841} = 29\text{ m}\). Since the walkway borders both sides, its width is \((29 - 23) \div 2 = 3\text{ m}\).
