qs.q: Courtyard A is a square with an area of \(2025\text{ ft}^2\), and Courtyard B is a square with an area of \(1296\text{ ft}^2\). How much longer is a side of Courtyard A than a side of Courtyard B?
qs.s: The side length of Courtyard A is \(\sqrt{2025} = 45\text{ ft}\) and of Courtyard B is \(\sqrt{1296} = 36\text{ ft}\). The difference in their side lengths is \(45 - 36 = 9\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A square park has an area of \(2500\text{ m}^2\). How far is it in a straight line from one corner of the park to the diagonally opposite corner?
qs.s: The side length of the park is \(s = \sqrt{2500} = 50\text{ m}\). The diagonal distance between opposite corners is \(d = \sqrt{50^2 + 50^2} = 50\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: The area of a softball diamond is \(3600\text{ ft}^2\). How far is it in a straight line from 1st base to 3rd base?
qs.s: The side length of the square diamond is \(s = \sqrt{3600} = 60\text{ ft}\). The distance from 1st base to 3rd base is the diagonal, \(d = \sqrt{60^2 + 60^2} = 60\sqrt{2}\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: The area of a square community garden is \(4900\text{ m}^2\). A straight stone pathway connects two opposite corners. What is the length of this pathway?
qs.s: The side length of the garden is \(s = \sqrt{4900} = 70\text{ m}\). The pathway along the diagonal has length \(d = \sqrt{70^2 + 70^2} = 70\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A square public plaza has an area of \(6400\text{ m}^2\). What is the straight-line distance between two opposite corners of the plaza?
qs.s: The side length of the plaza is \(s = \sqrt{6400} = 80\text{ m}\). The straight-line distance between opposite corners is \(d = \sqrt{80^2 + 80^2} = 80\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A youth baseball diamond is a square with an area of \(1600\text{ ft}^2\). How far is it in a straight line from home plate to second base?
qs.s: The side length of the diamond is \(s = \sqrt{1600} = 40\text{ ft}\). The distance from home plate to second base is the diagonal, \(d = \sqrt{40^2 + 40^2} = 40\sqrt{2}\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A rectangular storage yard has an area of \(4800\text{ m}^2\), and its length is three times its width. What is the straight-line distance between two opposite corners of the yard?
qs.s: Setting \(w \times 3w = 4800\) gives \(w^2 = 1600\), so the width is \(w = 40\text{ m}\) and the length is \(120\text{ m}\). The diagonal distance between opposite corners is \(d = \sqrt{40^2 + 120^2} = \sqrt{16000} = 40\sqrt{10}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A square solar farm has an area of \(9800\text{ m}^2\). What is the straight-line distance from one corner of the farm to the opposite corner?
qs.s: The side length of the square farm is \(s = \sqrt{9800} = 70\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\). The distance between opposite corners is the diagonal, \(d = s\sqrt{2} = 70\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} = 140\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular soccer field has an area of \(7200\text{ m}^2\), and its length is twice its width. What is the straight-line distance between two diagonally opposite corner flags?
qs.s: Setting \(w \times 2w = 7200\) gives \(w^2 = 3600\), so the width is \(w = 60\text{ m}\) and the length is \(120\text{ m}\). The diagonal distance between opposite corners is \(d = \sqrt{60^2 + 120^2} = \sqrt{18000} = 60\sqrt{5}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two identical square plots of land, each with an area of \(2500\text{ m}^2\), are joined side-by-side to form a single rectangular parcel. What is the straight-line distance between the two most distant corners of this parcel?
qs.s: Each square has a side length of \(\sqrt{2500} = 50\text{ m}\), forming a rectangle with width \(50\text{ m}\) and length \(100\text{ m}\). The distance between the most distant corners is the diagonal, \(d = \sqrt{50^2 + 100^2} = \sqrt{12500} = 50\sqrt{5}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A square nature reserve has an area of \(705\,600\text{ m}^2\). What is the straight-line distance between two opposite corners of the reserve?
qs.s: Factoring gives \(705\,600 = 2^6 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 \times 7^2\), so the side length is \(s = \sqrt{705\,600} = 840\text{ m}\). The distance between opposite corners is the diagonal, \(d = 840\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{3x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car that left a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car whose skid length is 48 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 48\) into the formula to get \(S = 2\sqrt{3(48)} = 2\sqrt{144}\). Since \(\sqrt{144} = 12\), the speed is \(2(12) = 24\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{6x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car that left a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car whose skid length is 96 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 96\) into the formula to get \(S = 2\sqrt{6(96)} = 2\sqrt{576}\). Since \(\sqrt{576} = 24\), the speed is \(2(24) = 48\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 5\sqrt{2x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle that left a skid of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a vehicle whose skid length is 32 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 32\) into the formula to get \(S = 5\sqrt{2(32)} = 5\sqrt{64}\). Since \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), the speed is \(5(8) = 40\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 3\sqrt{2x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle from a skid of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a vehicle whose skid length is 72 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 72\) into the formula to get \(S = 3\sqrt{2(72)} = 3\sqrt{144}\). Since \(\sqrt{144} = 12\), the speed is \(3(12) = 36\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 4\sqrt{3x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car that left a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car whose skid length is 75 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 75\) into the formula to get \(S = 4\sqrt{3(75)} = 4\sqrt{225}\). Since \(\sqrt{225} = 15\), the speed is \(4(15) = 60\) mph.

qs.q: To determine a vehicle's speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, on an inclined road, investigators use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{6x + 25}\), where \(x\) is the length of the skid mark in feet. Determine the speed of a vehicle that leaves a skid mark of 24 ft.
qs.s: Evaluate under the radical first: \(6(24) + 25 = 144 + 25 = 169\). The speed is then \(S = 2\sqrt{169} = 2(13) = 26\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{14x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle from a skid of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a vehicle whose skid mark length is 126 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 126\) to get \(S = 2\sqrt{14(126)} = 2\sqrt{1764}\). Factoring into primes gives \(1764 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7^2\), so \(\sqrt{1764} = 42\), which gives \(S = 2(42) = 84\) mph.

qs.q: An accident investigator uses the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{5x} + 12\) to determine the initial speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle before braking and colliding, where \(x\) is the skid mark length in feet. Determine the initial speed of a vehicle that left an 80 ft skid mark.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 80\) to get \(S = 2\sqrt{5(80)} + 12 = 2\sqrt{400} + 12\). Since \(\sqrt{400} = 20\), the initial speed is \(2(20) + 12 = 40 + 12 = 52\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{5x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car from its skid mark length, \(x\) in feet. In a zone with a posted speed limit of 35 mph, a car leaves a skid mark of 125 ft. By how many miles per hour did the driver exceed the speed limit?
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 125\) to calculate the vehicle's speed: \(S = 2\sqrt{5(125)} = 2\sqrt{625} = 2(25) = 50\) mph. The driver exceeded the posted speed limit by \(50 - 35 = 15\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{5x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car from its skid mark length, \(x\) in feet. At an accident scene, Car A left a skid mark of 180 ft and Car B left a skid mark of 80 ft. How many miles per hour faster was Car A travelling than Car B?
qs.s: Car A's speed is \(S_A = 2\sqrt{5(180)} = 2\sqrt{900} = 2(30) = 60\) mph, and Car B's speed is \(S_B = 2\sqrt{5(80)} = 2\sqrt{400} = 2(20) = 40\) mph. The difference between their speeds is \(60 - 40 = 20\) mph.

qs.q: Safety engineers use the formula \(S = 5\sqrt{2x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in kilometers per hour, of a vehicle with a skid mark of length \(x\) meters. Determine the speed of a vehicle whose skid length is 72 m.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 72\) into the formula to get \(S = 5\sqrt{2(72)} = 5\sqrt{144}\). Since \(\sqrt{144} = 12\), the speed is \(S = 5 \times 12 = 60\) km/h.

qs.q: Traffic investigators use the formula \(S = \sqrt{24x}\) to estimate the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle from a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a vehicle whose skid length is 150 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 150\) into the formula to get \(S = \sqrt{24(150)} = \sqrt{3600}\). Since \(60^2 = 3600\), the speed is 60 mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{5x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car that left a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car whose skid length is 80 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 80\) into the formula to get \(S = 2\sqrt{5(80)} = 2\sqrt{400}\). Since \(\sqrt{400} = 20\), the speed is \(S = 2 \times 20 = 40\) mph.

qs.q: On a wet asphalt road, investigators use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{3x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car from a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car whose skid length is 75 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 75\) into the formula to get \(S = 2\sqrt{3(75)} = 2\sqrt{225}\). Since \(\sqrt{225} = 15\), the speed is \(S = 2 \times 15 = 30\) mph.

qs.q: On an icy road, police use the formula \(S = \sqrt{6x}\) to find the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle that left a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car whose skid mark is 96 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 96\) into the formula to get \(S = \sqrt{6(96)} = \sqrt{576}\). Since \(24^2 = 576\), the speed is 24 mph.

qs.q: An accident investigator uses the formula \(S = 4\sqrt{3x}\) to estimate the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a vehicle from a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. At an intersection, Vehicle A left a skid mark of 48 ft and Vehicle B left a skid mark of 147 ft. How many miles per hour faster was Vehicle B traveling than Vehicle A?
qs.s: Vehicle A's speed is \(4\sqrt{3(48)} = 4\sqrt{144} = 4(12) = 48\) mph, and Vehicle B's speed is \(4\sqrt{3(147)} = 4\sqrt{441} = 4(21) = 84\) mph. Vehicle B was traveling \(84 - 48 = 36\) mph faster.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = \sqrt{21x}\) to determine the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car from a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. Determine the speed of a car that leaves a skid mark of 189 ft.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 189\) into the formula to get \(S = \sqrt{21(189)} = \sqrt{3969}\). Factoring gives \(3969 = 9 \times 441\), so \(\sqrt{3969} = 3 \times 21 = 63\) mph.

qs.q: When a vehicle skids across two different road surfaces, investigators use the formula \(S = \sqrt{18x_1 + 32x_2}\) to determine its speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, where \(x_1\) is the skid distance on asphalt and \(x_2\) is the skid distance on gravel. Determine the speed of a car that skidded 120 ft on asphalt and 45 ft on gravel.
qs.s: Substitute \(x_1 = 120\) and \(x_2 = 45\) to get \(S = \sqrt{18(120) + 32(45)} = \sqrt{2160 + 1440} = \sqrt{3600}\). Since \(\sqrt{3600} = 60\), the speed was 60 mph.

qs.q: A car skids for \(x\) ft before colliding with a barrier at 14 mph. Investigators use the formula \(S = \sqrt{20x + 196}\) to calculate the car's speed \(S\), in miles per hour, before braking. Determine the initial speed of the car if the skid mark was 55 ft long.
qs.s: Substitute \(x = 55\) into the formula to get \(S = \sqrt{20(55) + 196} = \sqrt{1100 + 196} = \sqrt{1296}\). Using prime factorization, \(\sqrt{1296} = \sqrt{16 \times 81} = 4 \times 9 = 36\) mph.

qs.q: Police use the formula \(S = 2\sqrt{5x}\) to estimate the speed, \(S\) in miles per hour, of a car that leaves a skid mark of length \(x\) ft. In a 50 mph speed zone, a car involved in an accident left a skid mark of 245 ft. By how many miles per hour was the driver exceeding the speed limit?
qs.s: The car's speed was \(S = 2\sqrt{5(245)} = 2\sqrt{1225} = 2(35) = 70\) mph. The driver exceeded the 50 mph speed limit by \(70 - 50 = 20\) mph.

qs.q: A rectangular poster has an area of \(450\text{ cm}^2\). If the length of the poster is twice as long as the width, determine the length of the poster.
qs.s: Since the area is \(2w^2 = 450\), we find \(w^2 = 225\), so the width is \(w = 15\text{ cm}\). Therefore, the length is \(2 \times 15 = 30\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The area of a rectangular floor is \(648\text{ ft}^2\). If its length is twice as long as its width, determine the width of the floor.
qs.s: With width \(w\), the area equation is \(2w^2 = 648\). Dividing by 2 gives \(w^2 = 324\), so the width is \(w = \sqrt{324} = 18\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: The area of a rectangular banner is \(968\text{ cm}^2\). If its length is twice as long as its width, what is the width of the banner?
qs.s: Let the width be \(w\); then \(2w^2 = 968\), so \(w^2 = 484\). Taking the square root gives \(w = \sqrt{484} = 22\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular garden has an area of \(242\text{ m}^2\). If the length of the garden is twice as long as its width, what is the length of the garden?
qs.s: Setting the width as \(w\), we have \(2w^2 = 242\), which gives \(w^2 = 121\) and \(w = 11\text{ m}\). The length is twice the width, so the length is \(2 \times 11 = 22\text{ m}\).

qs.q: The area of a rectangle with a length twice as long as its width is \(800\text{ m}^2\). Determine the width of the rectangle.
qs.s: Let the width be \(w\), so the length is \(2w\). Then \(2w^2 = 800\), which gives \(w^2 = 400\), so \(w = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular display board is made by placing three identical square panels side by side in a single row. The total area of the board is \(1083\text{ cm}^2\). Determine the perimeter of the display board.
qs.s: Each square panel has an area of \(1083 \div 3 = 361\text{ cm}^2\), so each side length is \(\sqrt{361} = 19\text{ cm}\). The board has dimensions \(57\text{ cm}\) by \(19\text{ cm}\), giving a perimeter of \(2(57 + 19) = 152\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The length of a rectangular field is \(1.5\) times its width. If the area of the field is \(384\text{ m}^2\), determine the perimeter of the field.
qs.s: Setting the length as \(1.5w\), the area is \(1.5w^2 = 384\), which gives \(w^2 = 256\) and \(w = \sqrt{256} = 16\text{ m}\). The length is \(1.5 \times 16 = 24\text{ m}\), so the perimeter is \(2(24 + 16) = 80\text{ m}\).

qs.q: The area of a rectangle whose length is 5 times its width is \(7220\text{ cm}^2\). Determine the width of the rectangle.
qs.s: Let the width be \(w\), so \(5w^2 = 7220\), which yields \(w^2 = 1444\). Factoring gives \(1444 = 2^2 \times 19^2\), so the width is \(w = 2 \times 19 = 38\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The area of a rectangular playground is \(1728\text{ m}^2\), and its length is three times its width. Determine the perimeter of the playground.
qs.s: The area is \(3w^2 = 1728\), giving \(w^2 = 576\) and \(w = \sqrt{576} = 24\text{ m}\). With width \(24\text{ m}\) and length \(3 \times 24 = 72\text{ m}\), the perimeter is \(2(72 + 24) = 192\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A square has the same perimeter as a rectangle whose length is three times its width. If the area of the rectangle is \(432\text{ cm}^2\), what is the area of the square?
qs.s: For the rectangle, \(3w^2 = 432\) gives \(w = 12\text{ cm}\) and length \(36\text{ cm}\), so its perimeter is \(2(36 + 12) = 96\text{ cm}\). The square has side length \(96 \div 4 = 24\text{ cm}\), giving an area of \(24^2 = 576\text{ cm}^2\).

qs.q: A solid wooden cube has a volume of \(64\text{ cm}^3\). Determine the length of each edge of the cube.
qs.s: The edge length is the cube root of the volume, so \(s = \sqrt[3]{64\text{ cm}^3} = 4\text{ cm}\) because \(4^3 = 64\).

qs.q: A cube-shaped box has a volume of \(125\text{ m}^3\). Determine the length of each edge of the box.
qs.s: The edge length is the cube root of the volume, so \(s = \sqrt[3]{125\text{ m}^3} = 5\text{ m}\) because \(5^3 = 125\).

qs.q: A cube has a volume of \(729\text{ mm}^3\). Determine the length of each side of the cube.
qs.s: The side length is the cube root of the volume, so \(s = \sqrt[3]{729\text{ mm}^3} = 9\text{ mm}\) because \(9^3 = 729\).

qs.q: A cube has a volume of \(343\text{ cm}^3\). Determine the length of each side of the cube.
qs.s: The side length is the cube root of the volume, so \(s = \sqrt[3]{343\text{ cm}^3} = 7\text{ cm}\) because \(7^3 = 343\).

qs.q: A cubic water tank has a capacity of \(512\text{ m}^3\). Determine the interior side length of the tank.
qs.s: The interior side length is the cube root of the volume, so \(s = \sqrt[3]{512\text{ m}^3} = 8\text{ m}\) because \(8^3 = 512\).

qs.q: A small cubic crystal has a volume of \(\frac{27}{512}\text{ mm}^3\). Determine the length of each side of the crystal.
qs.s: The side length is the cube root of the volume, so \(s = \sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{512}\text{ mm}^3} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{27}}{\sqrt[3]{512}} = \frac{3}{8}\text{ mm}\).

qs.q: A cube has a volume of \(3375\text{ cm}^3\). Determine the length of each side of the cube.
qs.s: Using prime factorization, \(3375 = 3^3 \times 5^3\), so the side length is \(s = \sqrt[3]{3375\text{ cm}^3} = 3 \times 5 = 15\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular storage trunk has a square base of side length \(w\) and a height equal to \(4\) times \(w\). If the trunk has a volume of \(2048\text{ cm}^3\), determine the width \(w\) of the base.
qs.s: The volume is given by \(V = w \times w \times 4w = 4w^3 = 2048\), which simplifies to \(w^3 = 512\). Taking the cube root gives \(w = \sqrt[3]{512} = 8\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: Five identical wooden cubes are placed in a row to form a rectangular prism with a total volume of \(1715\text{ cm}^3\). Determine the edge length of one of the individual cubes.
qs.s: The volume of one cube is \(\frac{1715}{5} = 343\text{ cm}^3\). Taking the cube root gives an edge length of \(s = \sqrt[3]{343} = 7\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A large cubic crate has a volume of \(1728\text{ dm}^3\) and a smaller cubic crate has a volume of \(343\text{ dm}^3\). How much longer is an edge of the large crate than an edge of the small crate?
qs.s: The edge of the large crate is \(\sqrt[3]{1728} = 12\text{ dm}\) and the edge of the small crate is \(\sqrt[3]{343} = 7\text{ dm}\). The difference in edge lengths is \(12 - 7 = 5\text{ dm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular solid has a length four times its width and a height twice its width. If the volume of the solid is \(216\text{ cm}^3\), what is its width?
qs.s: Let \(w\) be the width; then the volume is \(V = (4w)(w)(2w) = 8w^3 = 216\), which gives \(w^3 = 27\). Taking the cube root gives \(w = 3\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular solid has a length three times its width and a height four times its width. If the volume of the rectangular solid is \(96\text{ in}^3\), find its height.
qs.s: The volume equation is \(V = (3w)(w)(4w) = 12w^3 = 96\), giving \(w^3 = 8\) and \(w = 2\text{ in}\). Therefore, the height is \(4w = 4(2) = 8\text{ in}\).

qs.q: A rectangular solid has a length four times its width and a height three times its width. If the volume of the rectangular solid is \(1500\text{ ft}^3\), what is its width?
qs.s: The volume is given by \(V = (4w)(w)(3w) = 12w^3 = 1500\), which simplifies to \(w^3 = 125\). Taking the cube root yields \(w = 5\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A rectangular solid with a square base has a height three times the side length of its base. If its volume is \(375\text{ cm}^3\), what is the side length of the base?
qs.s: Letting \(s\) be the side length of the square base, \(V = s \cdot s \cdot 3s = 3s^3 = 375\), so \(s^3 = 125\). Taking the cube root gives \(s = 5\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: A rectangular storage container has a length five times its width and a height twice its width. If the volume of the container is \(640\text{ m}^3\), what is its length?
qs.s: The volume is \(V = (5w)(w)(2w) = 10w^3 = 640\), so \(w^3 = 64\) and \(w = 4\text{ m}\). Thus, the length is \(5w = 5(4) = 20\text{ m}\).

qs.q: A rectangular solid has a length three times its width and a height five times its width. If the volume of the rectangular solid is \(5145\text{ ft}^3\), what is the difference between its height and its length?
qs.s: The volume is \(V = (3w)(w)(5w) = 15w^3 = 5145\), so \(w^3 = 343\) and \(w = 7\text{ ft}\). The difference between the height and length is \(5w - 3w = 2w = 2(7) = 14\text{ ft}\).

qs.q: A rectangular solid has a height twice its width, and a length five times its height. If the volume of the solid is \(4320\text{ cm}^3\), what is its length?
qs.s: Since \(h = 2w\) and \(l = 5h = 10w\), the volume is \(V = (10w)(w)(2w) = 20w^3 = 4320\), so \(w^3 = 216\) and \(w = 6\text{ cm}\). The length is \(10w = 10(6) = 60\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The length of a rectangular box is \(1.5\) times its width, and its height is \(4\) times its width. If the volume of the box is \(3072\text{ in}^3\), find the sum of its length, width, and height.
qs.s: The volume is \(V = (1.5w)(w)(4w) = 6w^3 = 3072\), so \(w^3 = 512\) and \(w = 8\text{ in}\). The dimensions are \(w = 8\text{ in}\), \(l = 12\text{ in}\), and \(h = 32\text{ in}\), giving a sum of \(8 + 12 + 32 = 52\text{ in}\).

qs.q: A shipping container has a length that is \(\frac{4}{3}\) of its width, and a height that is twice its length. If the volume of the container is \(768\text{ m}^3\), find the area of its base (length \(\times\) width).
qs.s: Since \(l = \frac{4}{3}w\) and \(h = 2l = \frac{8}{3}w\), \(V = \left(\frac{4}{3}w\right)(w)\left(\frac{8}{3}w\right) = \frac{32}{9}w^3 = 768\), so \(w^3 = 216\) and \(w = 6\text{ m}\). Thus, \(l = 8\text{ m}\) and the base area is \(8 \times 6 = 48\text{ m}^2\).

qs.q: A rectangular block of stone has a length seven times its height and a width three times its height. If the volume of the block is \(57624\text{ cm}^3\), find its height.
qs.s: In terms of height \(h\), \(V = (7h)(3h)(h) = 21h^3 = 57624\), which simplifies to \(h^3 = 2744\). Factoring \(2744 = 8 \times 343 = 2^3 \times 7^3\), the cube root is \(h = 2 \times 7 = 14\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a cone whose height is equal to its base radius is given by the formula \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^3\), with \(r\) the radius of the base. Determine the radius of such a cone with volume \(\frac{64}{3}\pi\text{ m}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{1}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{64}{3}\pi\) gives \(r^3 = 64\). Taking the cube root gives \(r = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4\text{ m}\).

qs.q: The volume of a hemisphere is given by the formula \(V = \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3\), with \(r\) the radius of the hemisphere. Determine the radius of a hemisphere with volume \(\frac{250}{3}\pi\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{250}{3}\pi\) gives \(2r^3 = 250\), so \(r^3 = 125\). Taking the cube root gives \(r = \sqrt[3]{125} = 5\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a sphere is given by the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), with \(r\) the radius of the sphere. Determine the radius of a sphere with volume \(288\pi\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 288\pi\) gives \(r^3 = 288 \times \frac{3}{4} = 216\). Taking the cube root gives \(r = \sqrt[3]{216} = 6\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a sphere is given by the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), with \(r\) the radius of the sphere. Determine the radius of a sphere with volume \(36\pi\text{ in}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 36\pi\) gives \(r^3 = 36 \times \frac{3}{4} = 27\). Taking the cube root gives \(r = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\text{ in}\).

qs.q: The volume of a cylinder whose height is equal to its diameter is given by the formula \(V = 2\pi r^3\), with \(r\) the radius of the cylinder. Determine the radius of such a cylinder with volume \(686\pi\text{ mm}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(2\pi r^3 = 686\pi\) gives \(r^3 = 343\). Taking the cube root gives \(r = \sqrt[3]{343} = 7\text{ mm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a sphere is given by the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), where \(r\) is the radius of the sphere. Determine the diameter of a sphere with volume \(2304\pi\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 2304\pi\) gives \(r^3 = 2304 \times \frac{3}{4} = 1728\), so \(r = \sqrt[3]{1728} = 12\text{ cm}\). The diameter is \(d = 2r = 2 \times 12 = 24\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a sphere is given by the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), where \(r\) is the radius of the sphere. Determine the radius of a sphere with volume \(4500\pi\text{ m}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = 4500\pi\) gives \(r^3 = 4500 \times \frac{3}{4} = 3375\). Prime factorizing \(3375 = 3^3 \times 5^3\) gives \(r = 3 \times 5 = 15\text{ m}\).

qs.q: Two spheres have volumes of \(288\pi\text{ cm}^3\) and \(\frac{32}{3}\pi\text{ cm}^3\). Using the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), determine the difference between the radius of the larger sphere and the radius of the smaller sphere.
qs.s: Solving for each radius gives \(r_1 = \sqrt[3]{288 \times \frac{3}{4}} = \sqrt[3]{216} = 6\text{ cm}\) and \(r_2 = \sqrt[3]{\frac{32}{3} \times \frac{3}{4}} = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2\text{ cm}\). The difference is \(6 - 2 = 4\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a cube is given by the formula \(V = s^3\), where \(s\) is the edge length of the cube. Determine the perimeter of one square face of a cube with volume \(1728\text{ cm}^3\).
qs.s: The edge length of the cube is \(s = \sqrt[3]{1728} = 12\text{ cm}\). The perimeter of one square face is \(4s = 4 \times 12 = 48\text{ cm}\).

qs.q: The volume of a sphere is given by the formula \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), with \(r\) the radius of the sphere. Determine the radius of a sphere with volume \(\frac{9}{16}\pi\text{ m}^3\).
qs.s: Setting \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{9}{16}\pi\) gives \(r^3 = \frac{9}{16} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{27}{64}\). Taking the cube root of the numerator and denominator yields \(r = \frac{\sqrt[3]{27}}{\sqrt[3]{64}} = \frac{3}{4}\text{ m}\).

exercises.name: Classifying Radicals as Rational or Irrational

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{50}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 50 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(7^2 = 49\) and \(8^2 = 64\), 50 is not a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{50}\) cannot be written as a terminating or repeating decimal, so it is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{36}\).
d: Irrational, because 36 is not a perfect square
Irrational, because the square root of an even number is always irrational
qs.s: Since \(6^2 = 36\), 36 is a perfect square and \(\sqrt{36} = 6\). Because 6 is an integer, \(\sqrt{36}\) is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{121}\).
d: Irrational, because 121 is not a perfect square
Irrational, because 121 is an odd number
qs.s: Since \(11^2 = 121\), 121 is a perfect square and \(\sqrt{121} = 11\). Because 11 can be expressed as a fraction \(\frac{11}{1}\), it is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{80}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 80 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(8^2 = 64\) and \(9^2 = 81\), 80 does not have an integer square root. Therefore, \(\sqrt{80}\) is an irrational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{144}\).
d: Irrational, because 144 is not a perfect square
Irrational, because all square root expressions are irrational
qs.s: Since \(12^2 = 144\), 144 is a perfect square and \(\sqrt{144} = 12\). Because 12 is an integer, \(\sqrt{144}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{25 + 36}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because \(25 + 36 = 61\), which is not a perfect square
d: Rational, because both 25 and 36 are perfect squares
qs.s: Evaluating under the radical first gives \(\sqrt{25 + 36} = \sqrt{61}\). Because radicals cannot be distributed over addition and 61 is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{61}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{18}{50}}\).
d: Irrational, because neither 18 nor 50 is a perfect square
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction inside the radical gives \(\frac{18}{50} = \frac{9}{25}\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} = \frac{3}{5}\), which is a ratio of integers and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{16000}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 16000 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Although 16 is a perfect square, 16000 has an odd number of zeros (\(16000 = 1600 \times 10\)), which means it is not a perfect square (\(400^2 = 160000\)). Thus, \(\sqrt{16000} = 40\sqrt{10}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{81}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 81 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: While 81 is a perfect square (\(9^2 = 81\)), it is not a perfect cube because \(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{81} = 3\sqrt[3]{3}\), which is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.9}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because \(0.9 = \frac{9}{10}\) and 10 is not a perfect square
d: Irrational, because all decimal square roots are irrational
qs.s: Writing 0.9 as a fraction gives \(\frac{9}{10}\), so \(\sqrt{0.9} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\) (note that \(0.3^2 = 0.09\), not \(0.9\)). Since 10 is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.9}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{490}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 490 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(490 = 49 \times 10\), it has an odd number of trailing zeros and is not a perfect square (\(22^2 = 484\) and \(23^2 = 529\)). Therefore, \(\sqrt{490}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{640}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 640 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(640 = 64 \times 10\), it has an odd number of trailing zeros and is not a perfect square (\(25^2 = 625\) and \(26^2 = 676\)). Therefore, \(\sqrt{640}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{900}\).
d: Irrational, because 900 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(30^2 = 900\), 900 is a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{900} = 30\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{400}\).
d: Irrational, because 400 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(20^2 = 400\), 400 is a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{400} = 20\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{360}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 360 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(360 = 36 \times 10\), it has an odd number of trailing zeros and is not a perfect square (\(18^2 = 324\) and \(19^2 = 361\)). Therefore, \(\sqrt{360}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2}\).
d: Irrational, because 169 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Evaluating under the radical gives \(12^2 + 5^2 = 144 + 25 = 169\). Since \(13^2 = 169\), \(\sqrt{169} = 13\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{2700}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 2700 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: For a multiple of 10 to be a perfect cube, the number of trailing zeros must be a multiple of 3. Since 2700 has only 2 trailing zeros, it is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{2700}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{8}{18}}\).
d: Irrational, because neither 8 nor 18 is a perfect square
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction under the radical gives \(\frac{8}{18} = \frac{4}{9}\). Since both 4 and 9 are perfect squares, \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{2500000}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 2500000 is not a perfect square
qs.s: A power-of-10 multiple is a perfect square only if it has an even number of trailing zeros. Since 2,500,000 has 5 trailing zeros, it is not a perfect square, making \(\sqrt{2500000}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.009}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 0.009 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Writing the decimal as a fraction gives \(0.009 = \frac{9}{1000}\), which has an odd number of decimal places. Since 1000 is not a perfect square, \(0.009\) is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{0.009}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{18}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 18 is not a perfect square
d: Rational, because 18 is an even integer
qs.s: Since \(4^2 = 16\) and \(5^2 = 25\), 18 is not a perfect square; therefore, \(\sqrt{18}\) cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{75}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 75 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(8^2 = 64\) and \(9^2 = 81\), 75 is not a perfect square, which means its square root is a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{30}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 30 is not a perfect square
d: Rational, because 30 can be written as the fraction \(\frac{30}{1}\)
qs.s: Since \(5^2 = 25\) and \(6^2 = 36\), 30 is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{30}\) cannot be written as a fraction of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{64}\).
d: Irrational, because 64 is not divisible by 3
Irrational, because square roots of even numbers are irrational
qs.s: Since \(8^2 = 64\), 64 is a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{49}\).
d: Irrational, because 49 is an odd number
Irrational, because square roots of two-digit numbers are irrational
qs.s: Because \(7^2 = 49\), 49 is a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{49} = 7\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.4}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because \(0.4 = \frac{4}{10}\) and 10 is not a perfect square
d: Irrational, because any square root containing a decimal is irrational
qs.s: Writing \(0.4\) as a fraction yields \(\frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}\), and since neither numerator nor denominator is a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.4}\) is irrational (note that \((0.2)^2 = 0.04\), not \(0.4\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{16}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 16 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Although 16 is a perfect square (\(4^2 = 16\)), it is not a perfect cube because \(2^3 = 8\) and \(3^3 = 27\); therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{16}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{9 + 25}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because \(9 + 25 = 34\) and 34 is not a perfect square
d: Irrational, because the sum of two perfect squares is always irrational
qs.s: Adding the terms inside the radical gives \(9 + 25 = 34\). Because \(5^2 = 25\) and \(6^2 = 36\), 34 is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{34}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{20}{45}}\).
d: Irrational, because neither 20 nor 45 is a perfect square
Irrational, because the square root of a fraction is always irrational
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction gives \(\frac{20}{45} = \frac{4}{9}\). Since both 4 and 9 are perfect squares, \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{2 \times 50}\).
d: Irrational, because neither 2 nor 50 is a perfect square
Irrational, because the product of two non-perfect squares is always irrational
qs.s: Multiplying inside the radical gives \(2 \times 50 = 100\). Since \(10^2 = 100\), \(\sqrt{100} = 10\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{289}\).
qs.s: Since \(17^2 = 289\), \(\sqrt{289} = 17\). Because 17 is an integer, \(\sqrt{289}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{225}\).
qs.s: Since \(15^2 = 225\), \(\sqrt{225} = 15\). Because 15 is an integer, \(\sqrt{225}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{300}\).
qs.s: Because \(17^2 = 289\) and \(18^2 = 324\), 300 lies between two consecutive perfect squares and is not a perfect square itself, making \(\sqrt{300}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{90}\).
qs.s: Since \(9^2 = 81\) and \(10^2 = 100\), 90 is not a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{90}\) cannot be written as a terminating or repeating decimal, so it is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{625}\).
qs.s: Since \(25^2 = 625\), \(\sqrt{625} = 25\). Because 25 is an integer, \(\sqrt{625}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{10^2 + 5^2}\).
qs.s: Evaluating under the radical gives \(10^2 + 5^2 = 100 + 25 = 125\). Because \(11^2 = 121\) and \(12^2 = 144\), 125 is not a perfect square, making \(\sqrt{125}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{4900000}\).
qs.s: For a multiple of 10 to be a perfect square, it must have an even number of trailing zeros; since 4,900,000 has 5 zeros, it is not a perfect square and its square root is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{15^2 - 9^2}\).
qs.s: Evaluating inside the radical gives \(15^2 - 9^2 = 225 - 81 = 144\). Since \(\sqrt{144} = 12\), the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{50}{72}}\).
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction under the radical gives \(\frac{50}{72} = \frac{25}{36}\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} = \frac{5}{6}\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{2.5}\)
qs.s: Writing \(2.5\) as a fraction yields \(\frac{25}{10} = \frac{5}{2}\); since the denominator \(10\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{2.5}\) is irrational (note that \(0.5^2 = 0.25 \neq 2.5\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{0.9}\)
qs.s: Expressing \(0.9\) as the fraction \(\frac{9}{10}\), \(10\) is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{0.9}\) is irrational (note that \(0.3^2 = 0.09 \neq 0.9\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{0.49}\)
qs.s: Since \(0.49 = \frac{49}{100}\) and both \(49\) and \(100\) are perfect squares, \(\sqrt{0.49} = \frac{7}{10} = 0.7\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{0.4}\)
qs.s: Writing \(0.4\) as a fraction gives \(\frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}\); since \(10\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.4}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers and is irrational (note that \(0.2^2 = 0.04 \neq 0.4\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{0.81}\)
qs.s: Since \(0.81 = \frac{81}{100}\) and both \(81\) and \(100\) are perfect squares, \(\sqrt{0.81} = \frac{9}{10} = 0.9\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{3.2 \times 0.2}\)
qs.s: First calculate the product inside the radical: \(3.2 \times 0.2 = 0.64 = \frac{64}{100}\). Since \(\sqrt{\frac{64}{100}} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8\), the result is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{0.5^2 - 0.3^2}\)
qs.s: Evaluate inside the radical first: \(0.5^2 - 0.3^2 = 0.25 - 0.09 = 0.16 = \frac{16}{100}\), and taking the square root gives \(\frac{4}{10} = 0.4\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.64}\)
qs.s: Writing \(0.64\) as \(\frac{64}{100}\), \(64\) is a perfect cube (\(4^3\)) but \(100\) is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.64}\) is irrational (since \(0.4^3 = 0.064 \neq 0.64\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{\frac{50}{72}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the fraction by dividing numerator and denominator by \(2\) to obtain \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{36}}\); since both \(25\) and \(36\) are perfect squares, the value is \(\frac{5}{6}\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and state its value if rational: \(\sqrt{0.00064}\)
qs.s: Writing \(0.00064\) as \(\frac{64}{100000}\), \(100000\) has an odd number of zeros and is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{0.00064}\) is irrational (note that \(0.08^2 = 0.0064\) and \(0.008^2 = 0.000064\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.09}\).
qs.s: Expressing \(0.09\) as \(\frac{9}{100}\), we find \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}} = \frac{3}{10} = 0.3\), so the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.25}\).
qs.s: Write \(0.25\) as the fraction \(\frac{25}{100}\). Since \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{100}} = \frac{5}{10} = 0.5\), the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.81}\).
qs.s: Since \(0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.81\), we have \(\sqrt{0.81} = 0.9 = \frac{9}{10}\), which is a terminating decimal and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.064}\).
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.64 + 0.36}\).
qs.s: Evaluate inside the radical first: \(0.64 + 0.36 = 1\). Then \(\sqrt{1} = 1\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.004}\).
qs.s: Convert \(0.004\) to the fraction \(\frac{4}{1000} = \frac{1}{250}\). Because \(250\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.004}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(-\sqrt{0.000144}\).
qs.s: Express \(0.000144\) as \(\frac{144}{1000000}\). Taking the square root gives \(-\frac{12}{1000} = -0.012\), which is a terminating decimal and thus rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.0081}\).
qs.s: Since \((0.09)^2 = 0.0081\), we have \(\sqrt{0.0081} = 0.09\). Because it equals the terminating decimal \(0.09\) (or fraction \(\frac{9}{100}\)), it is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.025}\).
qs.s: Writing the decimal as a fraction gives \(\sqrt{0.025} = \sqrt{\frac{25}{1000}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{40}}\). Because \(40\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.025}\) cannot be written as a fraction of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.04}\).
qs.s: Since \((0.2)^2 = 0.04\), we have \(\sqrt{0.04} = 0.2\). Because it equals the terminating decimal \(0.2\) (or fraction \(\frac{1}{5}\)), it is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{400{,}000}\).
qs.s: Factoring powers of ten gives \(\sqrt{400{,}000} = \sqrt{4 \times 10^5} = 200\sqrt{10}\). Because \(10\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{400{,}000}\) cannot be written as an integer or fraction, making it irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{16}{54}}\).
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction gives \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{16}{54}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{27}}\). Since both \(8\) and \(27\) are perfect cubes, \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{27}} = \frac{2}{3}\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.00008}\).
qs.s: In fraction form, \(\sqrt[3]{0.00008} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{100{,}000}}\). Although the numerator \(8 = 2^3\) is a perfect cube, the denominator \(100{,}000 = 10^5\) is not because \(5\) is not divisible by \(3\), so the number is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.000064}\).
qs.s: Writing the radicand as a fraction gives \(\sqrt[3]{0.000064} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{64}{1{,}000{,}000}} = \frac{4}{100} = 0.04\). Because \((0.04)^3 = 0.000064\), the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.0025}\).
qs.s: Since \(0.0025 = \frac{25}{10000}\), its square root is \(\frac{5}{100} = 0.05\), which is a terminating decimal and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.0144}\).
qs.s: Since \(0.0144 = \frac{144}{10000}\), its square root is \(\frac{12}{100} = 0.12\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.04 + 0.09}\).
qs.s: Adding inside the radical first gives \(\sqrt{0.13} = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{10}\); since \(13\) is not a perfect square, the number is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.0036} + \sqrt{0.0064}\).
qs.s: Evaluating each term gives \(\sqrt{0.0036} = 0.06\) and \(\sqrt{0.0064} = 0.08\), and their sum is \(0.06 + 0.08 = 0.14\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.0008}\).
qs.s: Writing \(0.0008\) as \(\frac{8}{10000}\), the numerator is a perfect cube (\(2^3\)) but the denominator \(10000\) is not, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.0008}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.000289}\).
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.2} \times \sqrt{0.8}\).
qs.s: Multiplying under one radical gives \(\sqrt{0.2 \times 0.8} = \sqrt{0.16} = 0.4\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{20000}\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(20000 = 10000 \times 2 = 100^2 \times 2\), and since 2 is not a perfect square, 20000 is not a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{20000} = 100\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{19600}\).
qs.s: Since \(19600 = 140^2\), the square root simplifies exactly to the integer 140. Therefore, \(\sqrt{19600}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{25000}\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(25000 = 2500 \times 10 = 50^2 \times 10\), which has an odd number of zeros and is not a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{25000} = 50\sqrt{10}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{32400}\).
qs.s: Since \(32400 = 180^2\), the square root simplifies exactly to the integer 180. Therefore, \(\sqrt{32400}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{14400}\).
qs.s: Since \(14400 = 120^2\), the square root simplifies exactly to the integer 120. Therefore, \(\sqrt{14400}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{72900}\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(72900 = 9^3 \times 100\), and since 100 is not a perfect cube, 72900 is not a perfect cube. Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{72900} = 9\sqrt[3]{100}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{50}{98}}\).
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction gives \(\frac{50}{98} = \frac{25}{49}\). Since \(\sqrt{\frac{25}{49}} = \frac{5}{7}\), which is a ratio of integers, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.049}\).
qs.s: Writing the decimal as a fraction gives \(\frac{49}{1000} = \frac{7^2}{10^3}\), which cannot be written as a ratio of perfect squares because 1000 is not a square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{0.049}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.000441}\).
qs.s: Writing the decimal as a fraction gives \(\frac{441}{1000000} = \left(\frac{21}{1000}\right)^2\), so \(\sqrt{0.000441} = 0.021\). Because it equals a terminating decimal, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{640000}\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(640000 = 40^3 \times 10\), and since 10 is not a perfect cube, 640000 is not a perfect cube. Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{640000} = 40\sqrt[3]{10}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{2.5}\).
qs.s: Rewrite \(2.5\) as the fraction \(\frac{25}{10} = \frac{5}{2}\); since neither \(5\) nor \(2\) is a perfect square, \(\sqrt{2.5} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{2}}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers, so it is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.36}\).
qs.s: Rewrite \(0.36\) as the fraction \(\frac{36}{100}\). Since \(\sqrt{\frac{36}{100}} = \frac{6}{10} = 0.6\), which is a ratio of integers, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{8.1}\).
qs.s: Rewrite \(8.1\) as \(\frac{81}{10}\). Since \(10\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{8.1} = \frac{9}{\sqrt{10}}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers, so it is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.27}\).
qs.s: Write \(0.27\) as \(\frac{27}{100}\); while \(27 = 3^3\) is a perfect cube, the denominator \(100\) is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.27} = \frac{3}{\sqrt[3]{100}}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{9.8}{2}}\).
qs.s: First perform the division under the radical: \(\frac{9.8}{2} = 4.9 = \frac{49}{10}\). Since the denominator \(10\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{\frac{49}{10}} = \frac{7}{\sqrt{10}}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers, so it is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.25 + 1.44}\).
qs.s: First add the numbers inside the radical to get \(0.25 + 1.44 = 1.69\). Since \(1.69 = \frac{169}{100}\) and \(\sqrt{\frac{169}{100}} = \frac{13}{10} = 1.3\), the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{12}{75}}\).
qs.s: Simplify the fraction under the radical by dividing numerator and denominator by \(3\): \(\frac{12}{75} = \frac{4}{25}\). Then \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{25}} = \frac{2}{5}\), which is a ratio of integers, so the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{3^3}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 27 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Evaluating the power gives \(3^3 = 27\). Because 27 is not a perfect square (\(5^2 = 25\) and \(6^2 = 36\)), \(\sqrt{27}\) cannot be written as a fraction of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{15^3}\).
d: Irrational, because 15 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: The cube root and cubing operations are inverses, so \(\sqrt[3]{15^3} = 15\). Because 15 is an integer, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{24^2}\).
d: Irrational, because 24 is not a perfect square
qs.s: The square root and squaring operations undo each other, giving \(\sqrt{24^2} = 24\). Since 24 is an integer, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{45^2}\).
d: Irrational, because 45 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Taking the principal square root of \(45^2\) yields the base itself, so \(\sqrt{45^2} = 45\). Because 45 is an integer, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{6^2}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 36 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Evaluating the exponent gives \(6^2 = 36\). Although 36 is a perfect square, it is not a perfect cube (\(3^3 = 27\) and \(4^3 = 64\)), so \(\sqrt[3]{36}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{8^2 + 15^2}\).
d: Irrational, because 289 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Evaluating under the radical gives \(8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289\). Since \(17^2 = 289\), \(\sqrt{289} = 17\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{18}{32}}\).
d: Irrational, because 18 and 32 are not perfect squares
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction gives \(\frac{18}{32} = \frac{9}{16}\). Because both 9 and 16 are perfect squares, \(\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} = \frac{3}{4}\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{3^2 + 5^2}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 34 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Evaluating under the radical gives \(3^2 + 5^2 = 9 + 25 = 34\). Since 34 is not a perfect square (\(5^2 = 25\) and \(6^2 = 36\)), \(\sqrt{34}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{9^2}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 81 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Evaluating the power gives \(9^2 = 81\). While 81 is a perfect square, it is not a perfect cube (\(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\)), so \(\sqrt[3]{81}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{18 \times 12}\).
d: Irrational, because neither 18 nor 12 is a perfect cube
qs.s: Multiplying under the radical gives \(18 \times 12 = 216\). Since \(6^3 = 216\), \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{1.4^2}\).
qs.s: The principal square root of \(1.4^2\) simplifies directly to \(1.4\). Because \(1.4 = \frac{14}{10} = \frac{7}{5}\) is a terminating decimal, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.45^2}\).
qs.s: Since the square root and the square are inverse operations, \(\sqrt{0.45^2} = 0.45\). Because \(0.45 = \frac{45}{100} = \frac{9}{20}\) can be expressed as a ratio of integers, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.08^3}\).
qs.s: Since the cube root and the cube are inverse operations, \(\sqrt[3]{0.08^3} = 0.08\). Because \(0.08 = \frac{8}{100} = \frac{2}{25}\) is a terminating decimal, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)^2}\).
qs.s: Evaluating the square root of a squared positive fraction gives the fraction itself, so \(\sqrt{\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)^2} = \frac{5}{13}\). Because it is written as a quotient of two integers, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(-\sqrt{0.75^2}\).
qs.s: Evaluating the radical gives \(\sqrt{0.75^2} = 0.75\), so \(-\sqrt{0.75^2} = -0.75\). Because \(-0.75 = -\frac{3}{4}\) can be written as a ratio of integers, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.3^2 + 0.5^2}\).
qs.s: First compute the radicand: \(0.3^2 + 0.5^2 = 0.09 + 0.25 = 0.34 = \frac{34}{100}\). Since \(34\) is not a perfect square, its square root cannot be written as a ratio of integers, making \(\sqrt{0.34} \approx 0.58\) an irrational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.5^2 + 0.5^2}\).
qs.s: First evaluate the radicand: \(0.5^2 + 0.5^2 = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5 = \frac{1}{2}\). Since \(2\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.71\) cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers, making it irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{1.3^2 - 1.2^2}\).
qs.s: First calculate inside the square root: \(1.3^2 - 1.2^2 = 1.69 - 1.44 = 0.25\). Then \(\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5 = \frac{1}{2}\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.6^2 + 0.8^2}\).
qs.s: First evaluate inside the radical: \(0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.00\). Then \(\sqrt{1.00} = 1\), which is an integer and therefore a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.2^3 + 0.019}\).
qs.s: First evaluate inside the cube root: \(0.2^3 + 0.019 = 0.008 + 0.019 = 0.027\). Since \(0.3^3 = 0.027\), we have \(\sqrt[3]{0.027} = 0.3 = \frac{3}{10}\), which is a rational number.

exercises.name: Classifying Radicals as Rational or Irrational

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{8}\).
qs.s: Since \(2^3 = 8\), the cube root simplifies to the integer \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\). Therefore, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{27}\).
qs.s: Since \(3^3 = 27\), the cube root evaluates exactly to \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\). Therefore, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{9}\).
qs.s: Although 9 is a perfect square (\(3^2 = 9\)), it is not a perfect cube because \(2^3 = 8\) and \(3^3 = 27\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{9}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{64}\).
qs.s: Since \(4^3 = 64\), the cube root simplifies exactly to \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\). Therefore, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{1000}}\).
qs.s: Both 27 and 1000 are perfect cubes since \(3^3 = 27\) and \(10^3 = 1000\). Taking the cube root gives \(\frac{3}{10}\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{100 - 36}\).
qs.s: First evaluate the subtraction inside the radical: \(100 - 36 = 64\). Then \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), which is an integer, so the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{100}\).
qs.s: While 100 is a perfect square (\(10^2 = 100\)), it is not a perfect cube because \(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{100}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{25}\).
qs.s: Since \(2^3 = 8\) and \(3^3 = 27\), 25 is not a perfect cube. Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{25}\) cannot be written as a fraction of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{270000}\).
qs.s: Factoring gives \(270000 = 27 \times 10^4\). While 27 is a perfect cube (\(3^3\)), \(10^4\) is not because the exponent 4 is not divisible by 3, making \(\sqrt[3]{270000}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{3 \times 72}\).
qs.s: Multiplying the terms inside the radical first gives \(3 \times 72 = 216\). Since \(6^3 = 216\), \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{9}{64}}\).
qs.s: Although the denominator 64 is a perfect cube (\(4^3 = 64\)), the numerator 9 is not a perfect cube. Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{9}{64}}\) cannot be simplified to a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{125}\).
qs.s: Although 125 is a perfect cube (\(5^3 = 125\)), it is not a perfect square because \(11^2 = 121\) and \(12^2 = 144\), so \(\sqrt{125}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{216}\).
qs.s: Since \(6^3 = 216\), the cube root simplifies exactly to the integer 6, which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{1000}\).
qs.s: Since \(10^3 = 1000\), \(\sqrt[3]{1000} = 10\), which is an integer and therefore a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{225} - \sqrt[3]{343}\).
qs.s: Evaluate each radical: \(\sqrt{225} = 15\) and \(\sqrt[3]{343} = 7\). Subtracting them gives \(15 - 7 = 8\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{25}{64}}\).
qs.s: Although 64 is a perfect cube (\(4^3 = 64\)), the numerator 25 is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{25}{64}} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{25}}{4}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{54}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 54 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: The consecutive cubes around 54 are \(3^3 = 27\) and \(4^3 = 64\). Since 54 is not a perfect cube, \(\sqrt[3]{54}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{169}\).
d: Irrational, because 169 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Since \(13^2 = 169\), \(\sqrt{169} = 13\). Because 13 is an integer, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{343}\).
d: Irrational, because 343 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Since \(7^3 = 7 \times 7 \times 7 = 343\), the cube root is exactly 7. Because 7 is an integer, \(\sqrt[3]{343}\) is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the value of the expression is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{225} - \sqrt[3]{1728}\).
d: Irrational, because 1728 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Evaluating the components gives \(\sqrt{225} = 15\) and \(\sqrt[3]{1728} = 12\). Their difference is \(15 - 12 = 3\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the value of the expression is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{400} \times \sqrt[3]{0.008}\).
d: Irrational, because 0.008 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Evaluate each part: \(\sqrt{400} = 20\) and \(\sqrt[3]{0.008} = 0.2\) since \(0.2^3 = 0.008\). Multiplying them gives \(20 \times 0.2 = 4\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{49\,000}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 49,000 is not a perfect square
qs.s: Factoring gives \(49\,000 = 49 \times 10^3\); since the power of 10 has an odd exponent, \(49\,000\) is not a perfect square. Thus, \(\sqrt{49\,000} = 70\sqrt{10}\) is an irrational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{216000}\).
qs.s: Since \(6^3 = 216\) and \(10^3 = 1000\), \((60)^3 = 216000\), which means \(\sqrt[3]{216000} = 60\). Because 60 is an integer, the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{8}{25}}\).
qs.s: Taking square roots gives \(\frac{\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{\sqrt{8}}{5}\). Because 8 is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{8}\) is irrational, so the entire expression is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{48}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 48 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Since \(3^3 = 27\) and \(4^3 = 64\), 48 is not a perfect cube. Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{48}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{90}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 90 is not a perfect cube
qs.s: Since \(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\), 90 is not a perfect cube. Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{90}\) cannot be simplified to an integer and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.08}\).
qs.a: Irrational, because 0.08 is not a perfect cube
d: Rational, because 8 is a perfect cube
qs.s: Although 8 is a perfect cube, 0.08 has only two decimal places rather than a multiple of 3 (note that \(0.2^3 = 0.008\)). Since \(0.4^3 = 0.064\) and \(0.5^3 = 0.125\), 0.08 is not a perfect cube, making \(\sqrt[3]{0.08}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{3375}\).
d: Irrational, because 3375 is not a perfect cube
Irrational, because 3375 is an odd number
qs.s: Testing values between 10 and 20 that end in 5 gives \(15^3 = 15 \times 15 \times 15 = 3375\). Since \(\sqrt[3]{3375} = 15\) is an integer, it is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.027}\).
qs.s: Since \(0.3^3 = 0.027\), the cube root is \(0.3 = \frac{3}{10}\). Because it can be expressed as a fraction of integers, it is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{125000}\).
qs.s: Since \(125 = 5^3\) and \(1000 = 10^3\), we have \(125{,}000 = 50^3\). Thus, \(\sqrt[3]{125000} = 50\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{4000}\).
qs.s: While \(4 = 2^2\) is a perfect square, 4000 has an odd number of zeros, meaning it is not a perfect square. Therefore, \(\sqrt{4000}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{21600000}\).
qs.s: Although \(216 = 6^3\), the number \(21{,}600{,}000\) has 5 trailing zeros, which is not divisible by 3. Therefore, \(21{,}600{,}000\) is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{21600000}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{16}{250}}\).
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction inside the radical gives \(\frac{16}{250} = \frac{8}{125}\). Taking the cube root of the numerator and denominator yields \(\frac{2}{5}\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{5^2 + 7^2}\).
qs.s: Evaluating the radicand gives \(5^2 + 7^2 = 25 + 49 = 74\). Since 74 is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{74}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{25 \times 40}\).
qs.s: Multiplying the terms under the radical gives \(25 \times 40 = 1000\). Since \(10^3 = 1000\), \(\sqrt[3]{1000} = 10\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.00000081}\).
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{64\,000}\)
qs.s: Since \(40^3 = 64\,000\), \(\sqrt[3]{64\,000} = 40\), which is an integer and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{36\,000}\)
qs.s: While \(1000 = 10^3\) is a perfect cube, 36 is a perfect square (\(6^2\)) and not a perfect cube (\(3^3 = 27, 4^3 = 64\)), so \(\sqrt[3]{36\,000}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(-\sqrt[3]{16\,000\,000}\)
qs.s: Writing the radicand as \(16 \times 10^6\), the factor \(10^6 = (10^2)^3\) is a perfect cube, but 16 is not a perfect cube (\(2^3 = 8, 3^3 = 27\)). Therefore, \(-\sqrt[3]{16\,000\,000}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{54}{250}}\)
qs.s: Simplifying the fraction by dividing numerator and denominator by 2 yields \(\frac{27}{125}\). Since \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) and \(\sqrt[3]{125} = 5\), \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{54}{250}} = \frac{3}{5}\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.00027}\)
qs.s: Writing the decimal as a fraction gives \(\frac{27}{100\,000}\); although \(27 = 3^3\), \(100\,000 = 10^5\) is not a perfect cube because the exponent 5 is not divisible by 3, making \(\sqrt[3]{0.00027}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{3^3 + 4^3 + 5^3}\)
qs.s: Evaluating the sum inside the radicand gives \(27 + 64 + 125 = 216\). Since \(6^3 = 216\), \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{500 \times 16}\)
qs.s: Multiplying under the radical gives \(500 \times 16 = 8000\). Since \(20^3 = 8000\), \(\sqrt[3]{8000} = 20\), which is a rational number.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.008}\).
qs.s: Writing \(0.008\) as \(\frac{8}{1000}\), both \(8\) and \(1000\) are perfect cubes (\(2^3 = 8\) and \(10^3 = 1000\)), so \(\sqrt[3]{0.008} = \frac{2}{10} = 0.2\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.25 - 0.09}\).
qs.s: Subtracting inside the radical first gives \(\sqrt{0.25 - 0.09} = \sqrt{0.16} = 0.4\). Since \(0.4 = \frac{2}{5}\) is a ratio of integers, it is rational (note that radicals cannot be distributed across subtraction, so it does not equal \(0.5 - 0.3\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{9}}\).
qs.s: Finding a common denominator and adding gives \(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{9} = \frac{9 + 4}{36} = \frac{13}{36}\). Since \(13\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{\frac{13}{36}} = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{6}\) is irrational (note that the radical cannot be distributed to give \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{6}\)).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.00009}\).
qs.s: Writing \(0.00009\) as \(\frac{9}{100000}\), the numerator \(9\) is a perfect square, but the denominator \(100000 = 10^5\) is not a perfect square because the exponent of \(10\) is odd. Therefore, \(\sqrt{0.00009}\) is irrational (note that \(0.003^2 = 0.000009\), which has \(6\) decimal places).

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{1 - \frac{19}{27}}\).
qs.s: Subtracting inside the cube root gives \(1 - \frac{19}{27} = \frac{8}{27}\). Since both \(8\) and \(27\) are perfect cubes, \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{8}{27}} = \frac{2}{3}\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt[3]{0.64}\)
qs.s: Write \(0.64\) as \(\frac{64}{100}\). Although \(64 = 4^3\) is a perfect cube, the denominator \(100\) is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.64}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt[3]{0.027}\)
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt{0.4}\)
qs.s: We can write \(0.4\) as \(\frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}\). Since neither 2 nor 5 is a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.4}\) cannot be written as a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt{0.009}\)
qs.s: Write \(0.009\) as \(\frac{9}{1000}\). While \(9 = 3^2\) is a perfect square, \(1000\) is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{0.009}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt{0.0049}\)
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt{0.2} \times \sqrt{0.8}\)
qs.s: Multiply under a single radical to get \(\sqrt{0.2 \times 0.8} = \sqrt{0.16}\). Since \((0.4)^2 = 0.16\), the value is \(0.4\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt[3]{2700000}\)
qs.s: Write \(2700000\) as \(27 \times 10^5\). Although \(27 = 3^3\), \(10^5\) has 5 zeros (not a multiple of 3), so \(2700000\) is not a perfect cube and the number is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{0.16}{2}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the fraction inside the radical: \(\frac{0.16}{2} = 0.08 = \frac{8}{100}\). While \(8 = 2^3\) is a perfect cube, the denominator \(100\) is not, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.08}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt{1.44} - \sqrt[3]{0.064}\)
qs.s: Evaluate each radical: \(\sqrt{1.44} = 1.2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{0.064} = 0.4\). Subtracting gives \(1.2 - 0.4 = 0.8\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational (state its value if rational): \(\sqrt{0.16 + 0.09}\)
qs.s: Add the terms under the radical first: \(0.16 + 0.09 = 0.25\). Since \((0.5)^2 = 0.25\), \(\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{\frac{0.08}{0.18}}\).
qs.s: Simplify the fraction under the radical by multiplying the numerator and denominator by \(100\) and reducing: \(\frac{0.08}{0.18} = \frac{8}{18} = \frac{4}{9}\). Taking the square root gives \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{0.81} - \sqrt[3]{0.027}\).
qs.s: Evaluate each radical separately: \(\sqrt{0.81} = 0.9\) and \(\sqrt[3]{0.027} = 0.3\). Subtracting gives \(0.9 - 0.3 = 0.6\), which is a terminating decimal and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.0064}\).
qs.s: Write \(0.0064\) as the fraction \(\frac{64}{10\,000}\), so \(\sqrt[3]{0.0064} = \frac{4}{\sqrt[3]{10\,000}}\). Because \(10\,000\) is not a perfect cube, this number cannot be written as a ratio of integers and is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt{1 - 0.36}\).
qs.s: Evaluate the subtraction under the radical first: \(1 - 0.36 = 0.64\). Since \(\sqrt{0.64} = \sqrt{\frac{64}{100}} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8\), the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.000216}\).
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.00027}\).
qs.s: Write \(0.00027\) as \(\frac{27}{100\,000}\). Because \(100\,000 = 10^5\) has an exponent not divisible by \(3\), it is not a perfect cube, so \(\sqrt[3]{0.00027}\) is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.027}\).
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt{0.000081}\).
Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt{0.00016}\).
qs.s: Write \(0.00016\) as \(\frac{16}{100\,000}\). Since \(100\,000\) has \(5\) zeros (an odd number), it is not a perfect square, making \(\sqrt{0.00016}\) irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt{0.009}\).
qs.s: Write \(0.009\) as the fraction \(\frac{9}{1000}\). Since \(1000\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.009} = \frac{3}{10\sqrt{10}}\), which is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt{\frac{0.032}{0.5}}\).
qs.s: Simplifying the division gives \(\frac{0.032}{0.5} = 0.064 = \frac{64}{1000}\). Since \(1000\) is not a perfect square, \(\sqrt{0.064} = \frac{8}{10\sqrt{10}}\), which is irrational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt{0.0064} + \sqrt[3]{0.008}\).
qs.s: Evaluate each radical: \(\sqrt{0.0064} = 0.08\) and \(\sqrt[3]{0.008} = 0.2\). Their sum is \(0.08 + 0.2 = 0.28\), which is a terminating decimal and therefore rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt[3]{0.000000064}\).
qs.s: Write the decimal as \(\frac{64}{10^9}\). Since \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\) and \(\sqrt[3]{10^9} = 10^3 = 1000\), the cube root is \(\frac{4}{1000} = 0.004\), which is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt{\frac{0.08}{0.18}}\).
qs.s: Multiply the numerator and denominator by \(100\) to get \(\frac{8}{18}\), then divide both by \(2\) to simplify to \(\frac{4}{9}\). Since \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} = \frac{2}{3}\), the number is rational.

qs.q: Without a calculator, decide if the number is rational or irrational, and evaluate it if rational: \(\sqrt[3]{270\,000\,000}\).
qs.s: Write \(270\,000\,000\) as \(27 \times 10^7\). While \(27 = 3^3\) is a perfect cube, \(10^7\) is not because \(7\) is not divisible by \(3\), so the cube root is irrational.

qs.q: Using a calculator, approximate the irrational number to 2 decimal places: \(\sqrt[3]{29}\).
qs.s: Evaluating \(\sqrt[3]{29}\) on a calculator gives approximately \(3.0723\). Rounding to two decimal places yields \(3.07\).

qs.q: Using a calculator, approximate the irrational number to 2 decimal places: \(\sqrt{13.4}\).
qs.s: Evaluating \(\sqrt{13.4}\) on a calculator gives approximately \(3.6606\). Rounding to two decimal places yields \(3.66\).

qs.q: Using a calculator, approximate the irrational number to 2 decimal places: \(\sqrt[3]{6.5}\).
qs.s: Evaluating \(\sqrt[3]{6.5}\) on a calculator gives approximately \(1.8663\). Rounding to two decimal places yields \(1.87\).

qs.q: Using a calculator, approximate the irrational number to 2 decimal places: \(\sqrt{0.85}\).
qs.s: Evaluating \(\sqrt{0.85}\) on a calculator gives approximately \(0.92195\). Rounding to two decimal places yields \(0.92\).

qs.q: Using a calculator, approximate the irrational number to 2 decimal places: \(\sqrt{5.6}\).
qs.s: Evaluating \(\sqrt{5.6}\) on a calculator gives approximately \(2.3664\). Rounding to two decimal places yields \(2.37\).
