qs.q: Given \(\sqrt[3]{25} \doteq 2.92\), \(\sqrt[3]{250} \doteq 6.30\), and \(\sqrt[3]{2500} \doteq 13.57\), determine the value of the expression: \(\sqrt[3]{0.00025} - \sqrt[3]{0.000025}\).

exercises.name: Estimating Irrational Numbers on a Number Line

qs.q: Between which two consecutive integers on a number line does \(-\sqrt{39}\) lie?
qs.s: Since \(6^2 = 36\) and \(7^2 = 49\), we have \(6 < \sqrt{39} < 7\). Multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the inequality to \(-7 < -\sqrt{39} < -6\), so \(-\sqrt{39}\) lies between \(-7\) and \(-6\).

qs.q: Between which two consecutive integers on a number line does \(-\sqrt[3]{115}\) lie?
qs.s: Since \(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\), we have \(4 < \sqrt[3]{115} < 5\). Negating the inequality gives \(-5 < -\sqrt[3]{115} < -4\), so \(-\sqrt[3]{115}\) lies between \(-5\) and \(-4\).

qs.q: Between which two consecutive integers on a number line does \(-\sqrt{2.8}\) lie?
qs.s: Since \(1^2 = 1\) and \(2^2 = 4\), we have \(1 < \sqrt{2.8} < 2\). Multiplying by \(-1\) gives \(-2 < -\sqrt{2.8} < -1\), so \(-\sqrt{2.8}\) lies between \(-2\) and \(-1\).

qs.q: Between which two consecutive integers on a number line does \(\sqrt[3]{68}\) lie?
qs.s: Since \(4^3 = 64\) and \(5^3 = 125\), we have \(64 < 68 < 125\), which gives \(4 < \sqrt[3]{68} < 5\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{68}\) lies between \(4\) and \(5\).

qs.q: Between which two consecutive integers on a number line does \(\sqrt{19}\) lie?
qs.s: Since \(4^2 = 16\) and \(5^2 = 25\), we have \(16 < 19 < 25\), which means \(4 < \sqrt{19} < 5\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{19}\) lies between \(4\) and \(5\).

qs.q: Between which two consecutive integers on a number line does \(6 + \sqrt{45}\) lie?

qs.q: Without using the root functions of a calculator, approximate the irrational number to one decimal place: \(\sqrt{22}\).
qs.s: Since \(4^2 = 16\) and \(5^2 = 25\), 22 is 6 units from 16 and 3 units from 25. Using the ratio \(\frac{6}{6+3} = \frac{6}{9} \approx 0.7\), we approximate \(\sqrt{22} \approx 4.7\).

exercises.name: Ordering Irrational Numbers on a Number Line

qs.q: When the irrational numbers \(\sqrt{15}, \pi, -\sqrt{32}, -\sqrt{21}, \sqrt{8}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the middle (third)?
qs.s: Comparing the negative values gives \(-\sqrt{32} < -\sqrt{21} < 0\), while comparing the positives gives \(\sqrt{8} < 3 < \pi < \sqrt{15} < 4\). The complete order from least to greatest is \(-\sqrt{32}, -\sqrt{21}, \sqrt{8}, \pi, \sqrt{15}\), so \(\sqrt{8}\) is the middle number.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{28}, \sqrt{17}, -\sqrt{35}, \pi, \sqrt{7}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is fourth?
qs.s: Comparing values gives \(-\sqrt{35} < -\sqrt{28} < 0\) for the negatives and \(\sqrt{7} < 3 < \pi \approx 3.14 < 4 < \sqrt{17}\) for the positives. In increasing order, the list is \(-\sqrt{35}, -\sqrt{28}, \sqrt{7}, \pi, \sqrt{17}\), so the fourth number is \(\pi\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{40}, \sqrt{13}, -\sqrt{45}, \sqrt{26}, \pi\) are placed on a number line, which number is fourth from left to right?
qs.s: Arranging from least to greatest gives \(-\sqrt{45}, -\sqrt{40}, \pi, \sqrt{13}, \sqrt{26}\) because \(-\sqrt{45} < -\sqrt{40} < 0 < \pi \approx 3.14 < \sqrt{13} \approx 3.61 < \sqrt{26} \approx 5.10\). Therefore, the fourth number is \(\sqrt{13}\).

qs.q: When the irrational numbers \(\sqrt{20}, -\sqrt{14}, \pi, -\sqrt{19}, \sqrt{11}\) are arranged in order from least to greatest, which number is second?
qs.s: Since \(19 > 14\), we have \(-\sqrt{19} < -\sqrt{14} < 0\), and for the positives, \(0 < \pi \approx 3.14 < \sqrt{11} \approx 3.32 < \sqrt{20} \approx 4.47\). The numbers in order are \(-\sqrt{19}, -\sqrt{14}, \pi, \sqrt{11}, \sqrt{20}\), so the second number is \(-\sqrt{14}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{23}, -\sqrt{13}, \sqrt{5}, -\sqrt{18}, \pi\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the middle (third)?
qs.s: The negative numbers order as \(-\sqrt{18} < -\sqrt{13} < 0\), and the positive numbers order as \(\sqrt{5} < 3 < \pi < 4 < \sqrt{23}\). The complete order is \(-\sqrt{18}, -\sqrt{13}, \sqrt{5}, \pi, \sqrt{23}\), making \(\sqrt{5}\) the middle number.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{55}, -\sqrt[3]{90}, \pi, -\sqrt{40}, \sqrt[3]{70}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is second?
qs.s: For the negatives, \(-\sqrt{40} \in (-7, -6)\) and \(-\sqrt[3]{90} \in (-5, -4)\), so \(-\sqrt{40} < -\sqrt[3]{90} < 0\). The positives satisfy \(3 < \pi < 4 < \sqrt[3]{70} < 5 < 7 < \sqrt{55} < 8\), giving the full order \(-\sqrt{40}, -\sqrt[3]{90}, \pi, \sqrt[3]{70}, \sqrt{55}\), so the second number is \(-\sqrt[3]{90}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{80}, \sqrt{70}, -\sqrt{95}, \sqrt[3]{20}, -\pi, \pi\) are placed on a number line, which number is third from the left?
qs.s: The negative values order as \(-\sqrt{95} \approx -9.7 < -\sqrt{80} \approx -8.9 < -\pi \approx -3.14 < 0\), while the positives are \(\sqrt[3]{20} < 3 < \pi < \sqrt{70} \approx 8.4\). From left to right, the sequence begins \(-\sqrt{95}, -\sqrt{80}, -\pi\), so the third number is \(-\pi\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(2\pi, -\sqrt{110}, \sqrt{130}, -\sqrt{150}, \sqrt[3]{100}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the middle (third)?
qs.s: Estimating each value between consecutive integers yields \(-\sqrt{150} \in (-13, -12)\), \(-\sqrt{110} \in (-11, -10)\), \(\sqrt[3]{100} \in (4, 5)\), \(2\pi \approx 6.28 \in (6, 7)\), and \(\sqrt{130} \in (11, 12)\). Ordering gives \(-\sqrt{150}, -\sqrt{110}, \sqrt[3]{100}, 2\pi, \sqrt{130}\), so \(\sqrt[3]{100}\) is the middle number.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{52}, \sqrt[3]{60}, -\sqrt[3]{200}, \pi, \sqrt{45}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the middle (third)?
qs.s: Bounding by integers gives \(-\sqrt{52} \in (-8, -7)\), \(-\sqrt[3]{200} \in (-6, -5)\), \(\pi \approx 3.14\), \(\sqrt[3]{60} \in (3, 4)\) (with \(\pi^3 \approx 31 < 60\)), and \(\sqrt{45} \in (6, 7)\). Thus, the ordered list is \(-\sqrt{52}, -\sqrt[3]{200}, \pi, \sqrt[3]{60}, \sqrt{45}\), and \(\pi\) is in the middle.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt[3]{250}, -\sqrt{60}, \sqrt{85}, -\pi, \sqrt[3]{500}\) are arranged in order from least to greatest, which number is fourth?
qs.s: Using integer benchmarks, \(-\sqrt{60} \in (-8, -7)\), \(-\sqrt[3]{250} \in (-7, -6)\), \(-\pi \in (-4, -3)\), \(\sqrt[3]{500} \in (7, 8)\), and \(\sqrt{85} \in (9, 10)\). The values in increasing order are \(-\sqrt{60}, -\sqrt[3]{250}, -\pi, \sqrt[3]{500}, \sqrt{85}\), so the fourth number is \(\sqrt[3]{500}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{28}\), \(\sqrt{5}\), \(\pi\), \(\sqrt[3]{100}\), and \(\sqrt{60}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the fourth position?
qs.s: Finding the integer bounds for each number gives \(-\sqrt{28} \in (-6, -5)\), \(\sqrt{5} \in (2, 3)\), \(\pi \in (3, 4)\), \(\sqrt[3]{100} \in (4, 5)\), and \(\sqrt{60} \in (7, 8)\). In increasing order, the numbers are \(-\sqrt{28} < \sqrt{5} < \pi < \sqrt[3]{100} < \sqrt{60}\), so the fourth number is \(\sqrt[3]{100}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt[3]{10}\), \(\sqrt{10}\), \(e\), \(\sqrt[3]{300}\), and \(-\sqrt{40}\) are arranged from least to greatest, which number is the least (farthest to the left on a number line)?
qs.s: Since \(6^2 = 36 < 40 < 49 = 7^2\), we have \(-\sqrt{40} \approx -6.3\), while \(2^3 = 8 < 10 < 27 = 3^3\) gives \(-\sqrt[3]{10} \approx -2.2\). Comparing all values, \(-\sqrt{40} < -\sqrt[3]{10} < e < \sqrt{10} < \sqrt[3]{300}\), making \(-\sqrt{40}\) the least.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{67}\), \(-\sqrt[3]{75}\), \(\sqrt[3]{25}\), \(\pi\), and \(\sqrt{135}\) are placed on a number line from left to right, which number is in the middle (third position)?
qs.s: Approximating each value gives \(-\sqrt[3]{75} \approx -4.2\), \(\sqrt[3]{25} \approx 2.9\), \(\pi \approx 3.14\), \(\sqrt{67} \approx 8.2\), and \(\sqrt{135} \approx 11.6\). Ordered from least to greatest, the numbers are \(-\sqrt[3]{75} < \sqrt[3]{25} < \pi < \sqrt{67} < \sqrt{135}\), so \(\pi\) is in the middle position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{50}\), \(e\), \(\sqrt[3]{220}\), \(-\sqrt[3]{50}\), and \(\sqrt{17}\) are plotted on a number line from left to right, which number is in the second position?
qs.s: Approximating each value between consecutive integers gives \(-\sqrt[3]{50} \approx -3.7\), \(e \approx 2.7\), \(\sqrt{17} \approx 4.1\), \(\sqrt[3]{220} \approx 6.0\), and \(\sqrt{50} \approx 7.1\). Ordered from least to greatest, the list is \(-\sqrt[3]{50} < e < \sqrt{17} < \sqrt[3]{220} < \sqrt{50}\), so \(e\) is in the second position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{38}\), \(\pi\), \(\sqrt[3]{70}\), \(-\sqrt{15}\), and \(\sqrt{85}\) are arranged in order from least to greatest, which number is in the middle (third position)?
qs.s: Approximating each value gives \(-\sqrt{15} \approx -3.9\), \(\pi \approx 3.1\), \(\sqrt[3]{70} \approx 4.1\), \(\sqrt{38} \approx 6.2\), and \(\sqrt{85} \approx 9.2\). In increasing order, the numbers are \(-\sqrt{15} < \pi < \sqrt[3]{70} < \sqrt{38} < \sqrt{85}\), so \(\sqrt[3]{70}\) is in the middle.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{50}\), \(\sqrt[3]{350}\), \(2\pi\), \(-\sqrt[3]{150}\), and \(\sqrt{30}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the fourth position?
qs.s: Approximating gives \(-\sqrt[3]{150} \approx -5.3\), \(\sqrt{30} \approx 5.5\), and \(2\pi \approx 6.3\). Since \((\sqrt[3]{350})^6 = 350^2 = 122{,}500\) and \((\sqrt{50})^6 = 50^3 = 125{,}000\), we have \(\sqrt[3]{350} < \sqrt{50}\), placing \(\sqrt[3]{350}\) in the fourth position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{150}\), \(-\sqrt[3]{1700}\), \(\sqrt[3]{900}\), \(\sqrt{200}\), and \(3e\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the second position?
qs.s: For the negative numbers, \(12^2 = 144 < 150 \implies -\sqrt{150} \approx -12.2\), while \(12^3 = 1728 > 1700 \implies -\sqrt[3]{1700} \approx -11.9\), so \(-\sqrt{150} < -\sqrt[3]{1700}\). Since the positive values are all greater, \(-\sqrt[3]{1700}\) is in the second position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{60}\), \(\sqrt{28}\), \(\sqrt[3]{700}\), \(\sqrt{80}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{1100}\) are arranged from least to greatest, which number is in the middle (third position)?
qs.s: Comparing the two numbers between 8 and 9 by their 6th powers gives \((\sqrt[3]{700})^6 = 490{,}000\) and \((\sqrt{80})^6 = 512{,}000\), so \(\sqrt[3]{700} < \sqrt{80}\). In increasing order, \(-\sqrt{60} < \sqrt{28} < \sqrt[3]{700} < \sqrt{80} < \sqrt[3]{1100}\), so \(\sqrt[3]{700}\) is in the middle.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{45}\), \(\sqrt[3]{150}\), \(\sqrt{32}\), \(2\pi\), and \(\sqrt{90}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the third position?
qs.s: Both \(\sqrt[3]{150}\) and \(\sqrt{32}\) lie between 5 and 6, but \((\sqrt[3]{150})^6 = 150^2 = 22{,}500\) while \((\sqrt{32})^6 = 32^3 = 32{,}768\), showing \(\sqrt[3]{150} < \sqrt{32}\). The ordered set is \(-\sqrt{45} < \sqrt[3]{150} < \sqrt{32} < 2\pi < \sqrt{90}\), placing \(\sqrt{32}\) in the third position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{85}\), \(-\sqrt[3]{600}\), \(\sqrt[3]{75}\), \(\sqrt{21}\), and \(\sqrt{65}\) are arranged from least to greatest, which number is in the fourth position?
qs.s: Both \(\sqrt[3]{75}\) and \(\sqrt{21}\) lie between 4 and 5; comparing their 6th powers gives \(75^2 = 5625 < 21^3 = 9261\), so \(\sqrt[3]{75} < \sqrt{21}\). The full increasing order is \(-\sqrt{85} < -\sqrt[3]{600} < \sqrt[3]{75} < \sqrt{21} < \sqrt{65}\), which places \(\sqrt{21}\) in the fourth position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{7}, \sqrt[3]{7}, -\sqrt{18}, -\sqrt[3]{18}, \sqrt{35}, \sqrt[3]{35}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the fourth position?
qs.s: Bounding each radical between integers yields \(-\sqrt{18} \approx -4.2\), \(-\sqrt[3]{18} \approx -2.6\), \(\sqrt[3]{7} \approx 1.9\), \(\sqrt{7} \approx 2.6\), \(\sqrt[3]{35} \approx 3.3\), and \(\sqrt{35} \approx 5.9\). In order from least to greatest, the fourth value is \(\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt[3]{2}, -\sqrt{11}, -\sqrt[3]{11}, \sqrt{22}, \sqrt[3]{22}\) are placed on a number line from left to right, which number appears immediately to the left of \(\sqrt{2}\)?
qs.s: Arranging the numbers from least to greatest yields \(-\sqrt{11} \approx -3.32\), \(-\sqrt[3]{11} \approx -2.22\), \(\sqrt[3]{2} \approx 1.26\), \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\), \(\sqrt[3]{22} \approx 2.80\), and \(\sqrt{22} \approx 4.69\). Therefore, \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is positioned immediately to the left of \(\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{12}, \sqrt[3]{12}, -\sqrt{19}, -\sqrt[3]{19}, \sqrt{30}, \sqrt[3]{30}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the fifth position?
qs.s: Both \(\sqrt[3]{30}\) and \(\sqrt{12}\) fall between 3 and 4, but comparing sixth powers shows \((\sqrt[3]{30})^6 = 30^2 = 900\) and \((\sqrt{12})^6 = 12^3 = 1728\), so \(\sqrt[3]{30} < \sqrt{12}\). The full order from least to greatest is \(-\sqrt{19}, -\sqrt[3]{19}, \sqrt[3]{12}, \sqrt[3]{30}, \sqrt{12}, \sqrt{30}\), placing \(\sqrt{12}\) fifth.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{6}, \sqrt[3]{6}, -\sqrt{15}, -\sqrt[3]{15}, \sqrt{29}, \sqrt[3]{29}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the third position?
qs.s: Approximating each value using consecutive integer bounds gives \(-\sqrt{15} \approx -3.9\), \(-\sqrt[3]{15} \approx -2.5\), \(\sqrt[3]{6} \approx 1.8\), \(\sqrt{6} \approx 2.4\), \(\sqrt[3]{29} \approx 3.1\), and \(\sqrt{29} \approx 5.4\). Ordering from least to greatest places \(\sqrt[3]{6}\) in the third position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{3}, \sqrt[3]{3}, -\sqrt{12}, -\sqrt[3]{12}, \sqrt{20}, \sqrt[3]{20}\) are placed on a number line, which number lies between \(-3\) and \(-2\)?
qs.s: Since \(2^3 = 8 < 12 < 27 = 3^3\), we have \(2 < \sqrt[3]{12} < 3\), which means \(-3 < -\sqrt[3]{12} < -2\). The square root \(-\sqrt{12}\) lies between \(-4\) and \(-3\), so \(-\sqrt[3]{12}\) is the only number in the interval \((-3, -2)\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{12}, -\pi, -\sqrt[3]{35}, \sqrt{8}, \sqrt[3]{25}, \pi\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the fourth position?
qs.s: Approximating gives \(-\sqrt{12} \approx -3.46\), \(-\sqrt[3]{35} \approx -3.27\), \(-\pi \approx -3.14\), \(\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83\) (since \(8^3 = 512 < 25^2 = 625\)), \(\sqrt[3]{25} \approx 2.92\), and \(\pi \approx 3.14\). The fourth number in the ordered sequence is \(\sqrt{8}\).

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{150}, \sqrt[3]{150}, -\sqrt{200}, -\sqrt[3]{200}, \sqrt{350}, \sqrt[3]{350}\) are ordered from least to greatest on a number line, which number is in the fourth position?
qs.s: Estimating each root using perfect squares and cubes gives \(-\sqrt{200} \approx -14.1\), \(-\sqrt[3]{200} \approx -5.8\), \(\sqrt[3]{150} \approx 5.3\), \(\sqrt[3]{350} \approx 7.0\), \(\sqrt{150} \approx 12.2\), and \(\sqrt{350} \approx 18.7\). From least to greatest, \(\sqrt[3]{350}\) is in the fourth position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(-\sqrt{60}, -\sqrt[3]{500}, \sqrt{75}, \sqrt[3]{75}, -\sqrt{20}, \sqrt[3]{300}\) are arranged in order from least to greatest, which number is in the second position?
qs.s: Both \(-\sqrt[3]{500}\) and \(-\sqrt{60}\) lie between \(-8\) and \(-7\), but \((\sqrt[3]{500})^6 = 500^2 = 250000\) exceeds \((\sqrt{60})^6 = 60^3 = 216000\), which means \(-\sqrt[3]{500} < -\sqrt{60}\). Ordering all values produces \(-\sqrt[3]{500}, -\sqrt{60}, -\sqrt{20}, \sqrt[3]{75}, \sqrt[3]{300}, \sqrt{75}\), so \(-\sqrt{60}\) is in the second position.

qs.q: When the expressions \(1 - \sqrt{10}, -\sqrt[3]{9}, -\sqrt{2}, 5 - \sqrt[3]{30}, \sqrt[3]{70} - 1, 2 + \sqrt{5}\) are arranged from least to greatest on a number line, which number is in the third position?
qs.s: Approximating each term gives \(1 - \sqrt{10} \approx -2.16\), \(-\sqrt[3]{9} \approx -2.08\), \(-\sqrt{2} \approx -1.41\), \(5 - \sqrt[3]{30} \approx 1.89\), \(\sqrt[3]{70} - 1 \approx 3.12\), and \(2 + \sqrt{5} \approx 4.24\). Arranged from least to greatest, \(-\sqrt{2}\) occupies the third position.

qs.q: When the numbers \(\sqrt{14}, \sqrt[3]{45}, -\sqrt{14}, -\sqrt[3]{45}, \sqrt{50}, -\sqrt[3]{100}\) are ordered from least to greatest, which number is in the third position?
qs.s: Both \(-\sqrt{14}\) and \(-\sqrt[3]{45}\) lie between \(-4\) and \(-3\); since \((\sqrt{14})^6 = 14^3 = 2744\) is greater than \((\sqrt[3]{45})^6 = 45^2 = 2025\), we have \(\sqrt{14} > \sqrt[3]{45}\) and thus \(-\sqrt{14} < -\sqrt[3]{45}\). The ordered list is \(-\sqrt[3]{100}, -\sqrt{14}, -\sqrt[3]{45}, \sqrt[3]{45}, \sqrt{14}, \sqrt{50}\), making \(-\sqrt[3]{45}\) the third number.

exercises.name: Multiply powers with the same base

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5^3 \times 5^5\)
qs.s: Using the product rule \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), add the exponents: \(5^3 \times 5^5 = 5^{3+5} = 5^8\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(3^2 \times 3^4\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the exponents while keeping the base the same: \(3^2 \times 3^4 = 3^{2+4} = 3^6\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(4^3 \times 4^6\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the exponents: \(4^3 \times 4^6 = 4^{3+6} = 4^9\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(7^4 \times 7^5\)
qs.s: Keep the base of \(7\) and add the exponents: \(7^4 \times 7^5 = 7^{4+5} = 7^9\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(6^5 \times 6^6\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule for exponents: \(6^5 \times 6^6 = 6^{5+6} = 6^{11}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(y^4 \times y \times y^5 \times y^7\)
qs.s: Rewrite \(y\) as \(y^1\) and add the exponents using the product rule: \(y^4 \times y^1 \times y^5 \times y^7 = y^{4+1+5+7} = y^{17}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(3^7 \times 3^4 \times 3^8\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add all three exponents together: \(3^7 \times 3^4 \times 3^8 = 3^{7+4+8} = 3^{19}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(4^{2x} \times 4^{5x} \times 4^x\)
qs.s: Since \(4^x = 4^{1x}\), use the product rule to add the exponents: \(4^{2x} \times 4^{5x} \times 4^{1x} = 4^{2x+5x+1x} = 4^{8x}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(2^{16} \times 2^{25} \times 2^{31}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding the exponents: \(2^{16} \times 2^{25} \times 2^{31} = 2^{16+25+31} = 2^{72}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5 \times 5^3 \times 5^6 \times 5^4\)
qs.s: Write \(5\) as \(5^1\) and apply the product rule by adding all the exponents: \(5^1 \times 5^3 \times 5^6 \times 5^4 = 5^{1+3+6+4} = 5^{14}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(2^4 \times 2^6\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the base the same and add the exponents: \(2^4 \times 2^6 = 2^{4+6} = 2^{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(7^2 \times 7^5\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the base the same and add the exponents: \(7^2 \times 7^5 = 7^{2+5} = 7^7\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(6^6 \times 6^3\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the base the same and add the exponents: \(6^6 \times 6^3 = 6^{6+3} = 6^9\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5^3 \times 5^8\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the base the same and add the exponents: \(5^3 \times 5^8 = 5^{3+8} = 5^{11}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(10^4 \times 10^5\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the base the same and add the exponents: \(10^4 \times 10^5 = 10^{4+5} = 10^9\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5^{11} \times 5^{24} \times 5^6 \times 5^{13}\)
qs.s: Keep the base 5 and find the sum of all four exponents: \(5^{11+24+6+13} = 5^{54}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(7 \times 7^5 \times 7^0 \times 7^8\)
qs.s: Recall that \(7 = 7^1\) and \(7^0\) contributes \(0\) to the sum of exponents: \(7^{1+5+0+8} = 7^{14}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^4 \times \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^3 \times \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^5\)
qs.s: Keep the common fraction base and add the exponents together: \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{4+3+5} = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{12}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(2^{14} \times 2^8 \times 2^{11}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule across all three factors by keeping the base and adding the exponents: \(2^{14+8+11} = 2^{33}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-4)^3 \times (-4) \times (-4)^5\)
qs.s: Rewrite the middle factor as \((-4)^1\) and add the exponents: \((-4)^{3+1+5} = (-4)^9\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(7^5 \times 7^{-8}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents while keeping the base the same: \(5 + (-8) = -3\). Thus, the answer is \(7^{-3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(2^{-2} \times 2^6\)
qs.s: Keep the base 2 and add the exponents: \(-2 + 6 = 4\). Therefore, the answer is \(2^4\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(3^{-5} \times 3^4\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the exponents: \(-5 + 4 = -1\). The simplified expression is \(3^{-1}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5^{-4} \times 5^2\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by keeping the base 5 and adding the exponents: \(-4 + 2 = -2\). The result is \(5^{-2}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(6^2 \times 6^{-5}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(2 + (-5) = -3\). The result is \(6^{-3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(12^{-15} \times 12^{23} \times 12^{-11}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents for the common base 12: \(-15 + 23 + (-11) = -3\). This simplifies to \(12^{-3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(10^{-12} \times 10^{25} \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{-2}\)
qs.s: Add the four exponents using the product rule: \(-12 + 25 + (-8) + (-2) = 3\). The result is \(10^3\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(3^{-7} \times 3^4 \times 3^{-2}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule across all three factors by adding their exponents: \(-7 + 4 + (-2) = -5\). This gives \(3^{-5}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-4)^{-6} \times (-4)^9 \times (-4)^{-5}\)
qs.s: Keep the base \((-4)\) and add the exponents: \(-6 + 9 + (-5) = -2\). The result is \((-4)^{-2}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{-4} \times \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^7 \times \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{-1}\)
qs.s: Keep the fractional base \(\frac{2}{5}\) and add the exponents: \(-4 + 7 + (-1) = 2\). The answer is \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3 \times \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^0\)
qs.s: Add the exponents while keeping the fractional base the same: \(3 + 0 = 3\), resulting in \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(3^5 \times 3^0\)
qs.s: Add the exponents while keeping the base unchanged: \(5 + 0 = 5\), giving \(3^5\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(7^0 \times 7^4\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(0 + 4 = 4\). Keeping the base 7 gives \(7^4\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(10^0 \times 10^6\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the exponents: \(0 + 6 = 6\). The base remains 10, so the answer is \(10^6\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-2)^0 \times (-2)^5\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding the exponents: \(0 + 5 = 5\). The base remains \((-2)\), giving \((-2)^5\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(4^3 \times 4^0 \times 4^5 \times 4^2\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding all the exponents: \(3 + 0 + 5 + 2 = 10\). The base remains 4, yielding \(4^{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(10^{18} \times 10^0 \times 10^{27}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(18 + 0 + 27 = 45\). The base stays 10, giving \(10^{45}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(6^5 \times 6^{-2} \times 6^0 \times 6^4\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the exponents: \(5 + (-2) + 0 + 4 = 7\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \(6^7\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(2^{3x+4} \times 2^0 \times 2^{2x-1}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents by combining like terms: \((3x + 4) + 0 + (2x - 1) = 5x + 3\). This gives \(2^{5x+3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5^{\frac{2}{5}} \times 5^0 \times 5^{\frac{1}{2}}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents using a common denominator: \(\frac{2}{5} + 0 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{4}{10} + \frac{5}{10} = \frac{9}{10}\). In exponential form, this is \(5^{\frac{9}{10}}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(y^3 \times y \times y^7\)
qs.s: Express \(y\) as \(y^1\). By the product rule, add the exponents: \(3 + 1 + 7 = 11\), giving \(y^{11}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(x \times x^3 \times x^4\)
qs.s: Write \(x\) as \(x^1\) and add the exponents using the product rule: \(1 + 3 + 4 = 8\), so the result is \(x^8\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(m^5 \times m \times m^4\)
qs.s: Since \(m = m^1\), use the product rule to add the exponents: \(5 + 1 + 4 = 10\), giving \(m^{10}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(b^4 \times b^2 \times b\)
qs.s: Write \(b\) as \(b^1\). Add the exponents of the like bases: \(4 + 2 + 1 = 7\), yielding \(b^7\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(5 \times 5^2 \times 5^4\)
qs.s: Write the first factor as \(5^1\). Keep the base the same and add the exponents: \(1 + 2 + 4 = 7\), resulting in \(5^7\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(x \times x^{14} \times x^{23} \times x^{31}\)
qs.s: Write \(x\) as \(x^1\) and add all exponents together: \(1 + 14 + 23 + 31 = 69\), which gives \(x^{69}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(a^{4k-3} \times a \times a^{2k+7} \times a^{5k}\)
qs.s: Express \(a\) as \(a^1\) and combine the exponents: \((4k - 3) + 1 + (2k + 7) + 5k = 11k + 5\), giving \(a^{11k+5}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(y^{3n} \times y^{2n+5} \times y^{4n+1}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding the variable expressions in the exponents: \(3n + (2n + 5) + (4n + 1) = 9n + 6\), yielding \(y^{9n+6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(2^x \times 2^{3x+2} \times 2 \times 2^{4x-1}\)
qs.s: Write \(2\) as \(2^1\). Keep the base \(2\) and add all exponents: \(x + (3x + 2) + 1 + (4x - 1) = 8x + 2\), resulting in \(2^{8x+2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(3^8 \times 3^{15} \times 3 \times 3^{11} \times 3^4\)
qs.s: Write the middle factor \(3\) as \(3^1\). Keep the base \(3\) and sum the exponents: \(8 + 15 + 1 + 11 + 4 = 39\), giving \(3^{39}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(w^{-7} \times w^4 \times w\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(-7 + 4 + 1 = -2\). Thus, \(w^{-7} \times w^4 \times w = w^{-2}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(m^5 \times m^{-8} \times m\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(5 + (-8) + 1 = -2\). Thus, \(m^5 \times m^{-8} \times m = m^{-2}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(a^6 \times a^{-2} \times a\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(6 + (-2) + 1 = 5\). Thus, \(a^6 \times a^{-2} \times a = a^5\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(p^{-6} \times p^2 \times p\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(-6 + 2 + 1 = -3\). Thus, \(p^{-6} \times p^2 \times p = p^{-3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(x^{-4} \times x^7 \times x\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(-4 + 7 + 1 = 4\). Thus, \(x^{-4} \times x^7 \times x = x^4\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(c^{14} \times c^{-9} \times c \times c^{-11} \times c^2\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add all the exponents: \(14 + (-9) + 1 + (-11) + 2 = -3\). Therefore, the product is \(c^{-3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-12} \times \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^7 \times \left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \times \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2\)
qs.s: Since the bases are identical, apply the product rule by adding the exponents: \(-12 + 7 + 1 + 2 = -2\). The result is \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-2}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(k^{-15} \times k^{28} \times k \times k^{-6}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(-15 + 28 + 1 + (-6) = 8\). Therefore, the product is \(k^8\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-4)^{-8} \times (-4)^{15} \times (-4) \times (-4)^{-3}\)
qs.s: Since the bases are all \((-4)\), add the exponents using the product rule: \(-8 + 15 + 1 + (-3) = 5\). Thus, the result is \((-4)^5\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(z^{-23} \times z^{45} \times z \times z^{-18} \times z^{-9}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents of the like bases using the product rule: \(-23 + 45 + 1 + (-18) + (-9) = -4\). This gives \(z^{-4}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(2^0 \times 2^1 \times 2^5\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(0 + 1 + 5 = 6\). Therefore, \(2^0 \times 2^1 \times 2^5 = 2^6\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(10^0 \times 10^3 \times 10^4\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(0 + 3 + 4 = 7\). Therefore, \(10^0 \times 10^3 \times 10^4 = 10^7\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(5^0 \times 5^1 \times 5^3\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(0 + 1 + 3 = 4\). Therefore, \(5^0 \times 5^1 \times 5^3 = 5^4\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(6^1 \times 6^0 \times 6^4\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(1 + 0 + 4 = 5\). Therefore, \(6^1 \times 6^0 \times 6^4 = 6^5\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(9^2 \times 9^0 \times 9^1\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(2 + 0 + 1 = 3\). Therefore, \(9^2 \times 9^0 \times 9^1 = 9^3\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(3^{\frac{1}{4}} \times 3^{\frac{1}{2}} \times 3^{\frac{2}{3}}\)
qs.s: Find a common denominator of 12 to add the exponents: \(\frac{3}{12} + \frac{6}{12} + \frac{8}{12} = \frac{17}{12}\). Thus, the product is \(3^{\frac{17}{12}}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(4^{3n - 1} \times 4^{2n + 5} \times 4^{2 - 4n}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents by combining like terms: \((3n - 1) + (2n + 5) + (2 - 4n) = n + 6\). Therefore, the product is \(4^{n + 6}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(10^{\frac{3}{5}} \times 10^{-\frac{1}{2}} \times 10^{\frac{7}{10}}\)
qs.s: Using a common denominator of 10, add the exponents: \(\frac{6}{10} - \frac{5}{10} + \frac{7}{10} = \frac{8}{10} = \frac{4}{5}\). Thus, the product is \(10^{\frac{4}{5}}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{-2} \times \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^5 \times \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^0 \times \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{-1}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(-2 + 5 + 0 + (-1) = 2\). Therefore, the expression simplifies to \(\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(6^{-3} \times 6^5 \times 6^0 \times 6^{-4} \times 6^7\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add all exponents: \(-3 + 5 + 0 + (-4) + 7 = 5\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \(6^5\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(-\frac{4}{9}\right)^2 \times \left(-\frac{4}{9}\right)^7\)
qs.s: Using the product rule \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), keep the base and add the exponents: \(\left(-\frac{4}{9}\right)^{2+7} = \left(-\frac{4}{9}\right)^9\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^5 \times \left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^3\)
qs.s: Using the product rule \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), keep the base and add the exponents: \(\left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^{5+3} = \left(\frac{5}{7}\right)^8\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^4 \times \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^5\)
qs.s: Using the product rule \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), keep the base and add the exponents: \(\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^{4+5} = \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^9\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)^3 \times \left(\frac{7}{3}\right)^7\)
qs.s: Using the product rule \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), keep the base and add the exponents: \(\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)^{3+7} = \left(\frac{7}{3}\right)^{10}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^2 \times \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^6\)
qs.s: Using the product rule \(a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}\), keep the base and add the exponents: \(\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2+6} = \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^8\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)^5 \times \left(\frac{2}{7}\right) \times \left(\frac{2}{7}\right)^6\)
qs.s: Recall that \(\left(\frac{2}{7}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{7}\right)^1\). By the product rule, add all exponents: \(5 + 1 + 6 = 12\), yielding \(\left(\frac{2}{7}\right)^{12}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^3 \times \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^4 \times \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^2 \times \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^5\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding the exponents across all four factors: \(3 + 4 + 2 + 5 = 14\). The simplified form is \(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{14}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^6 \times \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^3 \times \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right) \times \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^8\)
qs.s: The third factor has an implied exponent of 1. Summing the exponents gives \(6 + 3 + 1 + 8 = 18\), resulting in \(\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^{18}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{18} \times \left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{27} \times \left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{35}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, keep the common base and add the exponents: \(18 + 27 + 35 = 80\). Thus, the answer is \(\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)^{80}\).

qs.q:
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form.

\(\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^{3x+2} \times \left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^{4x+5}\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the algebraic exponents: \((3x + 2) + (4x + 5) = 7x + 7\). The expression simplifies to \(\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^{7x+7}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-7)^5 \times (-7)^2 \times (-7)^1\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the base and add the exponents: \(5 + 2 + 1 = 8\), giving \((-7)^8\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-2)^5 \times (-2)^3 \times (-2)^1\)
qs.s: By the product rule, keep the common base and add the exponents: \(5 + 3 + 1 = 9\), which gives \((-2)^9\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-5)^3 \times (-5)^4 \times (-5)^1\)
qs.s: Keep the base of \(-5\) and add the exponents: \(3 + 4 + 1 = 8\), giving \((-5)^8\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-4)^2 \times (-4)^5 \times (-4)^1\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by keeping the base and adding the exponents: \(2 + 5 + 1 = 8\), yielding \((-4)^8\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-6)^4 \times (-6)^1 \times (-6)^2\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(4 + 1 + 2 = 7\), resulting in \((-6)^7\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-2)^9 \times (-2)^{-5} \times (-2)^4 \times (-2)^{-8} \times (-2)^7\)
qs.s: Add the positive and negative exponents: \(9 + (-5) + 4 + (-8) + 7 = 7\), giving \((-2)^7\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-3)^{15} \times (-3)^{24} \times (-3)^8 \times (-3)^{31}\)
qs.s: Keep the base and add all four exponents together: \(15 + 24 + 8 + 31 = 78\), so the expression equals \((-3)^{78}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-10)^{18} \times (-10)^{-7} \times (-10) \times (-10)^{12} \times (-10)^{-9}\)
Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^7 \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-3} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^5 \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-1}\)
qs.s: Add the exponents for the common base: \(7 + (-3) + 5 + (-1) = 8\), which leaves \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^8\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \((-5)^6 \times (-5)^0 \times (-5)^{11} \times (-5) \times (-5)^4\)
qs.s: Note that \((-5) = (-5)^1\). Applying the product rule gives an exponent sum of \(6 + 0 + 11 + 1 + 4 = 22\), resulting in \((-5)^{22}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right) \times \left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^7 \times \left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^{-3}\)
qs.s: The first factor has an unwritten exponent of \(1\). Adding the exponents gives \(1 + 7 + (-3) = 5\), so the expression simplifies to \(\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^5\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^4 \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-3} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, add the exponents: \(4 + (-3) + 1 = 2\). Thus, the product is \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^2\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^6 \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{-4} \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\)
qs.s: By the product rule, add the exponents, recalling that \(\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^1\): \(6 + (-4) + 1 = 3\). The result in exponential form is \(\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^3\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^2 \times \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^{-6} \times \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)\)
qs.s: Add the exponents of the identical bases: \(2 + (-6) + 1 = -3\). Leaving the answer in exponential form yields \(\left(-\frac{1}{5}\right)^{-3}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{-5} \times \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) \times \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^8\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding the exponents of the common base: \(-5 + 1 + 8 = 4\). This gives \(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^4\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-27} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{41} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-19} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{18} \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^{-9}\)
qs.s: Sum the exponents of the common base: \((41 + 18) + (-27 - 19 - 9) = 59 - 55 = 4\). In exponential form, this is \(\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)^4\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{5}{6}\right) \times \left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^{-11} \times \left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^7 \times \left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^0 \times \left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^{-2} \times \left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)\)
qs.s: Add all six exponents, including \(1\) for each of the two terms without an explicit exponent and \(0\) for \(\left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^0\): \(1 + (-11) + 7 + 0 + (-2) + 1 = -4\). This simplifies to \(\left(-\frac{5}{6}\right)^{-4}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{3}{8}\right)^{32} \times \left(-\frac{3}{8}\right)^{-45} \times \left(-\frac{3}{8}\right) \times \left(-\frac{3}{8}\right)^{26} \times \left(-\frac{3}{8}\right)^{-18} \times \left(-\frac{3}{8}\right)^7\)
qs.s: Group and add the positive and negative exponents: \((32 + 1 + 26 + 7) + (-45 - 18) = 66 - 63 = 3\). The result is \(\left(-\frac{3}{8}\right)^3\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^{-8} \times \left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^{12} \times \left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^0 \times \left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^{-6} \times \left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule by adding the exponents, noting that \(\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^0\) has exponent \(0\) and \(\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)\) has exponent \(1\): \(-8 + 12 + 0 + (-6) + 1 = -1\). The result is \(\left(-\frac{3}{7}\right)^{-1}\).

qs.q: Multiply. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^{15} \times \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^{-23} \times \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^{14} \times \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)\)
qs.s: Add the exponents for the common base: \(15 + (-23) + 14 + 1 = 7\). The simplified exponential form is \(\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^7\).

exercises.name: Divide powers with the same base

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{6^8}{6^2}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by keeping the base and subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{6^8}{6^2} = 6^{8-2} = 6^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{3^{10}}{3^2}\)
qs.s: Subtract the exponents using the quotient rule: \(\frac{3^{10}}{3^2} = 3^{10-2} = 3^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{10^6}{10^2}\)
qs.s: Keep the base the same and subtract the exponents: \(\frac{10^6}{10^2} = 10^{6-2} = 10^4\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{2^9}{2^3}\)
qs.s: Use the quotient rule to subtract the exponent in the denominator from the exponent in the numerator: \(\frac{2^9}{2^3} = 2^{9-3} = 2^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{7^{12}}{7^3}\)
qs.s: Use the quotient rule for exponents, \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\). Subtract the exponents: \(7^{12-3} = 7^9\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{6^3}{6^8}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting the denominator's exponent from the numerator's exponent: \(6^{3-8} = 6^{-5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{5^7 \times 5^6}{5^4}\)
qs.s: First, apply the product rule in the numerator to get \(5^{7+6} = 5^{13}\). Then, use the quotient rule to divide: \(5^{13-4} = 5^9\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{3^{43}}{3^{17}}\)
qs.s: Use the quotient rule to subtract the larger two-digit exponents: \(3^{43-17} = 3^{26}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{2^8 \times 2^7}{2^4 \times 2^6}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \(2^{8+7} = 2^{15}\) and the denominator to \(2^{4+6} = 2^{10}\), then divide using the quotient rule: \(2^{15-10} = 2^5\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{7^{15}}{7^6 \times 7^2}\)
qs.s: First combine the denominator using the product rule: \(7^6 \times 7^2 = 7^{6+2} = 7^8\). Then use the quotient rule: \(\frac{7^{15}}{7^8} = 7^{15-8} = 7^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{7^{10}}{7^2}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{7^{10}}{7^2} = 7^{10-2} = 7^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{5^8}{5^2}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{5^8}{5^2} = 5^{8-2} = 5^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{2^{12}}{2^4}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{2^{12}}{2^4} = 2^{12-4} = 2^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{9^{15}}{9^5}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{9^{15}}{9^5} = 9^{15-5} = 9^{10}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{3^9}{3^3}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{3^9}{3^3} = 3^{9-3} = 3^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{3^{17} \cdot 3^{13}}{3^8 \cdot 3^7 \cdot 3^5}\)
qs.s: Add exponents in the numerator to get \(3^{30}\) and in the denominator to get \(3^{20}\), then subtract exponents using the quotient rule: \(3^{30-20} = 3^{10}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{5^9 \cdot 5^6}{5^8}\)
qs.s: Add exponents in the numerator to get \(5^{9+6} = 5^{15}\), then subtract the exponent in the denominator using the quotient rule: \(5^{15-8} = 5^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{7^8 \cdot 7^6}{7^3 \cdot 7^4}\)
qs.s: Simplify numerator and denominator by adding exponents to get \(\frac{7^{14}}{7^7}\), then subtract exponents using the quotient rule to obtain \(7^{14-7} = 7^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3)^{11}}{(-3)^4 \cdot (-3)^2}\)
qs.s: Combine the powers in the denominator to get \((-3)^{4+2} = (-3)^6\), then subtract exponents using the quotient rule: \((-3)^{11-6} = (-3)^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^9}{\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{2}{5}}\)
qs.s: Write \(\frac{2}{5}\) as \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^1\) so the denominator becomes \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^4\), then subtract exponents using the quotient rule: \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{9-4} = \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{5^7}{5^3}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by keeping the base and subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{5^7}{5^3} = 5^{7 - 3} = 5^4\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{3^{11}}{3^4}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by keeping the base and subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{3^{11}}{3^4} = 3^{11 - 4} = 3^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{10^8}{10^5}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by keeping the base and subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{10^8}{10^5} = 10^{8 - 5} = 10^3\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{4^{12}}{4^3}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by keeping the base and subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{4^{12}}{4^3} = 4^{12 - 3} = 4^9\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{6^{10}}{6^4}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by keeping the base and subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{6^{10}}{6^4} = 6^{10 - 4} = 6^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{7^{23} \cdot 7^8}{7}\)
qs.s: Rewrite \(7\) as \(7^1\) and add the numerator exponents to get \(7^{23 + 8} = 7^{31}\). Then, subtract the denominator exponent: \(\frac{7^{31}}{7^1} = 7^{31 - 1} = 7^{30}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{2^{25} \cdot 2^{14}}{2^{11}}\)
qs.s: First, add the exponents in the numerator using the product rule: \(2^{25} \cdot 2^{14} = 2^{39}\). Then, apply the quotient rule to divide: \(\frac{2^{39}}{2^{11}} = 2^{39 - 11} = 2^{28}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{3^8 \cdot 3^{15} \cdot 3^6}{3^{11} \cdot 3^7}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \(3^{8 + 15 + 6} = 3^{29}\) and the denominator to \(3^{11 + 7} = 3^{18}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{3^{29}}{3^{18}} = 3^{29 - 18} = 3^{11}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{10^{18} \cdot 10^7}{10^9 \cdot 10^4}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \(10^{18 + 7} = 10^{25}\) and the denominator to \(10^{9 + 4} = 10^{13}\). Then, use the quotient rule: \(\frac{10^{25}}{10^{13}} = 10^{25 - 13} = 10^{12}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{5^{34}}{5^8 \cdot 5^{11}}\)
qs.s: First, combine the denominator powers using the product rule: \(5^8 \cdot 5^{11} = 5^{19}\). Then, apply the quotient rule to divide: \(\frac{5^{34}}{5^{19}} = 5^{34 - 19} = 5^{15}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{(-5)^6}{(-5)^3}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents while keeping the base the same: \(\frac{(-5)^6}{(-5)^3} = (-5)^{6-3} = (-5)^3\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{2^8}{2^2}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents while keeping the base the same: \(\frac{2^8}{2^2} = 2^{8-2} = 2^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{4^{10}}{4^5}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents while keeping the base the same: \(\frac{4^{10}}{4^5} = 4^{10-5} = 4^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{9^8}{9^4}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents while keeping the base the same: \(\frac{9^8}{9^4} = 9^{8-4} = 9^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{(2^4)^3}{2^6}\)
qs.s: First, apply the power rule to simplify the numerator: \((2^4)^3 = 2^{4 \times 3} = 2^{12}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{2^{12}}{2^6} = 2^{12-6} = 2^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{8^{9x}}{8^{4x}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the variable exponents: \(\frac{8^{9x}}{8^{4x}} = 8^{9x-4x} = 8^{5x}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{7^{18}}{7^4 \times 7^2}\)
qs.s: First, simplify the denominator using the product rule: \(7^4 \times 7^2 = 7^{4+2} = 7^6\). Then, use the quotient rule: \(\frac{7^{18}}{7^6} = 7^{18-6} = 7^{12}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form: \(\frac{5^7 \times 5^5}{5^4}\)
qs.s: First, use the product rule in the numerator to get \(5^{7+5} = 5^{12}\). Then, use the quotient rule to subtract exponents: \(\frac{5^{12}}{5^4} = 5^{12-4} = 5^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{n^{12}}{n^3}\)
qs.s: Subtract the exponents using the quotient rule: \(\frac{n^{12}}{n^3} = n^{12-3} = n^9\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{y^8}{y^2}\)
qs.s: Use the quotient rule to subtract the exponents: \(\frac{y^8}{y^2} = y^{8-2} = y^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{a^{10}}{a^2}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting the exponent of the denominator from the numerator: \(\frac{a^{10}}{a^2} = a^{10-2} = a^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{r^{10}}{r^5}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting the exponents: \(\frac{r^{10}}{r^5} = r^{10-5} = r^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{m^{15}}{m^5}\)
qs.s: Use the quotient rule to subtract the exponents: \(\frac{m^{15}}{m^5} = m^{15-5} = m^{10}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{b^{9n}}{b^{4n}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting the variable exponents: \(\frac{b^{9n}}{b^{4n}} = b^{9n - 4n} = b^{5n}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{x^8}{x^{-5}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the denominator's exponent from the numerator's: \(\frac{x^8}{x^{-5}} = x^{8 - (-5)} = x^{8 + 5} = x^{13}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{a^{52}}{a^{17}}\)
qs.s: Use the quotient rule to subtract the larger exponents: \(\frac{a^{52}}{a^{17}} = a^{52-17} = a^{35}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{y^7 \cdot y^6}{y^4}\)
qs.s: First combine the numerator using the product rule: \(y^7 \cdot y^6 = y^{7+6} = y^{13}\). Then apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{y^{13}}{y^4} = y^{13-4} = y^9\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{p^{-2}}{p^{-7}}\)
qs.s: Subtract the exponents according to the quotient rule: \(\frac{p^{-2}}{p^{-7}} = p^{-2 - (-7)} = p^{-2 + 7} = p^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{6^4}{6^4}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents while keeping the base unchanged: \(\frac{6^4}{6^4} = 6^{4-4} = 6^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{a^9}{a^9}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{a^9}{a^9} = a^{9-9} = a^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{y^5}{y^5}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{y^5}{y^5} = y^{5-5} = y^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{m^8}{m^8}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{m^8}{m^8} = m^{8-8} = m^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{w^{12}}{w^{12}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(\frac{w^{12}}{w^{12}} = w^{12-12} = w^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{m^9 \cdot m^7}{m^{16}}\)
qs.s: First, multiply the numerator powers: \(m^9 \cdot m^7 = m^{16}\). Then, use the quotient rule: \(\frac{m^{16}}{m^{16}} = m^{16-16} = m^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(a^4)^3}{a^5}\)
qs.s: First, apply the power rule to the numerator: \((a^4)^3 = a^{4 \times 3} = a^{12}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{a^{12}}{a^5} = a^{12-5} = a^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{y^{15}}{y^7 \cdot y^8}\)
qs.s: First, simplify the denominator using the product rule: \(y^7 \cdot y^8 = y^{15}\). Then, divide using the quotient rule: \(\frac{y^{15}}{y^{15}} = y^{15-15} = y^0\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{x^8 \cdot x^5}{x^7}\)
qs.s: First, multiply in the numerator by adding exponents: \(x^8 \cdot x^5 = x^{13}\). Then, use the quotient rule: \(\frac{x^{13}}{x^7} = x^{13-7} = x^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(b^3)^6}{(b^2)^7}\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule to simplify the numerator and denominator to \(b^{18}\) and \(b^{14}\), respectively. Then, subtract the exponents using the quotient rule: \(\frac{b^{18}}{b^{14}} = b^{18-14} = b^4\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-4)^5}{(-4)^{-2}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), subtract the exponents: \(5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \((-4)^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-5)^3}{(-5)^{-5}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), subtract the exponents: \(3 - (-5) = 3 + 5 = 8\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \((-5)^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{7^4}{7^{-3}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), subtract the exponents: \(4 - (-3) = 4 + 3 = 7\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \(7^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-2)^{-3}}{(-2)^{-7}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), subtract the exponents: $-3 - (-7) = -3 + 7 = 4. Thus, the expression simplifies to \((-2)^4\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-8)^2}{(-8)^{-4}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), subtract the exponents: \(2 - (-4) = 2 + 4 = 6\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \((-8)^6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-5)^7}{(-5)^{-4}} \div (-5)^{-3}\)
qs.s: First compute the quotient inside the fraction: \(7 - (-4) = 11\), giving \((-5)^{11}\). Then divide by \((-5)^{-3}\) by subtracting the exponent again: \(11 - (-3) = 14\), giving \((-5)^{14}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-2)^9 \cdot (-2)^{-3}}{(-2)^{-5} \cdot (-2)^4}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \((-2)^{9 + (-3)} = (-2)^6\) and the denominator to \((-2)^{-5 + 4} = (-2)^{-1}\). By the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(6 - (-1) = 7\), yielding \((-2)^7\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3)^8 \cdot (-3)^{-2}}{(-3)^{-5}}\)
qs.s: First combine the numerator powers using the product rule to get \((-3)^{8 + (-2)} = (-3)^6\). Then apply the quotient rule to subtract exponents: \(6 - (-5) = 11\), giving \((-3)^{11}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-10)^{14} \cdot (-10)^{-6}}{(-10)^{-8} \cdot (-10)^{-3}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \((-10)^{14 + (-6)} = (-10)^8\) and the denominator to \((-10)^{-8 + (-3)} = (-10)^{-11}\). Apply the quotient rule: \(8 - (-11) = 19\), resulting in \((-10)^{19}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^6 \cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{-1}}{\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{-4}}\)
qs.s: Combine the numerator using the product rule to get \(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^{6 + (-1)} = \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^5\). Then use the quotient rule to subtract exponents: \(5 - (-4) = 9\), giving \(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^9\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-7)^{-5}}{(-7)^{-8}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \((-7)^{-5 - (-8)} = (-7)^{-5 + 8} = (-7)^3\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-4)^{-2}}{(-4)^{-6}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \((-4)^{-2 - (-6)} = (-4)^{-2 + 6} = (-4)^4\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3)^{-2}}{(-3)^{-7}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \((-3)^{-2 - (-7)} = (-3)^{-2 + 7} = (-3)^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-6)^{-8}}{(-6)^{-5}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \((-6)^{-8 - (-5)} = (-6)^{-8 + 5} = (-6)^{-3}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-8)^{-3}}{(-8)^{-5}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \((-8)^{-3 - (-5)} = (-8)^{-3 + 5} = (-8)^2\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{[(-10)^{-2}]^3}{[(-10)^{-4}]^2}\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule to both parts to obtain \(\frac{(-10)^{-6}}{(-10)^{-8}}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \((-10)^{-6 - (-8)} = (-10)^2\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3)^{-5}}{(-3)^{-4} \cdot (-3)^{-7}}\)
qs.s: First, use the product rule in the denominator to get \((-3)^{-4 + (-7)} = (-3)^{-11}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \((-3)^{-5 - (-11)} = (-3)^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-2)^{-7} \cdot (-2)^{-5}}{(-2)^{-4} \cdot (-2)^{-13}}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \((-2)^{-12}\) and the denominator to \((-2)^{-17}\) using the product rule. Then, apply the quotient rule: \((-2)^{-12 - (-17)} = (-2)^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{[(-6)^{-2}]^4}{(-6)^{-11}}\)
qs.s: First, apply the power rule to the numerator: \([(-6)^{-2}]^4 = (-6)^{-8}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \((-6)^{-8 - (-11)} = (-6)^3\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-5)^{-4} \cdot (-5)^{-3}}{(-5)^{-11}}\)
qs.s: First, use the product rule in the numerator to get \((-5)^{-4 + (-3)} = (-5)^{-7}\). Then, apply the quotient rule: \((-5)^{-7 - (-11)} = (-5)^4\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3y)^2}{(-3y)^{-3}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponent of the denominator from that of the numerator: \(2 - (-3) = 2 + 3 = 5\). Therefore, \(\frac{(-3y)^2}{(-3y)^{-3}} = (-3y)^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-6b)^4}{(-6b)^{-2}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting the exponents: \(4 - (-2) = 4 + 2 = 6\). Hence, \(\frac{(-6b)^4}{(-6b)^{-2}} = (-6b)^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-4n)^5}{(-4n)^{-5}}\)
qs.s: Subtract the denominator's exponent from the numerator's exponent: \(5 - (-5) = 5 + 5 = 10\). Therefore, \(\frac{(-4n)^5}{(-4n)^{-5}} = (-4n)^{10}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(7k)^3}{(7k)^{-8}}\)
qs.s: Subtract the exponents using the quotient rule: \(3 - (-8) = 3 + 8 = 11\). Thus, \(\frac{(7k)^3}{(7k)^{-8}} = (7k)^{11}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(5a)^6}{(5a)^{-2}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting exponents: \(6 - (-2) = 6 + 2 = 8\). Thus, \(\frac{(5a)^6}{(5a)^{-2}} = (5a)^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3w)^5 \cdot (-3w)^{-1}}{(-3w)^{-4} \cdot (-3w)^2}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator to \((-3w)^{5 + (-1)} = (-3w)^4\) and the denominator to \((-3w)^{-4 + 2} = (-3w)^{-2}\). Finally, apply the quotient rule: \(4 - (-2) = 6\), giving \((-3w)^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-2y)^7}{(-2y)^{-4} \cdot (-2y)^3}\)
qs.s: First, use the product rule in the denominator to get \((-2y)^{-4 + 3} = (-2y)^{-1}\). Then, use the quotient rule to subtract exponents: \(7 - (-1) = 8\), yielding \((-2y)^8\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{[(-4p)^3]^2}{(-4p)^{-7}}\)
qs.s: First, simplify the numerator using the power rule: \([(-4p)^3]^2 = (-4p)^6\). Then, apply the quotient rule to subtract the exponents: \(6 - (-7) = 13\), giving \((-4p)^{13}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-3a^2b)^8}{(-3a^2b)^{-7}}\)
qs.s: Treat \((-3a^2b)\) as the common base and subtract exponents using the quotient rule: \(8 - (-7) = 15\). Thus, the result is \((-3a^2b)^{15}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{(-5k)^{4n+1}}{(-5k)^{n-3}}\)
qs.s: Subtract the exponent in the denominator from the exponent in the numerator: \((4n + 1) - (n - 3) = 4n + 1 - n + 3 = 3n + 4\). This gives \((-5k)^{3n+4}\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{x^{-3}}{x^{-8}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\) by subtracting the denominator's exponent from the numerator's exponent: \(-3 - (-8) = -3 + 8 = 5\). Thus, the answer is \(x^5\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{p^{-6}}{p^{-8}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule to subtract the exponents: \(-6 - (-8) = -6 + 8 = 2\). Therefore, the answer is \(p^2\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{w^{-2}}{w^{-9}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule, subtract the exponents: \(-2 - (-9) = -2 + 9 = 7\). Thus, the expression simplifies to \(w^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{m^{-5}}{m^{-11}}\)
qs.s: Subtract the exponent in the denominator from the exponent in the numerator: \(-5 - (-11) = -5 + 11 = 6\). The result is \(m^6\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{y^{-4}}{y^{-7}}\)
qs.s: Using the quotient rule \(\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\), subtract the exponents: \(-4 - (-7) = -4 + 7 = 3\). This gives \(y^3\).

qs.q: Divide and simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{y^{-4}}{y^{-9} \cdot y^{-3}}\)
qs.s: First use the product rule in the denominator to get \(y^{-9 + (-3)} = y^{-12}\), then subtract exponents using the quotient rule: \(-4 - (-12) = 8\). The result is \(y^8\).

qs.q: Divide and simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{x^{-5} \cdot x^{-7}}{x^{-18}}\)
qs.s: First combine the numerator using the product rule to get \(x^{-5 + (-7)} = x^{-12}\), then apply the quotient rule: \(-12 - (-18) = 6\). The simplified form is \(x^6\).

qs.q: Divide and simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{a^{-3} b^{-5}}{a^{-8} b^{-12}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule to each base separately: \(-3 - (-8) = 5\) for base \(a\), and \(-5 - (-12) = 7\) for base \(b\). The resulting expression is \(a^5 b^7\).

qs.q: Divide. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{k^{-17}}{k^{-42}}\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient rule by subtracting the denominator's exponent from the numerator's exponent: \(-17 - (-42) = -17 + 42 = 25\). The answer is \(k^{25}\).

qs.q: Divide and simplify. Leave answer in exponential form. \(\frac{6^{-5} \cdot 6^{-8}}{6^{-17}}\)
qs.s: Combine exponents in the numerator using the product rule to obtain \(6^{-5 + (-8)} = 6^{-13}\), then subtract the denominator's exponent: \(-13 - (-17) = 4\). The final answer is \(6^4\).

exercises.name: Power of a power and product

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((6^2)^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\) by multiplying the exponents to get \(6^{2 \times 3} = 6^6\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((3^2)^4\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\) by multiplying the exponents to get \(3^{2 \times 4} = 3^8\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((x^4)^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\) by multiplying the exponents to get \(x^{4 \times 3} = x^{12}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((y^2)^5\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\) by multiplying the exponents to get \(y^{2 \times 5} = y^{10}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((5^3)^2\)
qs.s: Apply the power rule \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\) by multiplying the exponents to get \(5^{3 \times 2} = 5^6\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((3x^4)^3\)
qs.s: Raise both the coefficient and the variable term to the third power: \(3^3 \cdot (x^4)^3 = 27x^{4 \times 3} = 27x^{12}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\(\frac{(m^5)^3}{(m^2)^4}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator and denominator using the power rule to get \(\frac{m^{15}}{m^8}\). Then apply the quotient rule by subtracting exponents to get \(m^{15-8} = m^7\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((-2a^3b^4)^4\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the fourth power to get \((-2)^4 \cdot (a^3)^4 \cdot (b^4)^4 = 16a^{12}b^{16}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\(\left(\frac{2x^3}{y^2}\right)^4\)
qs.s: Apply the power to both the numerator and the denominator to get \(\frac{2^4 (x^3)^4}{(y^2)^4} = \frac{16x^{12}}{y^8}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((p^3)^4 \cdot (p^2)^5\)
qs.s: First simplify each power using the power rule to get \(p^{12} \cdot p^{10}\). Then add the exponents using the product rule to get \(p^{12+10} = p^{22}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2^4)^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule by multiplying the exponents: \((2^4)^{-3} = 2^{4 \times (-3)} = 2^{-12}\). Rewriting with a positive exponent gives \(\frac{1}{2^{12}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((7^3)^{-2}\)
qs.s: Using the power of a power rule, multiply exponents to get \((7^3)^{-2} = 7^{3 \times (-2)} = 7^{-6}\). Write with a positive exponent as \(\frac{1}{7^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((10^4)^{-2}\)
qs.s: Multiply the exponents to get \((10^4)^{-2} = 10^{4 \times (-2)} = 10^{-8}\). Expressing with a positive exponent gives \(\frac{1}{10^8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((a^2b^{-3})^{-2}(a^{-1}b)^4\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule to each group to get \(a^{-4}b^6 \cdot a^{-4}b^4\). Then add exponents for like bases to obtain \(a^{-8}b^{10} = \frac{b^{10}}{a^8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2a^{-5}b^2)^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of \(-3\) to each factor: \(2^{-3}a^{(-5) \times (-3)}b^{2 \times (-3)} = 2^{-3}a^{15}b^{-6}\). Since \(2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}\) and \(b^{-6} = \frac{1}{b^6}\), this simplifies to \(\frac{a^{15}}{8b^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \(\left(\frac{3x^2}{y^4}\right)^{-2}\)
qs.s: Invert the fraction to change the outer exponent to positive: \(\left(\frac{y^4}{3x^2}\right)^2\). Squaring each factor in the numerator and denominator yields \(\frac{y^{4 \times 2}}{3^2 x^{2 \times 2}} = \frac{y^8}{9x^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((x^{-3}y^2)^{-4}\)
qs.s: Multiply each exponent inside the brackets by \(-4\): \((x^{-3}y^2)^{-4} = x^{(-3) \times (-4)}y^{2 \times (-4)} = x^{12}y^{-8}\). Expressing with positive exponents gives \(\frac{x^{12}}{y^8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((7^{-3})^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule, \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\). Multiply the exponents: \((-3) \times (-3) = 9\), which gives \(7^9\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((x^{-3})^{-4}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule, \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\). Multiply the exponents: \((-3) \times (-4) = 12\), which gives \(x^{12}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((5^{-2})^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule, \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\). Multiply the exponents: \((-2) \times (-3) = 6\), which gives \(5^6\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2^{-5})^{-2}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule, \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\). Multiply the exponents: \((-5) \times (-2) = 10\), which gives \(2^{10}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((a^{-3})^{-5}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a power rule, \((a^m)^n = a^{m \times n}\). Multiply the exponents: \((-3) \times (-5) = 15\), which gives \(a^{15}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \(\left(\frac{p^{-3}}{q^2}\right)^{-2}\)
qs.s: Apply the power to both terms to get \(\frac{(p^{-3})^{-2}}{(q^2)^{-2}} = \frac{p^6}{q^{-4}}\). Rewrite the denominator with a positive exponent to obtain \(p^6 q^4\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2x^{-4})^{-3}\)
qs.s: Raise both the coefficient and the variable term to the power of \(-3\): \(2^{-3} (x^{-4})^{-3} = \frac{1}{2^3} x^{12} = \frac{x^{12}}{8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((a^{-2} b^3)^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product rule to get \((a^{-2})^{-3} (b^3)^{-3} = a^6 b^{-9}\). Expressing with positive exponents gives \(\frac{a^6}{b^9}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \(\frac{(m^{-3})^{-3}}{(m^4)^3}\)
qs.s: Simplify the numerator and denominator using the power rule to obtain \(\frac{m^9}{m^{12}}\). Subtract exponents using the quotient rule: \(m^{9 - 12} = m^{-3} = \frac{1}{m^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((x^{-3})^{-2} \cdot (x^4)^{-2}\)
qs.s: Simplify each factor using the power of a power rule to get \(x^6 \cdot x^{-8}\). Then apply the product rule and negative exponent rule: \(x^{6 + (-8)} = x^{-2} = \frac{1}{x^2}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \(-(-6m^{-4})^0\)
qs.s: The expression inside the brackets evaluates to \((-6m^{-4})^0 = 1\), so the negative sign outside makes the final result \(-(1) = -1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \(-(5y^{-2})^0\)
qs.s: The exponent 0 applies only to the base inside the brackets, so \((5y^{-2})^0 = 1\), giving \(-(1) = -1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((-4x^{-3})^0\)
qs.s: Any non-zero expression raised to the power of 0 equals 1, so \((-4x^{-3})^0 = 1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((8t^{-5})^0\)
qs.s: Applying the zero exponent rule to the non-zero base \((8t^{-5})\) yields 1.

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((-7a^{-1})^0\)
qs.s: Since the entire expression is within brackets and raised to the power of 0, \((-7a^{-1})^0 = 1\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. $(-2x^{-3})^2(3x^0y^{-2})^{-2}
qs.s: Simplify the factors to \((-2)^2x^{-6} = 4x^{-6}\) and \(3^{-2}(y^{-2})^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}y^4\). Multiplying them together gives \(\frac{4y^4}{9x^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \left(\frac{-3a^{-2}b^0}{c^{-4}}\right)^2
qs.s: Since \(b^0 = 1\), square each factor in the numerator and denominator to obtain \(\frac{(-3)^2a^{-4}}{c^{-8}} = \frac{9a^{-4}}{c^{-8}}\). Moving negative exponents to opposite sides yields \(\frac{9c^8}{a^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((4x^{-3}y^0)^{-2}\)
qs.s: Since \(y^0 = 1\), apply the power of a product rule to get \(4^{-2}(x^{-3})^{-2} = 4^{-2}x^6\). Rewriting with positive exponents gives \(\frac{x^6}{16}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \frac{(-3x^{-4}y^2)^0}{(2x^{-2}y)^3}
qs.s: The numerator equals 1 because any non-zero expression raised to 0 is 1. The denominator expands to \(2^3(x^{-2})^3y^3 = 8x^{-6}y^3\), and moving \(x^{-6}\) to the numerator yields \(\frac{x^6}{8y^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. $(-3x^{-1}y^2)^2(2x^{-2}y^0)^{-1}
qs.s: Expand to get \(9x^{-2}y^4\) and \(2^{-1}x^2 = \frac{x^2}{2}\). Multiplying the factors combines \(x^{-2} \cdot x^2 = x^0 = 1\), leaving \(\frac{9y^4}{2}\).

qs.s: Apply the power of a product rule: \((3y)^3 = 3^3 \cdot y^3 = 27y^3\).

\((3n)^4\)

\((2x^3 y^2)^3 (3x y^4)^2\)
qs.s: Expand each power of a product to get \((8x^9y^6)(9x^2y^8)\), then multiply coefficients and add exponents of like bases to get \(72x^{11}y^{14}\).

qs.q:

\([(-2a^2 b^3)^2]^3\)
qs.s: Multiply the outer exponents to get \((-2a^2 b^3)^6\), then apply the exponent to each factor: \((-2)^6 \cdot a^{12} \cdot b^{18} = 64a^{12}b^{18}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((2x^{-3} y^2)^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the exponent to each factor to obtain \(2^{-3}x^9y^{-6}\), then rewrite with positive exponents as \(\frac{x^9}{8y^6}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((-2a^3 b^2 c^4)^4\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the fourth power: \((-2)^4 \cdot (a^3)^4 \cdot (b^2)^4 \cdot (c^4)^4 = 16a^{12}b^8c^{16}\).

qs.q:
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents.

\((-3x^2 y^4)^3\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the third power: \((-3)^3 \cdot (x^2)^3 \cdot (y^4)^3 = -27x^6y^{12}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2p^{-3})^4\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product and power of a power rules: \((2p^{-3})^4 = 2^4 \cdot p^{-3 \times 4} = 16p^{-12}\). Express with a positive exponent to get \(\frac{16}{p^{12}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((5a^{-2})^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product and power of a power rules: \((5a^{-2})^3 = 5^3 \cdot a^{-2 \times 3} = 125a^{-6}\). Express with a positive exponent as \(\frac{125}{a^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((4x^{-3})^2\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product rule and power of a power rule: \((4x^{-3})^2 = 4^2 \cdot x^{-3 \times 2} = 16x^{-6}\). Then rewrite using a positive exponent to get \(\frac{16}{x^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2y^{-5})^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product and power of a power rules: \((2y^{-5})^3 = 2^3 \cdot y^{-5 \times 3} = 8y^{-15}\). Rewrite using a positive exponent to get \(\frac{8}{y^{15}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((-3b^{-4})^2\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product rule: \((-3b^{-4})^2 = (-3)^2 \cdot b^{-4 \times 2} = 9b^{-8}\). Express with a positive exponent to obtain \(\frac{9}{b^8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((-4x^{-2}y^3)^3\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the third power: \((-4)^3 \cdot (x^{-2})^3 \cdot (y^3)^3 = -64x^{-6}y^9\). Rewriting with positive exponents gives \(-\frac{64y^9}{x^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((3a^4b^{-3})^{-2}\)
qs.s: Apply the exponent of \(-2\) to each factor: \(3^{-2} \cdot a^{4 \times (-2)} \cdot b^{-3 \times (-2)} = \frac{1}{9}a^{-8}b^6\). Rewriting with positive exponents yields \(\frac{b^6}{9a^8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((2x^{-3})^3(3x^2)^2\)
qs.s: Apply powers to both factors to get \((8x^{-9})(9x^4)\). Multiply coefficients and add exponents: \(72x^{-9+4} = 72x^{-5} = \frac{72}{x^5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \(\left(\frac{2x^{-4}}{3y^2}\right)^3\)
qs.s: Raise both the numerator and denominator to the power of 3: \(\frac{2^3 x^{-4 \times 3}}{3^3 y^{2 \times 3}} = \frac{8x^{-12}}{27y^6}\). Moving \(x^{-12}\) to the denominator gives \(\frac{8}{27x^{12}y^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents. \((-2a^{-3}b^{-1}c^2)^4\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the fourth power: \((-2)^4 \cdot a^{-3 \times 4} \cdot b^{-1 \times 4} \cdot c^{2 \times 4} = 16a^{-12}b^{-4}c^8\). Rewriting with positive exponents gives \(\frac{16c^8}{a^{12}b^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((5b^{-2})^3\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the third power to obtain \(5^3 b^{(-2)(3)} = 125b^{-6}\). Invert the variable with the negative exponent to get \(\frac{125}{b^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((3w^{-4})^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power rules to obtain \(3^3 w^{(-4)(3)} = 27w^{-12}\). Writing without negative exponents yields \(\frac{27}{w^{12}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((4y^{-3})^2\)
qs.s: Raise each factor to the second power to obtain \(4^2 y^{(-3)(2)} = 16y^{-6}\). Expressing with a positive exponent gives \(\frac{16}{y^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((2m^{-5})^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power rules to get \(2^3 m^{(-5)(3)} = 8m^{-15}\). Rewrite using a positive exponent as \(\frac{8}{m^{15}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((3x^{-2})^4\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product and power of a power rules to get \(3^4 x^{(-2)(4)} = 81x^{-8}\). Then rewrite using a positive exponent as \(\frac{81}{x^8}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \(\left(\frac{3a^{-2}}{2b^3}\right)^3\)
qs.s: Apply the quotient and power rules to get \(\frac{3^3 a^{-6}}{2^3 b^9} = \frac{27a^{-6}}{8b^9}\). Moving \(a^{-6}\) to the denominator gives \(\frac{27}{8a^6 b^9}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((2a^{-4}b^3)^{-3}\)
qs.s: Distribute the outer exponent \(-3\) to get \(2^{-3} a^{(-4)(-3)} b^{(3)(-3)} = \frac{1}{8} a^{12} b^{-9}\). Expressing with positive exponents gives \(\frac{a^{12}}{8b^9}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((-2x^2 y^{-3} z^{-1})^4\)
qs.s: Apply the outer exponent 4 to each factor: \((-2)^4 (x^2)^4 (y^{-3})^4 (z^{-1})^4 = 16x^8 y^{-12} z^{-4}\). Move factors with negative exponents to the denominator to get \(\frac{16x^8}{y^{12}z^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((-3x^{-3}y^2)^3\)
qs.s: Raise each factor inside the brackets to the power of 3: \((-3)^3 (x^{-3})^3 (y^2)^3 = -27x^{-9}y^6\). Rewrite \(x^{-9}\) in the denominator to get \(-\frac{27y^6}{x^9}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((4x^{-3} y^2)^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product and power of a power rules: \((4x^{-3} y^2)^3 = 4^3 x^{-3 \times 3} y^{2 \times 3} = 64x^{-9}y^6\). Rewriting with positive exponents yields \(\frac{64y^6}{x^9}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((2a^3 b^{-4})^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power of a product and power of a power rules: \((2a^3 b^{-4})^3 = 2^3 a^{3 \times 3} b^{-4 \times 3} = 8a^9 b^{-12}\). Rewriting with positive exponents gives \(\frac{8a^9}{b^{12}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((5p^{-2} q^3)^2\)
qs.s: Distribute the exponent to each factor: \(5^2 (p^{-2})^2 (q^3)^2 = 25p^{-4}q^6\). Expressing with positive exponents results in \(\frac{25q^6}{p^4}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((-3u^{-1} v^4)^3\)
qs.s: Apply the power to each factor: \((-3)^3 (u^{-1})^3 (v^4)^3 = -27u^{-3}v^{12}\). Rewriting without negative exponents gives \(-\frac{27v^{12}}{u^3}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \(\left(\frac{2m^{-3} n^4}{p^{-2}}\right)^{-4}\)
Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((-2a^{-3} b^2 c^{-4})^{-3}\)
qs.s: Apply the power \(-3\) to each factor: \((-2)^{-3} a^{(-3)(-3)} b^{(2)(-3)} c^{(-4)(-3)} = -\frac{1}{8} a^9 b^{-6} c^{12}\). Rewriting with positive exponents gives \(-\frac{a^9 c^{12}}{8b^6}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((2x^2 y^{-3})^3 (3x^{-4} y^2)^2\)
qs.s: Expand each factor using the power rules: \((2x^2 y^{-3})^3 = 8x^6 y^{-9}\) and \((3x^{-4} y^2)^2 = 9x^{-8} y^4\). Multiplying gives \((8 \times 9) x^{6+(-8)} y^{-9+4} = 72x^{-2}y^{-5} = \frac{72}{x^2 y^5}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \(\frac{(3x^3 y^{-2})^3}{(9x^{-1} y^4)^2}\)
qs.s: Expand numerator and denominator: \(\frac{27x^9 y^{-6}}{81x^{-2} y^8}\). Simplifying gives \(\frac{27}{81} x^{9 - (-2)} y^{-6 - 8} = \frac{1}{3} x^{11} y^{-14} = \frac{x^{11}}{3y^{14}}\).

qs.q: Simplify. Express without brackets or negative exponents: \((-4x^{-2} y^3 z^{-1})^2 (2x^3 y^{-1} z^{-2})^3\)
