qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{11}\)
qs.s: Use the product rule for cube roots to multiply the radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{11} = \sqrt[3]{2 \times 11} = \sqrt[3]{22}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{9}\)
qs.s: Use the product rule for cube roots, \(\sqrt[3]{A} \times \sqrt[3]{B} = \sqrt[3]{A \times B}\), to get \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{9} = \sqrt[3]{2 \times 9} = \sqrt[3]{18}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{9}\)
qs.s: Use the product rule for cube roots to multiply the radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{9} = \sqrt[3]{5 \times 9} = \sqrt[3]{45}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{6}\)
qs.s: Use the product rule for cube roots to multiply the radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{6} = \sqrt[3]{5 \times 6} = \sqrt[3]{30}\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{20} \times \sqrt[3]{50}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{20 \times 50} = \sqrt[3]{1000}\). Since \(10^3 = 1000\), the cube root simplifies to 10.

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 3 \times 18} = \sqrt[3]{108}\). Factor out the perfect cube 27 to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{27 \times 4} = 3\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{5}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{5} = \sqrt[3]{5 \times 5 \times 5} = \sqrt[3]{125} = 5\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{2}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{2} = \sqrt[3]{4 \times 2} = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{9} \times \sqrt[3]{3}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, \(\sqrt[3]{9} \times \sqrt[3]{3} = \sqrt[3]{9 \times 3} = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{8}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule, \(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{8} = \sqrt{2 \times 8} = \sqrt{16} = 4\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{12}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 3 \times 12} = \sqrt[3]{72}\). Then factor out the largest perfect cube: \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 9} = 2\sqrt[3]{9}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{9}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands using the product rule to get \(\sqrt[3]{4 \times 6 \times 9} = \sqrt[3]{216}\). Since \(6^3 = 216\), the cube root is \(6\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{3 \times 6 \times 10} = \sqrt{180}\). Then factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{36 \times 5} = 6\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{5}\)
qs.s: Multiply the factors under a common cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{3 \times 4 \times 5} = \sqrt[3]{60}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{7}\)
qs.s: Using the product rule for cube roots, multiply the radicands together: \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 3 \times 7} = \sqrt[3]{42}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{7}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule for radicals to multiply the values under a single radical: \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 5 \times 7} = \sqrt[3]{70}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{7}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands under a single cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{3 \times 5 \times 7} = \sqrt[3]{105}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{11}\)
qs.s: Combine the factors using the product rule for cube roots: \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 3 \times 11} = \sqrt[3]{66}\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{9}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{135}\), then simplify by extracting the perfect cube factor: \(\sqrt[3]{27 \times 5} = 3\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{25}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{1250}\), then factor out the perfect cube \(125\): \(\sqrt[3]{125 \times 10} = 5\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{5}\)
qs.s: Multiply all four radicands together to get \(\sqrt[3]{120}\), then factor out the perfect cube \(8\): \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 15} = 2\sqrt[3]{15}\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{7}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{56}\), then factor out the perfect cube: \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 7} = 2\sqrt[3]{7}\).

qs.q: Find the product in simplest form: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{216}\). Since \(6^3 = 216\), the expression simplifies completely to \(6\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{7} \times \sqrt[3]{9}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule for cube roots: \(\sqrt[3]{4 \times 7 \times 9} = \sqrt[3]{252}\). Factoring \(252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7\) shows there are no perfect cube factors, so \(\sqrt[3]{252}\) is in simplest form.

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{5} \times \sqrt[3]{11}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule for cube roots: \(\sqrt[3]{3 \times 5 \times 11} = \sqrt[3]{165}\). Since \(165\) has no perfect cube factors, the radical is in simplest form.

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{9} \times \sqrt[3]{5}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule for cube roots: \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 9 \times 5} = \sqrt[3]{90}\). Since \(90\) has no perfect cube factors, the expression cannot be simplified further.

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{6}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands using the product rule: \(\sqrt[3]{4 \times 10 \times 6} = \sqrt[3]{240}\). Factoring out the largest perfect cube factor gives \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 30} = 2\sqrt[3]{30}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{25} \times \sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands under the cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{25 \times 10 \times 18} = \sqrt[3]{4500}\). Factoring out the perfect cube \(125\) gives \(\sqrt[3]{125 \times 36} = 5\sqrt[3]{36}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{5}\)
qs.s: Multiply all four radicands under one cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 3 \times 4 \times 5} = \sqrt[3]{120}\). Factoring out the perfect cube factor \(8\) gives \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 15} = 2\sqrt[3]{15}\).

qs.q: Find the product: \(\sqrt[3]{16} \times \sqrt[3]{25} \times \sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands under the cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{16 \times 25 \times 10} = \sqrt[3]{4000}\). Factoring out the perfect cube \(1000\) gives \(\sqrt[3]{1000 \times 4} = 10\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{52}, \sqrt{54}, \sqrt{56}, \sqrt{58}\)
qs.s: We can simplify \(\sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13}\), \(\sqrt{54} = 3\sqrt{6}\), and \(\sqrt{56} = 2\sqrt{14}\) using the square factors 4 and 9. Because \(58 = 2 \times 29\) has no perfect square factor, \(\sqrt{58}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{32}, \sqrt{34}, \sqrt{40}, \sqrt{45}\)
qs.s: The numbers 32, 40, and 45 contain perfect square factors, giving \(\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\), \(\sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}\), and \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\). Since \(34 = 2 \times 17\) has no square factors greater than 1, \(\sqrt{34}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{63}, \sqrt{68}, \sqrt{70}, \sqrt{72}\)
qs.s: Factoring reveals that \(\sqrt{63} = 3\sqrt{7}\), \(\sqrt{68} = 2\sqrt{17}\), and \(\sqrt{72} = 6\sqrt{2}\). Since \(70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7\) has no perfect square factor, \(\sqrt{70}\) cannot be written as a mixed root.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{20}, \sqrt{24}, \sqrt{26}, \sqrt{28}\)
qs.s: The radicals \(\sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\), \(\sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}\), and \(\sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\) all contain a perfect square factor of 4. Since \(26 = 2 \times 13\) has no square factor greater than 1, \(\sqrt{26}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{75}, \sqrt{80}, \sqrt{82}, \sqrt{84}\)
qs.s: We can simplify \(\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5}\), and \(\sqrt{84} = 2\sqrt{21}\). Because 82 factors into \(2 \times 41\) with no repeated prime factors, \(\sqrt{82}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{135}, \sqrt{140}, \sqrt{147}, \sqrt{154}\)
qs.s: Factoring shows that \(\sqrt{135} = 3\sqrt{15}\), \(\sqrt{140} = 2\sqrt{35}\), and \(\sqrt{147} = 7\sqrt{3}\). Because \(154 = 2 \times 7 \times 11\) has no perfect square factor, \(\sqrt{154}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire cube roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt[3]{24}, \sqrt[3]{40}, \sqrt[3]{54}, \sqrt[3]{60}\)
qs.s: Using the perfect cube factors 8 and 27, we have \(\sqrt[3]{24} = 2\sqrt[3]{3}\), \(\sqrt[3]{40} = 2\sqrt[3]{5}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{54} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}\). Since \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\) has no perfect cube factor greater than 1, \(\sqrt[3]{60}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q:
Which of the following products of radicals cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{10}, \sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{21}, \sqrt{5} \times \sqrt{14}, \sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiplying gives \(\sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\), \(\sqrt{63} = 3\sqrt{7}\), and \(\sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10}\), which all simplify to mixed roots. However, \(\sqrt{5} \times \sqrt{14} = \sqrt{70} = \sqrt{2 \times 5 \times 7}\) contains no square factor and cannot be simplified.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{200}, \sqrt{242}, \sqrt{245}, \sqrt{246}\)
qs.s: The radicals simplify as \(\sqrt{200} = 10\sqrt{2}\), \(\sqrt{242} = 11\sqrt{2}\), and \(\sqrt{245} = 7\sqrt{5}\). Since \(246 = 2 \times 3 \times 41\) has no perfect square factor, \(\sqrt{246}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q:
Which one of the following entire cube roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt[3]{128}, \sqrt[3]{135}, \sqrt[3]{144}, \sqrt[3]{150}\)
qs.s: Simplifying using cube factors 64, 27, and 8 gives \(\sqrt[3]{128} = 4\sqrt[3]{2}\), \(\sqrt[3]{135} = 3\sqrt[3]{5}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{144} = 2\sqrt[3]{18}\). Because 150 has no perfect cube factor greater than 1 (\(150 = 2 \times 3 \times 5^2\)), \(\sqrt[3]{150}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{48}\), \(\sqrt{52}\), \(\sqrt{54}\), \(\sqrt{55}\)?
qs.s: Factoring out perfect squares gives \(\sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{52} = 2\sqrt{13}\), and \(\sqrt{54} = 3\sqrt{6}\). The number \(55\) has prime factors \(5\) and \(11\) with no squares, so \(\sqrt{55}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{56}\), \(\sqrt{60}\), \(\sqrt{63}\), \(\sqrt{65}\)?
qs.s: The radicals simplify as \(\sqrt{56} = 2\sqrt{14}\), \(\sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}\), and \(\sqrt{63} = 3\sqrt{7}\). The radicand \(65 = 5 \times 13\) has no square factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt{65}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{28}\), \(\sqrt{30}\), \(\sqrt{32}\), \(\sqrt{50}\)?
qs.s: The radicals \(\sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\), \(\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\), and \(\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\) simplify because their radicands have perfect square factors. Because \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\) has no perfect square factor greater than \(1\), \(\sqrt{30}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{8}\), \(\sqrt{12}\), \(\sqrt{14}\), \(\sqrt{27}\)?
qs.s: Since \(8 = 4 \times 2\), \(12 = 4 \times 3\), and \(27 = 9 \times 3\), each contains a perfect square factor and simplifies. The radicand \(14 = 2 \times 7\) has no perfect square factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt{14}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{35}\), \(\sqrt{40}\), \(\sqrt{44}\), \(\sqrt{45}\)?
qs.s: We can simplify \(\sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}\), \(\sqrt{44} = 2\sqrt{11}\), and \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\) using the square factors \(4\) and \(9\). Since \(35 = 5 \times 7\) is square-free, \(\sqrt{35}\) cannot be converted to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt[3]{72}\), \(\sqrt[3]{100}\), \(\sqrt[3]{108}\), \(\sqrt[3]{135}\)?
qs.s: Factoring out perfect cubes yields \(\sqrt[3]{72} = 2\sqrt[3]{9}\), \(\sqrt[3]{108} = 3\sqrt[3]{4}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{135} = 3\sqrt[3]{5}\). The number \(100 = 2^2 \times 5^2\) has no factor that is a perfect cube greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt[3]{100}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{200}\), \(\sqrt{210}\), \(\sqrt{242}\), \(\sqrt{252}\)?
qs.s: We can simplify \(\sqrt{200} = 10\sqrt{2}\), \(\sqrt{242} = 11\sqrt{2}\), and \(\sqrt{252} = 6\sqrt{7}\) because \(100\), \(121\), and \(36\) are perfect square factors. Since \(210 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\) has no repeated prime factors, \(\sqrt{210}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{150}\), \(\sqrt{154}\), \(\sqrt{162}\), \(\sqrt{175}\)?
qs.s: We can simplify \(\sqrt{150} = 5\sqrt{6}\), \(\sqrt{162} = 9\sqrt{2}\), and \(\sqrt{175} = 5\sqrt{7}\) using square factors \(25\) and \(81\). Because \(154 = 2 \times 7 \times 11\) contains no repeated prime factors, \(\sqrt{154}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt{108}\), \(\sqrt{110}\), \(\sqrt{112}\), \(\sqrt{117}\)?
qs.s: The radicands \(108 = 36 \times 3\), \(112 = 16 \times 7\), and \(117 = 9 \times 13\) all have perfect square factors greater than \(1\). In contrast, \(110 = 2 \times 5 \times 11\) is square-free, so \(\sqrt{110}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root: \(\sqrt[3]{24}\), \(\sqrt[3]{36}\), \(\sqrt[3]{54}\), \(\sqrt[3]{56}\)?
qs.s: For cube roots, we look for perfect cube factors: \(\sqrt[3]{24} = 2\sqrt[3]{3}\), \(\sqrt[3]{54} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{56} = 2\sqrt[3]{7}\). Although \(36\) is a perfect square, it has no perfect cube factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt[3]{36}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt[3]{16}, \sqrt[3]{32}, \sqrt[3]{90}, \sqrt[3]{135}\)
qs.s: We can simplify \(\sqrt[3]{16} = 2\sqrt[3]{2}\), \(\sqrt[3]{32} = 2\sqrt[3]{4}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{135} = 3\sqrt[3]{5}\) using the cube factors \(8\) and \(27\). Although \(90\) has a square factor (\(9\)), its prime factorization \(90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5\) contains no perfect cube factor, so \(\sqrt[3]{90}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt[3]{48}, \sqrt[3]{56}, \sqrt[3]{60}, \sqrt[3]{250}\)
qs.s: We have \(\sqrt[3]{48} = 2\sqrt[3]{6}\), \(\sqrt[3]{56} = 2\sqrt[3]{7}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{250} = 5\sqrt[3]{2}\) using the cube factors \(8\) and \(125\). The radicand \(60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5\) has no perfect cube factor, so \(\sqrt[3]{60}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt{28}, \sqrt{42}, \sqrt{45}, \sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: The roots \(\sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\), \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\), and \(\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\) simplify because they contain the perfect square factors \(4\), \(9\), and \(25\). Because \(42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7\) has no perfect square factor greater than \(1\), \(\sqrt{42}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt{54}, \sqrt{60}, \sqrt{66}, \sqrt{98}\)
qs.s: Factoring gives \(\sqrt{54} = 3\sqrt{6}\), \(\sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}\), and \(\sqrt{98} = 7\sqrt{2}\) using square factors \(9\), \(4\), and \(49\). Since \(66 = 2 \times 3 \times 11\) is square-free, \(\sqrt{66}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt[3]{24}, \sqrt[3]{54}, \sqrt[3]{70}, \sqrt[3]{128}\)
qs.s: The radicals \(\sqrt[3]{24} = 2\sqrt[3]{3}\), \(\sqrt[3]{54} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{128} = 4\sqrt[3]{2}\) each contain a perfect cube factor (\(8\), \(27\), or \(64\)). Since \(70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7\) has no perfect cube factor greater than \(1\), \(\sqrt[3]{70}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt[3]{350}, \sqrt[3]{375}, \sqrt[3]{432}, \sqrt[3]{500}\)
qs.s: Testing larger cube factors shows \(\sqrt[3]{375} = 5\sqrt[3]{3}\) (\(125 \times 3\)), \(\sqrt[3]{432} = 6\sqrt[3]{2}\) (\(216 \times 2\)), and \(\sqrt[3]{500} = 5\sqrt[3]{4}\) (\(125 \times 4\)). Although \(350\) is divisible by \(25\), its prime factorization \(2 \times 5^2 \times 7\) contains no perfect cube factor, so \(\sqrt[3]{350}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the following products of entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{10}, \sqrt{14} \times \sqrt{21}, \sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{22}, \sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{33}\)
qs.s: Multiplying gives \(\sqrt{60} = 2\sqrt{15}\), \(\sqrt{294} = 7\sqrt{6}\), and \(\sqrt{495} = 3\sqrt{55}\), which all simplify. In contrast, \(\sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{22} = \sqrt{330} = \sqrt{2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 11}\) has no square factors, so it cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt{175}, \sqrt{210}, \sqrt{245}, \sqrt{252}\)
qs.s: Factoring yields \(\sqrt{175} = 5\sqrt{7}\) (\(25 \times 7\)), \(\sqrt{245} = 7\sqrt{5}\) (\(49 \times 5\)), and \(\sqrt{252} = 6\sqrt{7}\) (\(36 \times 7\)). Since \(210 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\) has no perfect square factor greater than \(1\), \(\sqrt{210}\) cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt[3]{448}, \sqrt[3]{625}, \sqrt[3]{648}, \sqrt[3]{700}\)
qs.s: We find \(\sqrt[3]{448} = 4\sqrt[3]{7}\) (\(64 \times 7\)), \(\sqrt[3]{625} = 5\sqrt[3]{5}\) (\(125 \times 5\)), and \(\sqrt[3]{648} = 6\sqrt[3]{3}\) (\(216 \times 3\)). While \(700\) has square factors (\(4\) and \(25\)), its prime factorization \(2^2 \times 5^2 \times 7\) contains no perfect cube factor, so \(\sqrt[3]{700}\) cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Which one of the following products of entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root? \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{18}, \sqrt[3]{12} \times \sqrt[3]{15}, \sqrt[3]{14} \times \sqrt[3]{28}, \sqrt[3]{20} \times \sqrt[3]{25}\)
qs.s: Multiplying gives \(\sqrt[3]{72} = 2\sqrt[3]{9}\), \(\sqrt[3]{392} = 2\sqrt[3]{49}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{500} = 5\sqrt[3]{4}\), each having a cube factor of \(8\) or \(125\). The product \(\sqrt[3]{12} \times \sqrt[3]{15} = \sqrt[3]{180} = \sqrt[3]{2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5}\) has no cube factor, so it cannot be simplified to a mixed root.

qs.q: Which of the following entire radicals cannot be simplified to a mixed radical?
qs.s: Since \(49 = 7^2\), it has no perfect cube factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt[3]{49}\) cannot be simplified. The others simplify to \(2\sqrt[3]{3}\), \(3\sqrt[3]{3}\), and \(4\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Which of the following products of entire radicals cannot be simplified to a mixed radical?
qs.s: Multiplying gives \(\sqrt{14} \times \sqrt{15} = \sqrt{210}\), and \(210 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\) has no perfect square factor greater than \(1\). The other products simplify to \(3\sqrt{10}\), \(2\sqrt{35}\), and \(3\sqrt{35}\).

qs.q:
Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{48}, \sqrt[3]{48}, \sqrt{20}, \sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: The radicand \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\) has no perfect cube factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt[3]{20}\) cannot be simplified. The others simplify to \(4\sqrt{3}\), \(2\sqrt[3]{6}\), and \(2\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q:
Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{72}, \sqrt[3]{72}, \sqrt{45}, \sqrt[3]{45}\)
qs.s: Since \(45 = 9 \times 5\) contains no perfect cube factor greater than \(1\), \(\sqrt[3]{45}\) cannot be simplified. The other radicals simplify to \(6\sqrt{2}\), \(2\sqrt[3]{9}\), and \(3\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q:
Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{18}, \sqrt{30}, \sqrt[3]{40}, \sqrt[3]{54}\)
qs.s: The number \(30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5\) has no perfect square factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt{30}\) cannot be simplified. In contrast, the others simplify to \(3\sqrt{2}\), \(2\sqrt[3]{5}\), and \(3\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Which one of the entire roots cannot be simplified to a mixed root?
\(\sqrt{24}, \sqrt[3]{24}, \sqrt{50}, \sqrt[3]{50}\)
qs.s: Factoring gives \(50 = 2 \times 5^2\), which contains no perfect cube factor greater than \(1\), so \(\sqrt[3]{50}\) cannot be simplified. The others simplify to \(2\sqrt{6}\), \(2\sqrt[3]{3}\), and \(5\sqrt{2}\).

qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{216}\). Factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{36 \times 6} = 6\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{40}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{2 \times 40} = \sqrt{80}\). Factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{16 \times 5} = 4\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{30}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{3 \times 30} = \sqrt{90}\). Factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{9 \times 10} = 3\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three radicands to get \(\sqrt{2 \times 15 \times 20} = \sqrt{600}\). Factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{100 \times 6} = 10\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{16} \times \sqrt[3]{12}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{192}\). Since \(192 = 64 \times 3\) and \(64\) is a perfect cube, the simplified result is \(4\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{14} \times \sqrt{21}\)
qs.s: Combine the radicands to get \(\sqrt{14 \times 21} = \sqrt{(2 \times 7) \times (3 \times 7)} = \sqrt{49 \times 6} = 7\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{35}\)
qs.s: Combine the radicands: \(\sqrt{15 \times 35} = \sqrt{(3 \times 5) \times (5 \times 7)} = \sqrt{25 \times 21} = 5\sqrt{21}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{160}\), then factor out the perfect square: \(\sqrt{160} = \sqrt{16 \times 10} = 4\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{14} \times \sqrt{18} \times \sqrt{35}\)
qs.s: Combine under one radical using prime factors: \(\sqrt{(2 \times 7) \times (2 \times 3^2) \times (5 \times 7)} = \sqrt{2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7^2 \times 5} = (2 \times 3 \times 7)\sqrt{5} = 42\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{1800}\), then factor out the largest perfect square: \(\sqrt{1800} = \sqrt{900 \times 2} = 30\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{10} \times \sqrt{14} \times \sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Write under one radical using prime factors: \(\sqrt{(2 \times 5) \times (2 \times 7) \times (3 \times 5)} = \sqrt{2^2 \times 5^2 \times 21} = (2 \times 5)\sqrt{21} = 10\sqrt{21}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{48} \times \sqrt{45}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical first: \(\sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\) and \(\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\). Multiplying them gives \((4 \times 3)\sqrt{3 \times 5} = 12\sqrt{15}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt{32} \times \sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical first to get \(\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\). Multiply to obtain \(4\sqrt{2} \times 5\sqrt{3} = 20\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(4\sqrt{8} \times 3\sqrt{6}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \((4 \times 3)\sqrt{8 \times 6} = 12\sqrt{48}\). Simplify the radical by extracting the square root of 16: \(12\sqrt{16 \times 3} = 12 \times 4\sqrt{3} = 48\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(3\sqrt{10} \times 4\sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((3 \times 4)\sqrt{10 \times 15} = 12\sqrt{150}\). Factoring out the largest perfect square gives \(12\sqrt{25 \times 6} = 12 \times 5\sqrt{6} = 60\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(3\sqrt{10} \times 2\sqrt{8}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \((3 \times 2)\sqrt{10 \times 8} = 6\sqrt{80}\). Simplify by factoring 80 into \(16 \times 5\): \(6 \times 4\sqrt{5} = 24\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(5\sqrt{2} \times 3\sqrt{14}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((5 \times 3)\sqrt{2 \times 14} = 15\sqrt{28}\). Then simplify the radical: \(15\sqrt{4 \times 7} = 15 \times 2\sqrt{7} = 30\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(2\sqrt{15} \times 4\sqrt{6}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to find \((2 \times 4)\sqrt{15 \times 6} = 8\sqrt{90}\). Simplify the radical by factoring out 9: \(8\sqrt{9 \times 10} = 8 \times 3\sqrt{10} = 24\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(4\sqrt{45} \times 3\sqrt{60}\)
qs.s: Multiply the expressions to get \((4 \times 3)\sqrt{45 \times 60} = 12\sqrt{2700}\). Factoring out the largest perfect square gives \(12\sqrt{900 \times 3} = 12 \times 30\sqrt{3} = 360\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(2\sqrt{14} \times 3\sqrt{21} \times 2\sqrt{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(2 \times 3 \times 2 = 12\), and factor the radicand product: \(14 \times 21 \times 10 = (2 \times 7) \times (3 \times 7) \times (2 \times 5) = 196 \times 15\). This simplifies to \(12 \times 14\sqrt{15} = 168\sqrt{15}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(5\sqrt{42} \times 4\sqrt{35}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(5 \times 4 = 20\), and factor the radicands: \(\sqrt{(6 \times 7) \times (5 \times 7)} = \sqrt{49 \times 30} = 7\sqrt{30}\). The product is \(20 \times 7\sqrt{30} = 140\sqrt{30}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(3\sqrt{2} \times 2\sqrt{15} \times 4\sqrt{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands: \((3 \times 2 \times 4)\sqrt{2 \times 15 \times 10} = 24\sqrt{300}\). Since \(\sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3}\), the product is \(24 \times 10\sqrt{3} = 240\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\(2\sqrt{3} \times 3\sqrt{10} \times 4\sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three coefficients and radicands: \((2 \times 3 \times 4)\sqrt{3 \times 10 \times 15} = 24\sqrt{450}\). Simplify \(\sqrt{450} = \sqrt{225 \times 2} = 15\sqrt{2}\), giving \(24 \times 15\sqrt{2} = 360\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(-3\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(-3\sqrt{60}\). Simplify by factoring \(60 = 4 \times 15\), giving \(-3(2\sqrt{15}) = -6\sqrt{15}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(-5\sqrt{14} \times \sqrt{3}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(-5\sqrt{14 \times 3} = -5\sqrt{42}\). Since \(42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7\) has no perfect square factors, it cannot be simplified further.

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(-3\sqrt{7} \times \sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(-3\sqrt{7 \times 15} = -3\sqrt{105}\). Since \(105 = 3 \times 5 \times 7\) contains no perfect square factors, the radical cannot be simplified further.

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(-4\sqrt{10} \times \sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(-4\sqrt{150}\). Simplify by factoring \(150 = 25 \times 6\), giving \(-4(5\sqrt{6}) = -20\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(-2\sqrt{15} \times \sqrt{6}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(-2\sqrt{90}\). Simplify by factoring \(90 = 9 \times 10\), which yields \(-2(3\sqrt{10}) = -6\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-4\sqrt{15}) \times (-3\sqrt{10})\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands: \((-4)(-3)\sqrt{15 \times 10} = 12\sqrt{150}\). Simplify by factoring \(150 = 25 \times 6\), giving \(12(5\sqrt{6}) = 60\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-3\sqrt{14}) \times (2\sqrt{21})\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to obtain \((-3 \times 2)\sqrt{14 \times 21} = -6\sqrt{294}\). Factor out the perfect square \(49\) to get \(-6(7\sqrt{6}) = -42\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-2\sqrt{5}) \times (3\sqrt{6}) \times \sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply all three factors: \((-2 \times 3)\sqrt{5 \times 6 \times 15} = -6\sqrt{450}\). Simplify using \(\sqrt{450} = \sqrt{225 \times 2} = 15\sqrt{2}\) to get \(-6(15\sqrt{2}) = -90\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-5\sqrt{18}) \times (2\sqrt{24})\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to get \(-10\sqrt{432}\). Factor out the largest perfect square factor \(144\) to obtain \(-10(12\sqrt{3}) = -120\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((6\sqrt{35}) \times (-2\sqrt{14})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands: \((6)(-2)\sqrt{35 \times 14} = -12\sqrt{490}\). Simplify using \(\sqrt{490} = \sqrt{49 \times 10} = 7\sqrt{10}\), giving \(-12(7\sqrt{10}) = -84\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(4\sqrt{14} \times 3\sqrt{8}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to get \(12\sqrt{112}\). Factoring out the perfect square \(\sqrt{16 \times 7} = 4\sqrt{7}\) yields \(12 \times 4\sqrt{7} = 48\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt{6} \times 2\sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((3 \times 2)\sqrt{6 \times 15} = 6\sqrt{90}\). Simplify \(\sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10}\) to obtain \(6 \times 3\sqrt{10} = 18\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt{20} \times 4\sqrt{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \(12\sqrt{300}\). Since \(300 = 100 \times 3\), simplify \(12 \times 10\sqrt{3} = 120\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt{8} \times 3\sqrt{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to get \(6\sqrt{80}\). Simplify \(\sqrt{80} = \sqrt{16 \times 5} = 4\sqrt{5}\), giving \(6 \times 4\sqrt{5} = 24\sqrt{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(4\sqrt{14} \times 2\sqrt{21}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \((4 \times 2)\sqrt{14 \times 21} = 8\sqrt{294}\). Since \(294 = 49 \times 6\), simplify \(8 \times 7\sqrt{6} = 56\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(7\sqrt{48} \times 3\sqrt{125}\)
qs.s: Simplify the radicals to \(7(4\sqrt{3}) = 28\sqrt{3}\) and \(3(5\sqrt{5}) = 15\sqrt{5}\). Multiply the results to find \((28 \times 15)\sqrt{3 \times 5} = 420\sqrt{15}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt{14} \times 3\sqrt{21} \times 5\sqrt{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(30\), and factor the radicands as \(14 \times 21 \times 18 = (2 \times 7)(3 \times 7)(2 \times 9) = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 7^2\). The root simplifies to \(42\sqrt{3}\), giving \(30 \times 42\sqrt{3} = 1260\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-2\sqrt{14} \times 3\sqrt{21} \times (-4\sqrt{42})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-2 \times 3 \times -4 = 24)\) and combine radicands: \(\sqrt{14 \times 21 \times 42} = \sqrt{12348} = \sqrt{1764 \times 7} = 42\sqrt{7}\). The final product is \(24 \times 42\sqrt{7} = 1008\sqrt{7}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-3\sqrt{32} \times 4\sqrt{75}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to \(-3(4\sqrt{2}) = -12\sqrt{2}\) and \(4(5\sqrt{3}) = 20\sqrt{3}\). Multiplying them gives \((-12 \times 20)\sqrt{2 \times 3} = -240\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt{10} \times 2\sqrt{15} \times 4\sqrt{12}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((3 \times 2 \times 4 = 24)\) and the radicands \(\sqrt{10 \times 15 \times 12} = \sqrt{1800}\). Simplify \(\sqrt{1800} = 30\sqrt{2}\) to obtain \(24 \times 30\sqrt{2} = 720\sqrt{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-4\sqrt{15}) \times (2\sqrt{10})\)
qs.s: Multiply the outside coefficients to get \(-8\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt{150}\). Since \(\sqrt{150} = \sqrt{25 \times 6} = 5\sqrt{6}\), the product is \(-8 \times 5\sqrt{6} = -40\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-2\sqrt{27}) \times (3\sqrt{18})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \(-6\sqrt{486}\). Simplifying \(\sqrt{486} = \sqrt{81 \times 6} = 9\sqrt{6}\) yields \(-6 \times 9\sqrt{6} = -54\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-5\sqrt{18}) \times (-3\sqrt{20})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and the radicands to obtain \(15\sqrt{360}\). Simplifying \(\sqrt{360} = \sqrt{36 \times 10} = 6\sqrt{10}\) gives \(15 \times 6\sqrt{10} = 90\sqrt{10}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (2\sqrt{8}) \times (-4\sqrt{12})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and the radicands to get \(-8\sqrt{96}\). Since \(\sqrt{96} = \sqrt{16 \times 6} = 4\sqrt{6}\), the product simplifies to \(-8 \times 4\sqrt{6} = -32\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (3\sqrt{24}) \times (-2\sqrt{8})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(-6\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt{192}\). Simplifying \(\sqrt{192} = \sqrt{64 \times 3} = 8\sqrt{3}\) results in \(-6 \times 8\sqrt{3} = -48\sqrt{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-5\sqrt{48}) \times (2\sqrt{90})\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical first to \(-20\sqrt{3}\) and \(6\sqrt{10}\), respectively. Multiplying these together yields \((-20)(6)\sqrt{3 \times 10} = -120\sqrt{30}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-3\sqrt[3]{24}) \times (-2\sqrt[3]{90})\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients to get \(6\) and radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{2160}\). Since \(2160 = 216 \times 10\) and \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), the result is \(6 \times 6\sqrt[3]{10} = 36\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (3\sqrt{8}) \times (-2\sqrt{18}) \times (-5\sqrt{24})\)
qs.s: Simplify the first two terms to \(6\sqrt{2}\) and \(-6\sqrt{2}\), whose product is \(-72\). Multiplying \(-72\) by the simplified third term, \(-10\sqrt{6}\), gives \(720\sqrt{6}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-2\sqrt{6}) \times (-3\sqrt{10}) \times (2\sqrt{21})\)
qs.s: Multiply all coefficients to get \((-2)(-3)(2) = 12\), and multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt{1260}\). Simplify \(\sqrt{1260} = \sqrt{36 \times 35} = 6\sqrt{35}\), giving \(12 \times 6\sqrt{35} = 72\sqrt{35}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible:
\(\displaystyle (-4\sqrt[3]{12}) \times (5\sqrt[3]{36})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(-20\) and combine the cube roots to get \(\sqrt[3]{432}\). Since \(432 = 216 \times 2\) and \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), this simplifies to \(-20 \times 6\sqrt[3]{2} = -120\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{18} \times \sqrt[3]{3}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{54}\), then simplify using the perfect cube 27 to get \(\sqrt[3]{27 \times 2} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{9} \times \sqrt[3]{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply under the radical to get \(\sqrt[3]{135}\), then extract the perfect cube 27 to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{27 \times 5} = 3\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{40}\), then factor out the perfect cube 8 to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 5} = 2\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{12}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to find \(\sqrt[3]{72}\), then factor out the perfect cube 8 to simplify to \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 9} = 2\sqrt[3]{9}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{12} \times \sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{360}\), then simplify using the perfect cube 8 to find \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 45} = 2\sqrt[3]{45}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{14} \times 3\sqrt[3]{4}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \(6\sqrt[3]{56}\), then factor out \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\) to get \(6 \times 2\sqrt[3]{7} = 12\sqrt[3]{7}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(5\sqrt[3]{18} \times 2\sqrt[3]{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to get \(10\sqrt[3]{270}\), then extract \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) to obtain \(10 \times 3\sqrt[3]{10} = 30\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{25} \times \sqrt[3]{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{375}\), then factor out the perfect cube 125 to get \(\sqrt[3]{125 \times 3} = 5\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{25} \times \sqrt[3]{40}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{1000}\). Since \(10^3 = 1000\), the expression simplifies to \(10\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{40}\), then factor out the largest perfect cube: \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 5} = 2\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{18} \times \sqrt[3]{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{270}\), then simplify using the perfect cube 27: \(\sqrt[3]{27 \times 10} = 3\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{25} \times \sqrt[3]{75}\)
qs.s: Multiply to get \(\sqrt[3]{1875}\). Factor out the perfect cube 125: \(\sqrt[3]{125 \times 15} = 5\sqrt[3]{15}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{50} \times \sqrt[3]{60}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to find \(\sqrt[3]{3000}\). Since \(3000 = 1000 \times 3\), extract the cube root of 1000 to get \(10\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{40} \times \sqrt[3]{54}\)
qs.s: Simplify first as \(2\sqrt[3]{5} \times 3\sqrt[3]{2}\), then multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \(6\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply all three radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{4 \times 6 \times 18} = \sqrt[3]{432}\). Extracting the cube factor 216 yields \(\sqrt[3]{216 \times 2} = 6\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{32} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{576}\). Factoring out the largest perfect cube, 64, gives \(\sqrt[3]{64 \times 9} = 4\sqrt[3]{9}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{2}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule for cube roots: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{2} = \sqrt[3]{2 \times 2} = \sqrt[3]{4}\). Since 4 contains no perfect cube factors, the expression cannot be simplified further.

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{10} = \sqrt[3]{10 \times 10} = \sqrt[3]{100}\). Since 100 has no perfect cube factors, the expression cannot be simplified.

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{3}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands using the product rule: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{3} = \sqrt[3]{3 \times 3} = \sqrt[3]{9}\). Because 9 has no perfect cube factor, it is in simplest form.

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{6}\)
qs.s: Multiply under the radical: \(\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{6} = \sqrt[3]{6 \times 6} = \sqrt[3]{36}\). Since 36 has no perfect cube factors, the radical cannot be simplified further.

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{7} \times \sqrt[3]{7}\)
qs.s: Apply the product rule: \(\sqrt[3]{7} \times \sqrt[3]{7} = \sqrt[3]{7 \times 7} = \sqrt[3]{49}\). Since 49 has no perfect cube factors, the expression is already in simplest form.

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{4} \times 3\sqrt[3]{4}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to get \((2 \times 3)\sqrt[3]{4 \times 4} = 6\sqrt[3]{16}\). Since \(\sqrt[3]{16} = 2\sqrt[3]{2}\), the result is \(6 \times 2\sqrt[3]{2} = 12\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{4}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{24}\). Factor 24 as \(8 \times 3\), giving \(\sqrt[3]{8 \times 3} = 2\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{4} \times \sqrt[3]{4}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{16}\). Since \(16 = 8 \times 2\) and 8 is a perfect cube, simplify to \(\sqrt[3]{8} \times \sqrt[3]{2} = 2\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{9}\)
qs.s: Multiply all three radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 3 \times 9} = \sqrt[3]{54}\). Since \(54 = 27 \times 2\), simplify to get \(\sqrt[3]{27} \times \sqrt[3]{2} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{14} \times \sqrt[3]{49}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{14 \times 49} = \sqrt[3]{686}\). Factoring out the perfect cube \(343\) gives \(\sqrt[3]{343 \times 2} = 7\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{2} \times \sqrt[3]{32}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{2 \times 32} = \sqrt[3]{64}\). Since \(64 = 4^3\), the expression simplifies to \(4\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{36} \times \sqrt[3]{60}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{36 \times 60} = \sqrt[3]{2160}\). Factoring out the perfect cube \(216\) yields \(\sqrt[3]{216 \times 10} = 6\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{45} \times \sqrt[3]{75}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{45 \times 75} = \sqrt[3]{3375}\). Since \(3375 = 15^3\), the simplified value is \(15\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{3} \times \sqrt[3]{20} \times \sqrt[3]{50}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{3 \times 20 \times 50} = \sqrt[3]{3000}\). Factoring out the perfect cube \(1000\) yields \(\sqrt[3]{1000 \times 3} = 10\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply all three radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{6 \times 10 \times 18} = \sqrt[3]{1080}\). Factoring out the perfect cube \(216\) gives \(\sqrt[3]{216 \times 5} = 6\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(\sqrt[3]{28} \times \sqrt[3]{98}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{28 \times 98} = \sqrt[3]{2744}\). Since \(2744 = 14^3\), the simplified value is \(14\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{21} \times \sqrt[3]{18}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(2\sqrt[3]{378}\). Factor \(378 = 27 \times 14\) to obtain \(2 \times 3\sqrt[3]{14} = 6\sqrt[3]{14}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{18} \times \sqrt[3]{6}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(3\sqrt[3]{108}\). Since \(108 = 27 \times 4\), this simplifies to \(3 \times 3\sqrt[3]{4} = 9\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{14} \times \sqrt[3]{28}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(2\sqrt[3]{392}\). Factoring gives \(392 = 8 \times 49\), which simplifies to \(2 \times 2\sqrt[3]{49} = 4\sqrt[3]{49}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to obtain \(2\sqrt[3]{120}\). Since \(120 = 8 \times 15\), simplify to \(2 \times 2\sqrt[3]{15} = 4\sqrt[3]{15}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{10} \times \sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the radicands to get \(3\sqrt[3]{200}\). Since \(200 = 8 \times 25\), simplify to \(3 \times 2\sqrt[3]{25} = 6\sqrt[3]{25}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-2\sqrt[3]{15} \times 3\sqrt[3]{18} \times \sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(-6\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{5400}\). Since \(5400 = 216 \times 25\), simplify to \(-6 \times 6\sqrt[3]{25} = -36\sqrt[3]{25}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{40} \times 2\sqrt[3]{54}\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical to get \(3(2\sqrt[3]{5}) \times 2(3\sqrt[3]{2}) = 6\sqrt[3]{5} \times 6\sqrt[3]{2}\), then multiply to obtain \(36\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{50} \times 4\sqrt[3]{45}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \(12\sqrt[3]{2250}\). Since \(2250 = 125 \times 18\), simplify to \(12 \times 5\sqrt[3]{18} = 60\sqrt[3]{18}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{6} \times \sqrt[3]{10} \times 3\sqrt[3]{14}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(6\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{840}\). Since \(840 = 8 \times 105\), simplify to \(6 \times 2\sqrt[3]{105} = 12\sqrt[3]{105}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(4\sqrt[3]{18} \times 3\sqrt[3]{30}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \(12\sqrt[3]{540}\). Since \(540 = 27 \times 20\), simplify to \(12 \times 3\sqrt[3]{20} = 36\sqrt[3]{20}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-2\sqrt[3]{36} \times (-3\sqrt[3]{12})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \((-2) \times (-3) = 6\), then simplify \(\sqrt[3]{36 \times 12} = \sqrt[3]{432} = \sqrt[3]{216 \times 2} = 6\sqrt[3]{2}\). Multiplying gives \(6 \times 6\sqrt[3]{2} = 36\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(5\sqrt[3]{45} \times (-2\sqrt[3]{15})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(5 \times (-2) = -10\), then simplify \(\sqrt[3]{45 \times 15} = \sqrt[3]{675} = \sqrt[3]{27 \times 25} = 3\sqrt[3]{25}\). Combining gives \(-10 \times 3\sqrt[3]{25} = -30\sqrt[3]{25}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-4\sqrt[3]{28} \times 3\sqrt[3]{14}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(-4 \times 3 = -12\), then simplify \(\sqrt[3]{28 \times 14} = \sqrt[3]{392} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 49} = 2\sqrt[3]{49}\). Combining gives \(-12 \times 2\sqrt[3]{49} = -24\sqrt[3]{49}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-2\sqrt[3]{18} \times 5\sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(-2 \times 5 = -10\), then simplify the radical \(\sqrt[3]{18 \times 20} = \sqrt[3]{360} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 45} = 2\sqrt[3]{45}\). Combining them yields \(-10 \times 2\sqrt[3]{45} = -20\sqrt[3]{45}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{12} \times (-4\sqrt[3]{50})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(3 \times (-4) = -12\), then simplify the radical \(\sqrt[3]{12 \times 50} = \sqrt[3]{600} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 75} = 2\sqrt[3]{75}\). Combining them gives \(-12 \times 2\sqrt[3]{75} = -24\sqrt[3]{75}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-\frac{2}{5}\sqrt[3]{84} \times 15\sqrt[3]{98}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(-\frac{2}{5} \times 15 = -6\). Factor the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{84 \times 98} = \sqrt[3]{(2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7)(2 \cdot 7^2)} = \sqrt[3]{2^3 \cdot 7^3 \cdot 3} = 14\sqrt[3]{3}\), yielding \(-6 \times 14\sqrt[3]{3} = -84\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{12} \times (-5\sqrt[3]{18}) \times 3\sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the three coefficients to get \(2 \times (-5) \times 3 = -30\). Then simplify the radical product \(\sqrt[3]{12 \times 18 \times 10} = \sqrt[3]{2160} = \sqrt[3]{216 \times 10} = 6\sqrt[3]{10}\), giving a final result of \(-30 \times 6\sqrt[3]{10} = -180\sqrt[3]{10}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(-2\sqrt[3]{14} \times 3\sqrt[3]{21} \times (-4\sqrt[3]{36})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \((-2) \times 3 \times (-4) = 24\). Factor the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{14 \times 21 \times 36} = \sqrt[3]{(2 \cdot 7)(3 \cdot 7)(2^2 \cdot 3^2)} = \sqrt[3]{2^3 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 7^2} = 6\sqrt[3]{49}\), giving \(24 \times 6\sqrt[3]{49} = 144\sqrt[3]{49}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(5\sqrt[3]{108} \times (-2\sqrt[3]{80})\)
qs.s: Multiplying coefficients gives \(5 \times (-2) = -10\), and simplifying the product of radicands gives \(\sqrt[3]{108 \times 80} = \sqrt[3]{8640} = \sqrt[3]{1728 \times 5} = 12\sqrt[3]{5}\). The product is \(-10 \times 12\sqrt[3]{5} = -120\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(4\sqrt[3]{90} \times (-7\sqrt[3]{60})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(4 \times (-7) = -28\), and simplify the radicand product \(\sqrt[3]{90 \times 60} = \sqrt[3]{5400} = \sqrt[3]{216 \times 25} = 6\sqrt[3]{25}\). The result is \(-28 \times 6\sqrt[3]{25} = -168\sqrt[3]{25}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{15} \times 4\sqrt[3]{75}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \(8\sqrt[3]{1125}\). Factor \(1125 = 125 \times 9\), giving \(8 \times 5\sqrt[3]{9} = 40\sqrt[3]{9}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(5\sqrt[3]{4} \times 3\sqrt[3]{10}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \(15\sqrt[3]{40}\). Since \(40 = 8 \times 5\), extract \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\) to obtain \(15 \times 2\sqrt[3]{5} = 30\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(4\sqrt[3]{9} \times 2\sqrt[3]{12}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(8\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{108}\). Factor \(108 = 27 \times 4\), so \(8 \times 3\sqrt[3]{4} = 24\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{18} \times 4\sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(8\) and radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{360}\). Factor \(360 = 8 \times 45\) to obtain \(8 \times 2\sqrt[3]{45} = 16\sqrt[3]{45}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{14} \times 2\sqrt[3]{28}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \(6\sqrt[3]{392}\). Since \(392 = 8 \times 49\), simplify to \(6 \times 2\sqrt[3]{49} = 12\sqrt[3]{49}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{25} \times 2\sqrt[3]{10} \times 4\sqrt[3]{20}\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \(24\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{5000}\). Since \(5000 = 1000 \times 5\), extract \(\sqrt[3]{1000} = 10\) to get \(24 \times 10\sqrt[3]{5} = 240\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(2\sqrt[3]{4} \times 3\sqrt[3]{18} \times 5\sqrt[3]{15}\)
qs.s: Multiply all three coefficients \(2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30\) and the radicands \(4 \times 18 \times 15 = 1080\). Factor \(1080 = 216 \times 5\) to get \(30 \times 6\sqrt[3]{5} = 180\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(4\sqrt[3]{24} \times 3\sqrt[3]{36}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients to obtain \(12\) and radicands to obtain \(\sqrt[3]{864}\). Factor \(864 = 216 \times 4\), yielding \(12 \times 6\sqrt[3]{4} = 72\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(3\sqrt[3]{28} \times 2\sqrt[3]{147}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients to get \(6\) and radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{4116}\). Since \(4116 = 343 \times 12\) and \(\sqrt[3]{343} = 7\), the result is \(6 \times 7\sqrt[3]{12} = 42\sqrt[3]{12}\).

qs.q: Multiply, and simplify if possible: \(5\sqrt[3]{32} \times 2\sqrt[3]{36}\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients to get \(10\) and radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{1152}\). Factor \(1152 = 64 \times 18\) where \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\), giving \(10 \times 4\sqrt[3]{18} = 40\sqrt[3]{18}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-4\sqrt[3]{9})(3\sqrt[3]{6})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and the radicands to get \((-4)(3)\sqrt[3]{9 \times 6} = -12\sqrt[3]{54}\). Since \(54 = 27 \times 2\), simplify to \(-12(3\sqrt[3]{2}) = -36\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-2\sqrt[3]{16})(-5\sqrt[3]{4})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and the radicands to get \((-2)(-5)\sqrt[3]{16 \times 4} = 10\sqrt[3]{64}\). Since \(64 = 4^3\), evaluate \(10(4) = 40\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((3\sqrt[3]{25})(-2\sqrt[3]{10})\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients and radicands to obtain \((3)(-2)\sqrt[3]{25 \times 10} = -6\sqrt[3]{250}\). Simplify \(\sqrt[3]{250} = \sqrt[3]{125 \times 2} = 5\sqrt[3]{2}\) to arrive at \(-6(5\sqrt[3]{2}) = -30\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((2\sqrt[3]{4})(-5\sqrt[3]{10})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \((2)(-5)\sqrt[3]{4 \times 10} = -10\sqrt[3]{40}\). Simplify \(\sqrt[3]{40} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 5} = 2\sqrt[3]{5}\), giving \(-10(2\sqrt[3]{5}) = -20\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-2\sqrt[3]{15})(-4\sqrt[3]{18})\)

Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-3\sqrt[3]{4})(-2\sqrt[3]{14})(-5\sqrt[3]{49})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \((-3)(-2)(-5) = -30\), and prime-factor the radicands: \(\sqrt[3]{2^2 \times (2 \times 7) \times 7^2} = \sqrt[3]{2^3 \times 7^3} = 14\). Then \(-30 \times 14 = -420\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-3\sqrt[3]{50})(4\sqrt[3]{45})\)
qs.s: Multiply coefficients to get \((-3)(4) = -12\) and radicands to get \(50 \times 45 = (2 \times 5^2)(3^2 \times 5) = 125 \times 18\). The expression becomes \(-12(5\sqrt[3]{18}) = -60\sqrt[3]{18}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((2\sqrt[3]{6})(-3\sqrt[3]{12})(4\sqrt[3]{9})\)
qs.s: Multiply all three coefficients to get \((2)(-3)(4) = -24\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{6 \times 12 \times 9} = \sqrt[3]{648}\). Since \(648 = 216 \times 3 = 6^3 \times 3\), simplify \(-24(6\sqrt[3]{3}) = -144\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-5\sqrt[3]{32})(3\sqrt[3]{108})\)
qs.s: Simplify each radical first: \(\sqrt[3]{32} = 2\sqrt[3]{4}\) and \(\sqrt[3]{108} = 3\sqrt[3]{4}\), yielding \((-10\sqrt[3]{4})(9\sqrt[3]{4}) = -90\sqrt[3]{16}\). Since \(\sqrt[3]{16} = 2\sqrt[3]{2}\), the result is \(-90(2\sqrt[3]{2}) = -180\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(\left(\frac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{16}\right)\left(-\frac{9}{8}\sqrt[3]{20}\right)\)
qs.s: Multiply the fractions to get \(\frac{2}{3} \times \left(-\frac{9}{8}\right) = -\frac{3}{4}\) and the radicands to get \(\sqrt[3]{320} = \sqrt[3]{64 \times 5} = 4\sqrt[3]{5}\). Then \(-\frac{3}{4}(4\sqrt[3]{5}) = -3\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((4\sqrt[3]{12})(-3\sqrt[3]{10})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \(4 \times (-3) = -12\) and the radicands \(\sqrt[3]{12 \times 10} = \sqrt[3]{120} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 15} = 2\sqrt[3]{15}\). Multiplying gives \(-12 \times 2\sqrt[3]{15} = -24\sqrt[3]{15}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-2\sqrt[3]{16})(-3\sqrt[3]{12})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-2) \times (-3) = 6\) and the radicands \(\sqrt[3]{16 \times 12} = \sqrt[3]{192} = \sqrt[3]{64 \times 3} = 4\sqrt[3]{3}\). The final product is \(6 \times 4\sqrt[3]{3} = 24\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-2\sqrt[3]{25})(-4\sqrt[3]{10})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-2) \times (-4) = 8\) and the radicands \(\sqrt[3]{25 \times 10} = \sqrt[3]{250} = \sqrt[3]{125 \times 2} = 5\sqrt[3]{2}\). The result is \(8 \times 5\sqrt[3]{2} = 40\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((5\sqrt[3]{18})(-2\sqrt[3]{4})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \(5 \times (-2) = -10\) and the radicands \(\sqrt[3]{18 \times 4} = \sqrt[3]{72} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 9} = 2\sqrt[3]{9}\). Multiplying gives \(-10 \times 2\sqrt[3]{9} = -20\sqrt[3]{9}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((2\sqrt[3]{9})(-4\sqrt[3]{6})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \(2 \times (-4) = -8\) and the radicands \(\sqrt[3]{9 \times 6} = \sqrt[3]{54} = \sqrt[3]{27 \times 2} = 3\sqrt[3]{2}\). Multiplying these gives \(-8 \times 3\sqrt[3]{2} = -24\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{16}\right)\left(6\sqrt[3]{54}\right)\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \(\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) \times 6 = -\frac{9}{2}\). The radicand product is \(\sqrt[3]{16 \times 54} = \sqrt[3]{864} = 6\sqrt[3]{4}\), giving \(-\frac{9}{2} \times 6\sqrt[3]{4} = -27\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-5\sqrt[3]{54})(4\sqrt[3]{48})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-5)(4) = -20\). Under the radical, \(54 \times 48 = 2592 = 216 \times 12\), so \(\sqrt[3]{2592} = 6\sqrt[3]{12}\), giving \(-20 \times 6\sqrt[3]{12} = -120\sqrt[3]{12}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-4\sqrt[3]{35})(3\sqrt[3]{175})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-4)(3) = -12\). Factoring the radicand gives \(35 \times 175 = (5 \times 7)(5^2 \times 7) = 125 \times 49\), so \(\sqrt[3]{35 \times 175} = 5\sqrt[3]{49}\), giving \(-12 \times 5\sqrt[3]{49} = -60\sqrt[3]{49}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((3\sqrt[3]{16})(-2\sqrt[3]{25})(5\sqrt[3]{40})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \(3 \times (-2) \times 5 = -30\). The product of radicands is \(16 \times 25 \times 40 = 16000 = 8000 \times 2\), so \(\sqrt[3]{16000} = 20\sqrt[3]{2}\), giving \(-30 \times 20\sqrt[3]{2} = -600\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.
\((-2\sqrt[3]{6})(3\sqrt[3]{10})(-5\sqrt[3]{18})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-2)(3)(-5) = 30\). Under the radical, \(6 \times 10 \times 18 = 1080 = 216 \times 5\), so \(\sqrt[3]{1080} = 6\sqrt[3]{5}\), yielding \(30 \times 6\sqrt[3]{5} = 180\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((3\sqrt[3]{36})(-2\sqrt[3]{12})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((3 \cdot (-2))\sqrt[3]{36 \cdot 12} = -6\sqrt[3]{432}\). Factoring \(432 = 216 \cdot 2 = 6^3 \cdot 2\) yields \(-6 \cdot 6\sqrt[3]{2} = -36\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((3\sqrt[3]{16})(-2\sqrt[3]{20})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((3 \cdot (-2))\sqrt[3]{16 \cdot 20} = -6\sqrt[3]{320}\). Factoring \(320 = 64 \cdot 5 = 4^3 \cdot 5\), we obtain \(-6 \cdot 4\sqrt[3]{5} = -24\sqrt[3]{5}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((-3\sqrt[3]{25})(4\sqrt[3]{15})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((-3 \cdot 4)\sqrt[3]{25 \cdot 15} = -12\sqrt[3]{375}\). Since \(375 = 125 \cdot 3 = 5^3 \cdot 3\), simplifying gives \(-12 \cdot 5\sqrt[3]{3} = -60\sqrt[3]{3}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((4\sqrt[3]{18})(-2\sqrt[3]{12})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to obtain \((4 \cdot (-2))\sqrt[3]{18 \cdot 12} = -8\sqrt[3]{216}\). Since \(216 = 6^3\), the expression simplifies completely to \(-8 \cdot 6 = -48\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((-3\sqrt[3]{4})(5\sqrt[3]{54})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients and radicands to get \((-3 \cdot 5)\sqrt[3]{4 \cdot 54} = -15\sqrt[3]{216}\). Because \(\sqrt[3]{216} = 6\), simplifying gives \(-15 \cdot 6 = -90\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((-3\sqrt[3]{108})(5\sqrt[3]{144})\)
qs.s: Multiply to get \((-3 \cdot 5)\sqrt[3]{108 \cdot 144} = -15\sqrt[3]{15552}\). Factoring \(15552 = 1728 \cdot 9 = 12^3 \cdot 9\) yields \(-15 \cdot 12\sqrt[3]{9} = -180\sqrt[3]{9}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((-2\sqrt[3]{150})(7\sqrt[3]{180})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-2)(7) = -14\) and the radicands \(150 \cdot 180 = 27000\). Because \(\sqrt[3]{27000} = 30\), simplifying gives \(-14 \cdot 30 = -420\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((-2\sqrt[3]{4})(3\sqrt[3]{18})(-5\sqrt[3]{12})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \((-2)(3)(-5) = 30\) and the radicands \(4 \cdot 18 \cdot 12 = 864\). Since \(864 = 216 \cdot 4 = 6^3 \cdot 4\), simplifying gives \(30 \cdot 6\sqrt[3]{4} = 180\sqrt[3]{4}\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((-2\sqrt[3]{15})(5\sqrt[3]{50})(-3\sqrt[3]{36})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients to get \((-2)(5)(-3) = 30\), and multiply the radicands \(15 \cdot 50 \cdot 36 = 27000\). Since \(27000 = 30^3\), the final result is \(30 \cdot 30 = 900\).

qs.q:
Multiply, and simplify if possible.

\((4\sqrt[3]{24})(-2\sqrt[3]{45})(3\sqrt[3]{50})\)
qs.s: Multiply the coefficients \(4 \cdot (-2) \cdot 3 = -24\) and radicands \(24 \cdot 45 \cdot 50 = 54000\). Factoring \(54000 = 27000 \cdot 2 = 30^3 \cdot 2\) gives \(-24 \cdot 30\sqrt[3]{2} = -720\sqrt[3]{2}\).

qs.q:
Without a calculator, compare the expressions by converting each to an entire root first:

\(2\sqrt{15} \text{ \_\_\_ } 8\)

Which inequality correctly compares their entire roots?
qs.s: Convert \(2\sqrt{15}\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{2^2 \times 15} = \sqrt{4 \times 15} = \sqrt{60}\). Convert \(8\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{8^2} = \sqrt{64}\). Since \(60 < 64\), the correct inequality is \(\sqrt{60} < \sqrt{64}\) (which means \(2\sqrt{15} < 8\)).

qs.q:
Without a calculator, compare the expressions by converting each to an entire root first:

\(4\sqrt{5} \text{ \_\_\_ } 9\)

Which inequality correctly compares their entire roots?
qs.s: Convert \(4\sqrt{5}\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{4^2 \times 5} = \sqrt{16 \times 5} = \sqrt{80}\). Convert \(9\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{9^2} = \sqrt{81}\). Since \(80 < 81\), the correct inequality is \(\sqrt{80} < \sqrt{81}\) (which means \(4\sqrt{5} < 9\)).

qs.q:
Without a calculator, compare the expressions by converting each to an entire root first:

\(3\sqrt{11} \text{ \_\_\_ } 10\)

Which inequality correctly compares their entire roots?
qs.s: Convert \(3\sqrt{11}\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{3^2 \times 11} = \sqrt{9 \times 11} = \sqrt{99}\). Convert \(10\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{10^2} = \sqrt{100}\). Since \(99 < 100\), the correct inequality is \(\sqrt{99} < \sqrt{100}\) (which means \(3\sqrt{11} < 10\)).

qs.q:
Without a calculator, compare the expressions by converting each to an entire root first:

\(5\sqrt{2} \text{ \_\_\_ } 7\)

Which inequality correctly compares their entire roots?
qs.s: Convert \(5\sqrt{2}\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{5^2 \times 2} = \sqrt{25 \times 2} = \sqrt{50}\). Convert \(7\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{7^2} = \sqrt{49}\). Since \(50 > 49\), the correct inequality is \(\sqrt{50} > \sqrt{49}\) (which means \(5\sqrt{2} > 7\)).

qs.q:
Without a calculator, compare the expressions by converting each to an entire root first:

\(2\sqrt{7} \text{ \_\_\_ } 5\)

Which inequality correctly compares their entire roots?
qs.s: Convert \(2\sqrt{7}\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{2^2 \times 7} = \sqrt{4 \times 7} = \sqrt{28}\). Convert \(5\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{5^2} = \sqrt{25}\). Since \(28 > 25\), the correct inequality is \(\sqrt{28} > \sqrt{25}\) (which means \(2\sqrt{7} > 5\)).

qs.q:
Without a calculator, compare the expressions by converting each to an entire root first:

\(8\sqrt{5} \text{ \_\_\_ } 18\)

Which inequality correctly compares their entire roots?
qs.s: Convert \(8\sqrt{5}\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{8^2 \times 5} = \sqrt{64 \times 5} = \sqrt{320}\). Convert \(18\) to an entire root: \(\sqrt{18^2} = \sqrt{324}\). Since \(320 < 324\), the correct inequality is \(\sqrt{320} < \sqrt{324}\) (which means \(8\sqrt{5} < 18\)).

qs.q:
