qs.s: Between x = -1 and x = 2, the graph doubles back, so any vertical line in that interval intersects all three segments. Since it intersects more than once, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the relation shown. Which pair of points causes the relation to fail the vertical line test?
qs.s: The vertical line test fails when two points share the same x-coordinate, so a vertical line passes through both. The points (4, -1) and (4, 3) both lie on the vertical line x = 4, whereas the pairs sharing equal y-values lie on horizontal lines.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the circle shown in the graph. Is the relation a function?
qs.a: No, because a vertical line such as \(x = 0\) intersects the circle at two points.
d: Yes, because the circle has a constant radius of 3.
Yes, because the circle is centered at the origin \((0, 0)\).
No, because the circle does not pass through the origin.
qs.s: A vertical line drawn through the circle (for example, \(x = 0\), which crosses at \((0, 3)\) and \((0, -3)\)) intersects the graph twice. Therefore, the relation fails the vertical line test and is not a function.

qs.q: Use the graph of the relation to apply the vertical line test. Which statement correctly determines whether the relation is a function?
qs.a: It is not a function because the vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects the graph at two points, \((0, 2)\) and \((0, -2)\).
d: It is a function because every input in the domain has at least one output.
It is a function because the graph intersects the \(x\)-axis at \((-4, 0)\).
It is not a function because the graph does not extend into the region where \(x < -4\).
qs.s: By the vertical line test, if any vertical line intersects a graph at more than one point, the relation is not a function. The line \(x = 0\) intersects the curve at \((0, 2)\) and \((0, -2)\), so the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the cubic curve shown in the graph. Does the relation represent a function?
qs.a: Yes, because any vertical line intersects the graph at exactly one point.
d: No, because the horizontal line \(y = 0\) intersects the graph at three points.
No, because the curve changes direction from increasing to decreasing.
Yes, because the graph passes through the origin \((0, 0)\).
qs.s: The vertical line test requires that no vertical line intersect the curve more than once. Any vertical line drawn on the plane meets this curve at exactly one point, so the relation is a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the parabola shown in the graph. Does this relation represent a function?
qs.a: Yes, because every vertical line intersects the graph at most once.
d: No, because the horizontal line \(y = 1\) intersects the graph at two points.
No, because the graph has a minimum point at \((0, -3)\).
Yes, because the graph is symmetric across the \(y\)-axis.
qs.s: A relation is a function if no vertical line crosses its graph more than once. Since any vertical line intersects this parabola at exactly one point, it is a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the relation shown in the graph. Which statement is correct?
qs.a: The relation is not a function because the vertical line \(x = 1\) intersects the graph at \((1, 3)\) and \((1, -1)\).
d: The relation is a function because it has a single vertex at \((-3, 1)\).
The relation is a function because each ray extends indefinitely to the right.
The relation is not a function because it is composed of two straight line segments.
qs.s: The vertical line \(x = 1\) intersects both arms of the graph at \((1, 3)\) and \((1, -1)\). Because a vertical line intersects the graph at more than one point, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the piecewise relation shown in the graph. Which statement correctly evaluates whether it is a function?
qs.a: It is a function because each vertical line intersects the graph at exactly one point.
d: It is not a function because the horizontal lines \(y = -3\) and \(y = 3\) contain infinitely many points.
It is not a function because the relation contains sharp corners at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 2\).
It is a function because it passes both the vertical line test and the horizontal line test.
qs.s: A relation is a function if every vertical line crosses the graph at most once. While horizontal lines intersect the flat sections at infinitely many points, every vertical line intersects the graph exactly once, so it is a function.

qs.q: The graph shows a relation that includes three connected segments, one of which is vertical. Apply the vertical line test to determine whether this relation is a function.
qs.a: It is not a function because the vertical line \(x = -2\) intersects the graph at infinitely many points.
d: It is a function because the graph is continuous from \(x = -5\) to \(x = 4\).
It is not a function because the vertical line \(x = -2\) intersects the graph at exactly two points.
It is a function because every \(x\)-value in the domain has at least one \(y\)-value.
qs.s: The vertical segment along \(x = -2\) from \(y = 1\) to \(y = 4\) lies directly on the vertical line \(x = -2\), resulting in infinitely many points of intersection. Therefore, the relation fails the vertical line test.

qs.q: The graph shows a relation consisting of six plotted points. Apply the vertical line test to determine whether the relation is a function.
qs.a: Yes, because every vertical line passes through at most one point.
d: No, because the horizontal line \(y = 2\) passes through two points: \((-4, 2)\) and \((3, 2)\).
No, because the points do not follow a linear pattern.
Yes, because the relation contains an even number of points.
qs.s: Each plotted point has a distinct \(x\)-coordinate (\(-4, -2, 0, 1, 3, 5\)), so no vertical line intersects more than one point. Having multiple points with the same \(y\)-value (such as \(y = 2\)) does not violate the vertical line test.

qs.q: The graph shows a continuous zigzag relation. Apply the vertical line test to determine whether the relation is a function, and identify the number of points at which the vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects the graph.
qs.a: It is not a function; the vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects the graph at 3 points.
d: It is a function; the vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects the graph at 1 point.
It is not a function; the vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects the graph at 2 points.
It is a function; the relation is continuous and has rotational symmetry.
qs.s: A vertical line at \(x = 0\) cuts through all three segments of the zigzag path, intersecting the graph at 3 points. Since it intersects more than once, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Use the vertical line test to determine whether the graph represents a function.
qs.a: Yes, because no vertical line intersects the graph more than once.
d: No, because the curve changes direction and has peaks and troughs.
No, because the graph crosses the x-axis at three separate points.
Yes, because the relation passes through the origin.
qs.s: Every vertical line drawn across the domain intersects the curve at exactly one point. Therefore, the relation is a function.

qs.q: Use the vertical line test on the graph to determine whether the relation is a function.
qs.a: No, because a vertical line can intersect the graph at two points.
d: Yes, because every value in the domain produces at least one output.
Yes, because the curve is continuous and smooth.
No, because the relation crosses the x-axis.
qs.s: A vertical line, such as \(x = 1\), intersects the graph at two distinct points, \((1, 2)\) and \((1, -2)\). By the vertical line test, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the graph shown. Does the relation represent a function?
qs.a: No, because vertical lines pass through two points on the circle.
d: Yes, because the graph is centered at the origin.
Yes, because the relation has both a domain and a range.
No, because the radius is constant in all directions.
qs.s: A vertical line passing through the interior of the circle, such as \(x = 0\), intersects the circle at two points, \((0, 3)\) and \((0, -3)\). Therefore, the relation fails the vertical line test and is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the graph shown. Determine whether the relation is a function.
qs.a: Yes, because any vertical line intersects the graph at most once.
d: No, because a horizontal line can intersect the graph twice.
No, because the parabola opens upwards and extends indefinitely.
Yes, because the vertex is located at an integer coordinate.
qs.s: No vertical line intersects the parabola at more than one point. Therefore, the relation passes the vertical line test and is a function.

qs.q: Use the vertical line test to determine whether the relation shown in the graph is a function.
qs.a: No, because vertical lines intersect the relation at two points.
d: Yes, because both branches are straight line segments.
Yes, because the relation has a single vertex at \((-1, 0)\).
No, because the relation contains points with negative coordinates.
qs.s: Vertical lines to the right of \(x = -1\), such as \(x = 3\), intersect the graph at two points, \((3, 3)\) and \((3, -3)\). Because a vertical line intersects the graph more than once, it is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the piecewise connected relation shown. Which statement correctly evaluates whether the relation is a function?
qs.a: It is not a function because the vertical line \(x = 1\) contains infinitely many points of the relation.
d: It is a function because the relation is connected with no breaks or holes.
It is a function because horizontal lines intersect the graph at most once.
It is not a function because the relation spans across multiple quadrants.
qs.s: The relation includes a vertical line segment along \(x = 1\) from \(y = -2\) to \(y = 3\). Because the vertical line \(x = 1\) intersects the relation at infinitely many points, it fails the vertical line test.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the upper semicircle shown in the graph. Is the relation a function?
qs.a: Yes, because every vertical line on the domain intersects the graph at exactly one point.
d: No, because circles and semicircles always fail the vertical line test.
No, because horizontal lines intersect the semicircle at two points.
Yes, because the relation has a single y-intercept at \((0, 4)\).
qs.s: Unlike a full circle, this graph contains only the top half, so any vertical line between \(x = -4\) and \(x = 4\) intersects the curve at exactly one point. Therefore, this relation passes the vertical line test and is a function.

qs.q: A student applies the vertical line test to the sideways parabola shown in the graph. At which of the following vertical lines does the test fail, demonstrating that the relation is not a function?
qs.s: The vertical line \(x = 2\) intersects the relation at two points, \((2, 2)\) and \((2, 0)\), proving that it is not a function. At \(x = 3\) the line intersects at only one point (the vertex), at \(x = 4\) it does not intersect the relation, and \(y = 1\) is a horizontal line.

qs.q: The graph shows a discrete relation composed of individual points. Use the vertical line test to determine if the relation is a function, and identify the vertical line that justifies your answer.
qs.a: Not a function; the vertical line \(x = 2\) intersects two points.
d: A function; every plotted point has distinct coordinates.
Not a function; the horizontal line \(y = 2\) passes near two points.
A function; the points pass the vertical line test everywhere except at \(x = 2\).
qs.s: The vertical line \(x = 2\) passes through both \((2, 4)\) and \((2, -3)\), meaning a single input corresponds to two outputs. Since at least one vertical line intersects more than one point, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Use the vertical line test on the rational relation shown in the graph. Is the relation a function?
qs.a: Yes, because every vertical line intersects the graph at most once.
d: No, because the vertical line \(x = 0\) never intersects the graph.
No, because the relation consists of two disconnected branches.
Yes, because the graph displays point symmetry about the origin.
qs.s: The vertical line test requires that no vertical line intersects the graph more than once. For \(x \neq 0\), each vertical line intersects the curve exactly once, and at \(x = 0\) it intersects zero times; thus the test passes and the relation is a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the circular relation shown in the graph. Does this relation represent a function?
qs.a: No, because vertical lines such as \(x = 0\) intersect the graph at two points.
d: Yes, because the relation is symmetric about both the x-axis and the y-axis.
Yes, because every point on the circle is equidistant from the origin.
No, because the relation does not extend infinitely in all directions.
qs.s: The vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects the circle at \((0, 3)\) and \((0, -3)\). Since a vertical line intersects the relation at more than one point, it is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the V-shaped relation shown in the graph. Is this relation a function?
qs.a: No, because a vertical line can intersect the graph at two points.
d: Yes, because the two rays meet at a single vertex at \((2, 0)\).
Yes, because the graph is symmetric with respect to the x-axis.
No, because the rays extend indefinitely to the left.
qs.s: A vertical line such as \(x = -1\) intersects both the upper and lower rays of the graph. Because it intersects the relation more than once, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to determine whether the relation shown in the graph is a function.
qs.a: Yes, because every vertical line intersects the graph at most once.
d: No, because the horizontal line \(y = 1\) intersects the graph twice.
No, because the graph extends below the x-axis.
Yes, because the graph opens upward and has a minimum.
qs.s: Any vertical line drawn across the plane intersects the parabola at exactly one point. Therefore, the relation is a function.

qs.q: Use the vertical line test to determine whether the relation shown in the graph is a function.
qs.a: Yes, because every vertical line intersects the line at exactly one point.
d: No, because the line has a negative slope.
No, because the line intersects both the x-axis and the y-axis.
Yes, because the line has a y-intercept at \((0, 1)\).
qs.s: Any vertical line drawn through the coordinate plane intersects the given line at exactly one point. Therefore, each input \(x\) has exactly one output \(y\), so the relation is a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the relation shown in the graph. Is this relation a function?
qs.a: No, because a vertical line can intersect the graph at more than one point.
d: Yes, because every input has at least one corresponding output.
Yes, because a horizontal line intersects the graph at most once.
No, because the graph has an x-intercept at (-1, 0).
qs.s: A vertical line, such as \(x = 3\), intersects the curve at two distinct points, \((3, 2)\) and \((3, -2)\). By the vertical line test, the relation is not a function.

qs.q: Apply the vertical line test to the piecewise relation shown. Is the relation a function, and why?
qs.a: No, because the vertical line \(x = 1\) intersects the graph at two points: \((1, 1)\) and \((1, 4)\).
d: Yes, because each individual straight segment passes the vertical line test.
Yes, because the relation is defined for all \(x\)-values from \(-4\) to \(5\).
No, because the vertical line \(x = 0\) intersects both segments.
qs.s: At \(x = 1\), both segments have solid endpoints, meaning both \((1, 1)\) and \((1, 4)\) belong to the relation. The vertical line \(x = 1\) intersects the graph at two points, so it is not a function.

qs.q: The graph shows a relation consisting of six distinct points. Apply the vertical line test to determine which point could be removed so that the remaining relation is a function.
qs.s: The points \((2, 4)\) and \((2, -1)\) both have \(x = 2\), so the vertical line \(x = 2\) intersects two points. Removing \((2, -1)\) leaves each input with a unique output, making the remaining relation a function.

qs.q: The graph shows a sideways parabola with vertex \(V(-4, 0)\). Apply the vertical line test to determine whether the relation is a function, and identify the value of \(x\) at which a vertical line intersects the relation at exactly ONE point.
qs.a: Not a function; the vertical line intersects at exactly one point at \(x = -4\).
d: A function; the vertical line intersects at exactly one point at \(x = -4\).
Not a function; the vertical line intersects at exactly one point at \(x = 0\).
A function; every vertical line for \(x \ge -4\) intersects the graph.
qs.s: For \(x > -4\), vertical lines intersect the parabola at two points, so it is not a function. At the vertex \(x = -4\), the vertical line is tangent to the curve and intersects it at exactly one point, \((-4, 0)\).

qs.q: The graph shows a relation composed of three connected line segments. Over which interval of \(x\) does the relation fail the vertical line test by having a vertical line intersect the graph at more than one point?
qs.s: For any \(x\) between \(0\) and \(3\), the segments overlap, so a vertical line intersects the relation at two or three points. Outside \(0 \le x \le 3\), vertical lines intersect the graph at most once.

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -6 | -3 | 0 | 3 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | -10 | -7 | -4 | -1 | 2 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{-7 - (-10)}{-3 - (-6)} = \frac{3}{3} = 1\), and \(y = -4\) when \(x = 0\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to x - 4\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -2 | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | -13 | -9 | -5 | -1 | 3 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{-9 - (-13)}{-1 - (-2)} = 4\), and the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\) is \(-5\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to 4x - 5\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -4 | -2 | 0 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 7 | 3 | -1 | -5 | -9 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{3 - 7}{-2 - (-4)} = \frac{-4}{2} = -2\), and the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\) is \(-1\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to -2x - 1\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -2 | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 7 | 4 | 1 | -2 | -5 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{4 - 7}{-1 - (-2)} = -3\), and the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\) is \(1\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to -3x + 1\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -4 | -2 | 0 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | -5 | -1 | 3 | 7 | 11 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{-1 - (-5)}{-2 - (-4)} = \frac{4}{2} = 2\), and the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\) is \(3\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to 2x + 3\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -6 | -3 | 3 | 9 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 9 | 7 | 3 | -1 | -3 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{7 - 9}{-3 - (-6)} = -\frac{2}{3}\), and using the point \((3, 3)\), the constant term is \(b = 3 - \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)(3) = 5\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to -\frac{2}{3}x + 5\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | 2 | 5 | 8 | 12 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 26 | -10 | -46 | -94 | -130 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{-10 - 26}{5 - 2} = -12\), and using \((2, 26)\), the constant term is \(b = 26 - (-12)(2) = 50\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to -12x + 50\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | -2 | -1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{-1 - (-2)}{4 - 2} = \frac{1}{2}\), and using \((2, -2)\), the constant term is \(b = -2 - \frac{1}{2}(2) = -3\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to \frac{1}{2}x - 3\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | 4 | 7 | 10 | 13 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 3 | 24 | 45 | 66 | 87 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{24 - 3}{7 - 4} = 7\), and using \((4, 3)\), the constant term is \(b = 3 - 7(4) = -25\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to 7x - 25\).

qs.q:
A function \(f\) is defined by the table below:

| \(x\) | -8 | -4 | 4 | 8 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 4 | 1 | -5 | -8 | -14 |

Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The rate of change is \(\frac{1 - 4}{-4 - (-8)} = -\frac{3}{4}\), and using \((-4, 1)\), the constant term is \(b = 1 - \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)(-4) = -2\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(f: x \to -\frac{3}{4}x - 2\).

qs.s: The points to plot are \((-5, -4)\), \((-3, -2)\), \((-1, 0)\), \((0, 3)\), \((2, 1)\), and \((5, -2)\). Quadrant III requires both \(x < 0\) and \(y < 0\), so only \((-5, -4)\) and \((-3, -2)\) lie in Quadrant III, giving a total of 2 points.

qs.q: The graph of the quadratic function \(g\) is shown on the coordinate plane below. Express this function in vertex form using mapping notation.

qs.s: The graph consists of an increasing segment from \((-6, -2)\) to \((-2, 2)\), a horizontal segment at \(y = 2\) from \(x = -2\) to \(x = 2\), and a decreasing segment from \((2, 2)\) to \((6, -2)\). Evaluating at even integers gives \(y\)-values \(-2, 0, 2, 2, 2, 0, -2\).

qs.q:
The partial table of values represents the quadratic function \(f(x)\) shown in the graph:

\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline f(x) & A & 3 & B & 3 & C \end{array}\)

What are the values of \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\)?
qs.s: From the graph of the parabola, the \(y\)-value at \(x = -2\) is \(0\) (\(A = 0\)), the vertex at \(x = 0\) is \((0, 4)\) (\(B = 4\)), and the \(y\)-value at \(x = 2\) is \(0\) (\(C = 0\)).

qs.q: The graph of a linear function \(f\) is shown below. Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The line crosses the y-axis at \((0, -3)\) and passes through \((2, 1)\), giving a slope of \(m = \frac{1 - (-3)}{2 - 0} = 2\). In mapping notation, this function is written as \(f: x \to 2x - 3\).

qs.q: The graph of a linear function \(h\) is shown below. Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The line passes through \((0, 0)\) and \((1, -3)\), giving a slope of \(m = \frac{-3 - 0}{1 - 0} = -3\) and a y-intercept of \(0\). In mapping notation, this is \(h: x \to -3x\).

qs.q: The graph of a linear function \(g\) is shown below. Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The line has a y-intercept at \((0, 1)\) and passes through \((4, 3)\), which gives a slope of \(m = \frac{3 - 1}{4 - 0} = \frac{1}{2}\). Expressed in mapping notation, this is \(g: x \to (1/2)x + 1\).

qs.q: The graph of a quadratic function \(g\) is shown below. Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The vertex of the parabola is at \((-2, 3)\), and it passes through \((0, -1)\). In vertex form, \(-1 = a(0 + 2)^2 + 3 \implies 4a = -4 \implies a = -1\). In mapping notation, this is \(g: x \to -(x + 2)^2 + 3\).

qs.q: The graph of a quadratic function \(f\) is shown below. Express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: The parabola has its vertex at \((1, -4)\) and passes through \((3, 0)\). Using vertex form \(y = a(x - h)^2 + k\), we find \(0 = a(3 - 1)^2 - 4 \implies a = 1\), giving \(f: x \to (x - 1)^2 - 4\) in mapping notation.

qs.q: The graph shows a function \(f\). Express this function using ordered pair notation.
qs.s: Identify the coordinates \((x, y)\) of each marked point: \((-4, 1)\), \((-1, 3)\), \((2, -2)\), and \((4, 0)\). Writing these as a set gives \(\{(-4, 1), (-1, 3), (2, -2), (4, 0)\}\).

qs.q: Use the graph below to express the function as a set of ordered pairs.
qs.s: Read the coordinates \((x, y)\) of the plotted points: \((-4, -3)\), \((-2, 2)\), \((1, -1)\), and \((3, 5)\). In ordered pair notation, the set is \(\{(-4, -3), (-2, 2), (1, -1), (3, 5)\}\).

qs.q: The graph shows a function \(g\). Express this function using ordered pair notation.
The discrete function \(h\) is graphed below. Express \(h\) using ordered pair notation.
qs.s: Locate each point by its horizontal coordinate \(x\) and vertical coordinate \(y\): \((-2, 4)\), \((0, -3)\), \((2, 1)\), and \((4, 3)\). The function is \(\{(-2, 4), (0, -3), (2, 1), (4, 3)\}\).

qs.q: The graph shows a discrete function \(f\). Express the function \(g(x) = f(x) + 2\) using ordered pair notation.
The discrete function \(f\) is shown on the grid below. Express \(f\) using ordered pair notation.

The graph of the quadratic function \(f(x)\) is shown below. Express the function as a set of ordered pairs \((x, f(x))\) for all integer values of \(x\) in the interval \([-1, 3]\).
qs.s: Read the \(y\)-value for each integer \(x\) in \([-1, 3]\) from the graph: \(f(-1) = 0\), \(f(0) = 3\), \(f(1) = 4\), \(f(2) = 3\), and \(f(3) = 0\). In ordered pair notation, this is \(\{(-1, 0), (0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 0)\}\).

qs.q: The graph of a piecewise linear function \(f\) is shown below. Express the function as a set of ordered pairs \((x, f(x))\) for all integer values of \(x\) in the interval \([-2, 2]\).
qs.s: Find the \(y\)-value on the graph for each integer \(x\) from \(-2\) to \(2\): \(f(-2) = 0\), \(f(-1) = 2\), \(f(0) = 4\), \(f(1) = 3\), and \(f(2) = 2\). Writing these as ordered pairs gives \(\{(-2, 0), (-1, 2), (0, 4), (1, 3), (2, 2)\}\).

qs.q: Use the graph of the parabola below to identify the table of values representing the function for integer values of x from -2 to 2.
qs.s: Read the y-coordinates on the parabola corresponding to each x from -2 to 2: at x = -2, y = 0; at x = -1, y = 3; at x = 0, y = 4; at x = 1, y = 3; and at x = 2, y = 0.

qs.q: The graph shows a discrete function consisting of five plotted points. Which table of values represents this function?
qs.s: Read the coordinates (x, y) of each plotted point from left to right: (-4, 1), (-2, 3), (0, -1), (2, -3), and (3, 2). Listing these gives the corresponding table.

qs.q: Use the graph of the linear function below to express it as a table of values for integer values of x from -2 to 3.
qs.s: Trace the line to find the y-value for each given x: (-2, 4), (-1, 3), (0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 0), and (3, -1).

qs.q: Use the graph of the absolute value function below to choose the correct table of values for x from -3 to 1.
qs.s: Locate each x on the axis and read the graph's y-values: (-3, -1), (-2, -2), vertex at (-1, -3), (0, -2), and (1, -1).

qs.q: Use the graph of the linear function below to express it as a table of values for integer values of x from -1 to 3.
qs.s: Locate each x-value from -1 to 3 on the x-axis and find the corresponding y-value on the line: (-1, -5), (0, -3), (1, -1), (2, 1), and (3, 3).

qs.q: Use the graph of the quadratic function below to determine the correct table of values for x in {-3, -1, 1, 3, 5}.
qs.s: Locate each specified x-value on the curve: at x = -3, y = 4; at x = -1, y = -2; at the vertex x = 1, y = -4; at x = 3, y = -2; and at x = 5, y = 4.

qs.q: The graph of a piecewise linear function is shown below. Which table of values represents the function for the inputs x = -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, and 5?
qs.s: Reading points across all three segments gives (-4, -1) and (-2, 3) on the left segment, (0, 3) and (2, 3) on the horizontal segment, and (4, 1) and (5, 0) on the right segment.

qs.q: Use the graph of the cubic polynomial function shown below to express it as a table of values for integer values of x from -2 to 2.
qs.s: Examine the integer grid points along the curve: (-2, -2), local maximum at (-1, 2), origin at (0, 0), local minimum at (1, -2), and (2, 2).

qs.s: Read each coordinate pair from the graph: (0, 1), (1, 3), vertex at (2, 5), (3, 3), (4, 1), and (5, -1).

qs.q: The graph of a piecewise function is shown below. Express this function as a table of values for the given inputs: x = -3, -2, -1, 1, 3, and 5.
qs.s: Read each coordinate along both segments: on the left piece, (-3, 0), (-2, 2), (-1, 4); on the right piece, (1, 2), (3, 0), and (5, -2).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-5, -3), (-2, 4), (0, -1), (4, -3)\) is represented in the table of values below, where \(k\) is the output corresponding to \(x = 4\):
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -5 & -3 \\ \hline -2 & 4 \\ \hline 0 & -1 \\ \hline 4 & k \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(k\)?
qs.s: From the ordered pair \((4, -3)\), the output corresponding to the input \(x = 4\) is \(-3\). Thus, \(k = -3\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-4, -2), (0, 3), (2, -2), (5, 1)\) is represented in the table of values below, where \(p\) is the output corresponding to \(x = 5\):
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & -4 & 0 & 2 & 5 \\ \hline y & -2 & 3 & -2 & p \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(p\)?
qs.s: The ordered pair \((5, 1)\) shows that the output for \(x = 5\) is \(y = 1\). Therefore, \(p = 1\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-6, 1), (-2, -5), (1, 4), (3, 1)\) is represented in the table of values below, where \(c\) is the input corresponding to \(y = -5\):
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -6 & 1 \\ \hline c & -5 \\ \hline 1 & 4 \\ \hline 3 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(c\)?
qs.s: The ordered pair with output \(y = -5\) is \((-2, -5)\), which corresponds to the input \(x = -2\). Therefore, \(c = -2\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-4, 7), (-1, 2), (1, -3), (3, 2)\) is represented in the table of values below, where \(a\) is the output corresponding to \(x = -1\):
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -4 & 7 \\ \hline -1 & a \\ \hline 1 & -3 \\ \hline 3 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(a\)?
qs.s: In the ordered pair \((-1, 2)\), the input is \(x = -1\) and the output is \(y = 2\). Therefore, the missing value in the table is \(a = 2\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-3, 5), (-1, -4), (2, 6), (5, 5)\) is represented in the table of values below, where \(m\) is the output corresponding to \(x = -1\):
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & -3 & -1 & 2 & 5 \\ \hline y & 5 & m & 6 & 5 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(m\)?
qs.s: The ordered pair with an input of \(x = -1\) is \((-1, -4)\), which has an output of \(y = -4\). Therefore, \(m = -4\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \(\left(-\frac{5}{2}, \frac{1}{4}\right)\), \(\left(-\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{3}{4}\right)\), \(\left(\frac{3}{2}, \frac{5}{4}\right)\), and \(\left(\frac{7}{2}, -\frac{3}{4}\right)\) is represented in the table of values below:
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \hline -\frac{1}{2} & r \\ \hline \frac{3}{2} & s \\ \hline \frac{7}{2} & -\frac{3}{4} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(r + s\) in simplest form?
qs.s: From the ordered pairs, \(r = -\frac{3}{4}\) and \(s = \frac{5}{4}\). Adding these yields \(r + s = -\frac{3}{4} + \frac{5}{4} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-12, 8), (-4, -6), (3, -11), (9, 14), (16, -6)\) is represented in the table of values below:
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x & -12 & -4 & 3 & 9 & 16 \\ \hline y & 8 & m & n & 14 & -6 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(2m - 3n\)?
qs.s: From the ordered pairs, \(m = -6\) and \(n = -11\). Substituting gives \(2(-6) - 3(-11) = -12 + 33 = 21\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-15, 22), (-8, -13), (4, 31), (11, -13)\) is represented in the table of values below, where \(u < 0\):
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -15 & 22 \\ \hline u & -13 \\ \hline 4 & v \\ \hline 11 & -13 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(v - u\)?
qs.s: Because \(u < 0\) corresponds to \(y = -13\), we have \(u = -8\) from \((-8, -13)\), while \(v = 31\) from \((4, 31)\). Thus, \(v - u = 31 - (-8) = 39\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \(\left(-6, \frac{2}{3}\right)\), \(\left(-1, -\frac{4}{3}\right)\), \(\left(3, \frac{5}{3}\right)\), and \(\left(8, -\frac{4}{3}\right)\) is represented in the table of values below:
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -6 & \frac{2}{3} \\ \hline -1 & j \\ \hline 3 & k \\ \hline 8 & -\frac{4}{3} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(3j + 6k\)?
qs.s: From the ordered pairs, \(j = -\frac{4}{3}\) and \(k = \frac{5}{3}\). Evaluating gives \(3\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) + 6\left(\frac{5}{3}\right) = -4 + 10 = 6\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-18, 42), (-7, -15), (5, 29), (14, -36), (23, -15)\) is represented in the table of values below:
\(\displaystyle \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x & y \\ \hline -18 & 42 \\ \hline -7 & a \\ \hline 5 & 29 \\ \hline 14 & b \\ \hline 23 & -15 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
What is the value of \(a + b\)?
qs.s: From the pairs \((-7, -15)\) and \((14, -36)\), the table entries are \(a = -15\) and \(b = -36\). Adding them gives \(a + b = -15 + (-36) = -51\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-3, -3), (-1, 1), (1, -3), (3, 1)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Each ordered pair \((x, y)\) translates into the mapping arrow \(x \to y\). Writing each pair in this format gives \(\{-3 \to -3, -1 \to 1, 1 \to -3, 3 \to 1\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-4, -1), (-2, 5), (0, 5), (2, -1)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Each ordered pair \((x, y)\) corresponds to the arrow \(x \to y\), directing each domain element to its range value. This gives \(\{-4 \to -1, -2 \to 5, 0 \to 5, 2 \to -1\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-2, 6), (0, -4), (2, 6), (4, -4)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Each domain value \(x\) is mapped to its associated range value \(y\) as \(x \to y\). Therefore, the function in mapping notation is \(\{-2 \to 6, 0 \to -4, 2 \to 6, 4 \to -4\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-3, 4), (-1, -2), (1, 4), (3, -2)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: In mapping notation, each input \(x\) is mapped to its output \(y\) in the form \(x \to y\). Thus, the ordered pairs give the mapping \(\{-3 \to 4, -1 \to -2, 1 \to 4, 3 \to -2\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-5, 2), (-2, 0), (1, 2), (4, 0)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Mapping notation represents each relation pair \((x, y)\) as \(x \to y\). Pairing the given \(x\)-values with their corresponding \(y\)-values yields \(\{-5 \to 2, -2 \to 0, 1 \to 2, 4 \to 0\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-15, 30), (-8, 12), (0, 30), (8, -5), (15, 12)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Express each pair \((x, y)\) by mapping the domain element to its range output with an arrow \(x \to y\). This gives \(\{-15 \to 30, -8 \to 12, 0 \to 30, 8 \to -5, 15 \to 12\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \(\left(-\frac{3}{2}, 2\right), \left(-\frac{1}{2}, -1\right), \left(\frac{1}{2}, 2\right), \left(\frac{3}{2}, -1\right)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Writing each ordered pair \((x, y)\) as \(x \to y\) from the input to its corresponding output yields \(\{-\frac{3}{2} \to 2, -\frac{1}{2} \to -1, \frac{1}{2} \to 2, \frac{3}{2} \to -1\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-24, -10), (-16, 15), (0, -10), (12, 25), (20, 15)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Convert every ordered pair \((x, y)\) into the arrow notation \(x \to y\). Matching each domain element with its correct range value results in \(\{-24 \to -10, -16 \to 15, 0 \to -10, 12 \to 25, 20 \to 15\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \((-18, -4), (-9, 16), (0, -4), (9, 32), (18, 16)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: In mapping notation, every input maps to its output using an arrow \(x \to y\). Mapping each of the five given pairs results in \(\{-18 \to -4, -9 \to 16, 0 \to -4, 9 \to 32, 18 \to 16\}\).

qs.q: Use the ordered pairs \(\left(-1, \frac{3}{4}\right), \left(-\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{4}\right), \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{4}\right), \left(1, -\frac{1}{4}\right)\) to express this function using mapping notation.
qs.s: Each ordered pair \((x, y)\) maps the first component to the second component as \(x \to y\). Writing this for all pairs gives \(\{-1 \to \frac{3}{4}, -\frac{1}{2} \to -\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{2} \to \frac{3}{4}, 1 \to -\frac{1}{4}\}\).

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the ordered pairs \((-3, -4)\), \((0, 3)\), \((2, 0)\), and \((4, -2)\). When this function is graphed on a coordinate plane, which point lies on the \(x\)-axis?
qs.s: A point lies on the \(x\)-axis when its \(y\)-coordinate is \(0\). Among the given pairs, \((2, 0)\) has \(y = 0\), so it is located on the \(x\)-axis.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the ordered pairs \((-3, 5)\), \((-1, -2)\), \((0, 4)\), and \((3, -1)\). When this function is graphed on a coordinate plane, which point lies in Quadrant II?
qs.s: Points in Quadrant II have a negative \(x\)-coordinate and a positive \(y\)-coordinate. The point \((-3, 5)\) has \(x = -3 < 0\) and \(y = 5 > 0\), so it lies in Quadrant II.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the ordered pairs \((-4, 1)\), \((-2, -3)\), \((0, -2)\), and \((3, 2)\). When this function is graphed on a coordinate plane, which point lies on the \(y\)-axis?
qs.s: A point lies on the \(y\)-axis when its \(x\)-coordinate is \(0\). Among the given ordered pairs, \((0, -2)\) has \(x = 0\), so it lies on the \(y\)-axis.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the ordered pairs \((-5, -3)\), \((-1, 2)\), \((2, 4)\), and \((4, -1)\). When this function is plotted on a coordinate plane, which point lies in Quadrant III?
qs.s: Points in Quadrant III have both negative \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates. The pair \((-5, -3)\) has \(x = -5 < 0\) and \(y = -3 < 0\), so it lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the ordered pairs \((-2, 4)\), \((1, -3)\), \((3, 2)\), and \((-4, -1)\). When this function is plotted on a coordinate grid, which point lies in Quadrant IV?
qs.s: Points in Quadrant IV have a positive \(x\)-coordinate and a negative \(y\)-coordinate. The point \((1, -3)\) has \(x = 1 > 0\) and \(y = -3 < 0\), placing it in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by \(y = \frac{1}{2}x - 4\) for the domain \(\{-6, 0, 4, 10\}\). When this function is graphed on a coordinate plane, which point lies on the \(y\)-axis?
qs.s: Substituting the domain values yields the points \((-6, -7)\), \((0, -4)\), \((4, -2)\), and \((10, 1)\). The point \((0, -4)\) has an \(x\)-coordinate of \(0\), which places it on the \(y\)-axis.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the rule \(y = 3 - 2x\) for the domain \(\{-3, 0, 1, 4\}\). When this function is graphed on a coordinate plane, which point lies in Quadrant IV?
qs.s: Evaluating the function for each domain value gives the points \((-3, 9)\), \((0, 3)\), \((1, 1)\), and \((4, -5)\). The point \((4, -5)\) has \(x > 0\) and \(y < 0\), so it lies in Quadrant IV.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the equation \(y = 2x + 8\) for the domain \(\{-6, -4, 0, 3\}\). When the points of this function are plotted on a coordinate plane, which point lies on the \(x\)-axis?
qs.s: Calculating the outputs yields \((-6, -4)\), \((-4, 0)\), \((0, 8)\), and \((3, 14)\). A point lies on the \(x\)-axis when \(y = 0\), which corresponds to \((-4, 0)\).

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by the rule \(y = x^2 - 10\) for the domain \(\{-4, -2, 1, 4\}\). When this function is plotted on a coordinate plane, which point lies in Quadrant III?
qs.s: Evaluating \(y = x^2 - 10\) gives the ordered pairs \((-4, 6)\), \((-2, -6)\), \((1, -9)\), and \((4, 6)\). The point \((-2, -6)\) has both coordinates negative, so it lies in Quadrant III.

qs.q: A discrete function is defined by \(y = -5x + 20\) for the domain \(\{-3, 2, 4, 7\}\). When this function is graphed on a coordinate plane, which point lies in Quadrant II?
qs.s: Evaluating \(y = -5x + 20\) for each input gives \((-3, 35)\), \((2, 10)\), \((4, 0)\), and \((7, -15)\). The point \((-3, 35)\) has \(x < 0\) and \(y > 0\), placing it in Quadrant II.

qs.q:

| \(x\) | \(y\) |
| :---: | :---: |
| \(-4\) | \(-5\) |
| \(-1\) | \(-5\) |
| \(2\) | \(-5\) |
| \(5\) | \(c\) |

What is the value of \(c\)?
qs.s: Each row in the table corresponds to an ordered pair \((x, y)\). For the point \((5, -5)\), the input \(x = 5\) gives the output \(y = -5\), so \(c = -5\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-3, -1)\), \((0, 2)\), \((2, 4)\), and \((4, 6)\) is shown in the horizontal table of values below.

| \(x\) | \(-3\) | \(0\) | \(2\) | \(4\) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| \(y\) | \(-1\) | \(2\) | \(k\) | \(6\) |

What is the value of \(k\)?
qs.s: Each column represents an ordered pair \((x, y)\). For \(x = 2\), the corresponding ordered pair is \((2, 4)\), so \(k = 4\).

qs.q:
The function given by the ordered pairs \((-5, -3)\), \((-1, 0)\), \((2, 3)\), and \((6, 7)\) is represented in the table of values below.
